Winer’s Grammar, (and Buttmann, as above; also sec. 140, 16)); tou mh, “that ... not” (Latin ne), after katecw, Luke 4:42; kratoumai, Luke 24:16; kwluw, Acts 10:47; katapauw, Acts 131 14:18; pauw, 1 Peter 3:10; uJpostellomai, Acts 20:20,27; prosecw mh, Matthew 6:1; but tou mh is added also to other expressions in the sense of Latin ut ne, “that ... not”: Romans 7:3; ofqalmoi tou mh blepein, wta tou mh akouein, Romans 11:8,10. After clauses denoting necessity, advantage, power, fitness, mh is used with an infinitive specifying the thing (Buttmann, sec. 148, 6), kalon esti mh, 1 Corinthians 7:1; Galatians 4:18; followed by to mh, Romans 14:21; alogon mh, Acts 25:27; kreitton hn, 2 Peter 2:21; exousia tou (L T Tr WH omit tou) mh ergazesqai, a right to forbear working, 1 Corinthians 9:6; dei, Acts 27:21; ou dunamai mh, “I cannot but,” Acts 4:20; anendekton esti tou mh, Luke 17:1 (cf. anendektov). b. mh with an infinitive which has the article follows a preposition, to indicate the purpose or end: as, prov to mh, “that ... not,” 2 Corinthians 3:13; 1 Thessalonians 2:9; 2 Thessalonians 3:8; eiv to mh (Latin in id ... ne), “to the end (or intent) that ... not,” Acts 7:19; 1 Corinthians 10:6; 2 Corinthians 4:4; followed by an accusative and infinitive, 2 Thessalonians 2:2; 1 Peter 3:7; dia to mh, “because ... not,” Matthew 13:5f; Mark 4:5f; Luke 8:6; James 4:2 (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 482 (449)) (2 Macc. 4:19). c. in other expressions where an infinitive with the article is used substantively: tw mh (dative of the cause or reason (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 44, 5; Buttmann, 264 (227))), 2 Corinthians 2:13 (12); in the accusative, to mh: Romans 14:13; 1 Corinthians 4:6 (R G); 2 Corinthians 2:1; 10:2; 1 Thessalonians 4:6, cf. 3. d. in sentences expressing consequence or result: wJste mh, “so that ... not,” Matthew 8:28; Mark 3:20; 1 Corinthians 1:7; 2 Corinthians 3:7; 1 Thessalonians 1:8.

5. mh is joined with a participle (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 50, 5 g.; (Buttmann, sec. 148, 7; see C. J. Vaughan’s Commentary on Romans 2:14)), a. in sentences expressing a command, exhortation, purpose, etc.: Luke 3:11; John 9:39; Acts 15:38; 20:29; Romans 8:4; 14:3; 2 Corinthians 12:21; Ephesians 5:27; Philippians 1:28; 2:4 (here Rec. imperative); 1 Thessalonians 4:5; 2 Thessalonians 1:8; 1 Peter 2:16; Hebrews 6:1; 13:17, etc. b. in general sentences, in which no definite person is meant but it is merely assumed that there is someone of the character denoted by the participle: as oJ mh wn met’ emou, “he that is not on roy side,” whoever he is, or if there is any such person, Matthew 12:30; Luke 11:23; oJ de mh pisteuwn, whoever believeth not, John 3:18; oJi mh oJmologountev Ihsoun Criston if any do not 132 confess, or belong to the class that do not confess, 2 John 1:7; add, Matthew 10:28; Luke 6:49; 12:21,47f; 22:36; John 5:23; 10:1; 12:48; 14:24; Romans 4:5; 5:14; 10:20; 1 Corinthians 7:38; 11:22; 2 Thessalonians 1:8; James 2:13; 1 John 2:4, etc.; pav oJ mh, Matthew 7:26; (pan dendron mh, Matthew 3:10; 7:19); 1 John 3:10; 2 John 9; 2 Thessalonians 2:12 (here L marginal reading T Tr WH marginal reading aJpantev oJi mh etc.); makariov oJ mh, John 20:29; Romans 14:22. c. where, indeed, a definite person or thing is referred to, but in such a way that his (its) quality or action (indicated by the participle) is denied in the thought or judgment either of the writer or of some other person (cf. especially Winer’s Grammar, 484 (451)): ta mh onta, that are deemed as nothing, 1 Corinthians 1:28; wJv mh labwn, as if thou hadst not received, 1 Corinthians 4:7; wJv mh ercomenou mou, as though I were not coming, 1 Corinthians 4:18; wJv mh efiknoumenoi eiv uJmav, 2 Corinthians 10:14; add, 1 Corinthians 7:29. hdei ... tinev eisin oJi mh pisteuontev (according to the opinion of oJ eidwv), John 6:64; the same holds true of Acts 20:29; ta mh blepomena (in the opinion of oJi mh skopountev), 2 Corinthians 4:18 (on the other hand, in Hebrews 11:1, ou blepomena, actually invisible); ton mh gnonta aJmartian uJper hJmwn aJmartian epoihsen (mh gnonta is said agreeably to the judgment of oJ poihsav), 2 Corinthians 5:21 (ton ou gnonta would be equivalent to agnwunta). in predictions, where it expresses the opinion of those who predict: esh siwpwn kai mh dunamenov lalhsai, Luke 1:20; esh tuflov mh blepwn, Acts 13:11. where the writer or speaker does not regard the thing itself so much as the thought of the thing, which he wishes to remove from the mind of the reader or hearer (Klotz ad Devar. ii. 2, p. 666) — to be rendered “without” etc. (German ohne zu with an infinitive) (cf. Buttmann, sec. 148, 7 b.): exhlqe mh epistamenov, pou ercetai, Hebrews 11:8; add, Matthew 22:12; Luke 13:11 ((but cf. Buttmann, sec. 148, 7 c.)); Acts 5:7; 20:22; Hebrews 9:9. where the participles have a conditional, causal, or concessive force, and may be resolved into clauses introduced by “if, on condition that,” etc.: qerisomen mh ekluomenoi, Galatians 6:9; mh ontov nomou, Romans 5:13; “although”: nomon mh econtev,Ro. 2:14; mh wn autov uJpo nomon, 1 Corinthians 9:20 (Rec. omits); we have both the negative particles in oJn ouk eidotev (or (with L T Tr WH) idontev) ... mh oJrwntev, whom being ignorant of (in person) (or (according to the critical text) not having seen) ... although now not seeing, 1 Peter 1:8; also 133 with the article: ta mh nomon econta (German die doch nicht haben, “they that have not,” etc.), Romans 2:14; oJ de mh genealogoumenov, “but he, although not” etc. Hebrews 7:6; — or “since, because, inasmuch as”: mh asqenhsav th pistei ou (but G L T Tr WH omit ou; cf. Buttmann, sec. 148, 14) katenohse to eJautou swma ... nenekrwmenon (ouk asqenhsav would be equivalent to dunatov, “strong”), Romans 4:19; pwv oJutov grammata oide mh memaqhkwv; “since he has not learned” (Winer’s Grammar, 483 (450)), John 7:15; add, Matthew 18:25; 22:25,29; Luke 2:45; 7:30; 11:24; 12:47; 24:23; Acts 9:26; 17:6; 21:34; 27:7; 2 Corinthians 3:14; 5:19; also with the article: oJ mh ginwskwn ton nomon, since it knoweth not the law, John 7:49; add, Jude 1:5. d. where (with the participle) it can be resolved by (being) “such (a person) as not, of such a sort as not”: mh zhtwn to emautou sumforon, 1 Corinthians 10:33; add, Acts 9:9; Galatians 4:8. neuter plural as a substantive: ta mh onta, Romans 4:17; ta mh saleuomena, Hebrews 12:27; ta mh deonta, 1 Timothy 5:13; ta mh kaqhkonta, Romans 1:28; 2 Macc. 6:4 (on the other hand, in ta ouk anhkonta, Ephesians 5:4 (where L T Tr WH aJ ouk anhken), the ouk coalesces with anhkonta and forms a single idea, “unseemly, unlawful”).

6. in independent sentences of forbidding, dehorting, admonishing, desiring, etc., mh is Prohibitive (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 56,1),Latin ne, not;

a. with the 1 person plural of the subjunctive present: mh ginwmeqa kenodoxoi, Galatians 5:26; add, Galatians 6:9; 1 Thessalonians 5:6; 1 John 3:18; aorist: John 19:24; before the word depending on the exhortation, 1 Corinthians 5:8.

b. with a present imperative, generally where one is bidden to cease from something already begun, or repeated, or continued: Matthew 6:16,19; 7:1; 19:6; Mark 9:39; 13:11; Luke 6:30; 7:6,13; 8:49,52; 10:4,7,20; John 2:16; 5:28,45; 6:43; 7:24; 14:1,27; 19:21; Acts 10:15; 11:9; 20:10; Romans 6:12; 11:18,20; 12:2 (here L Tr marginal reading WH marginal reading give the infinitive), 14; 1 Corinthians 6:9; 7:5; 2 Corinthians 6:14, 17; Galatians 5:1; 6:7; Ephesians 4:30; Colossians 3:9, 19, 21; 1 Thessalonians 5:19; 2 Thessalonians 3:15; 1 Timothy 4:14; 5:16,19; Hebrews 12:5; 13:2; James 134 1:7,16; 1 Peter 4:12,15f; 1 John 2:15; 3:13; Revelation 5:5, and very often.

c. with the third person (nowhere in the N.T. with the second) of the aorist imperative where the prohibition relates to something not to be begun, and where things about to be done are forbidden: mh epistreyatw, Matthew 24:18; Luke 17:31; mh katabatw, Mark 13:15, and L T Tr WH in Matthew 24:17 (where R G badly katabainetw); mh gnwtw, Matthew 6:3; genesqw (but T Tr WH ginesqw), Luke 22:42; cf. Xenophon, Cyril 7, 5, 73; Aeschylus the Septuagint c. Theb. 1036.

d. as in the more elegant Greek writings where future things are forbidden (cf. Herm. ad Vig., p. 807), with the 2 person of the aorist subjunctive: mh doxhte, Matthew 3:9; 5:17; mh fobhqhv, Matthew 1:20; 10:26,31 (here L T Tr WH present imperative fobeisqe) (alternating with the imperative present fobeisqe in Matthew 10:28 (G L T Tr)); mh aJyh, Colossians 2:21; mh apostrafhv, Matthew 5:42; mh kthshsqe, Matthew 10:9; add, Matthew 6:2,7,13,31; Mark 5:7; 10:19; Luke 6:29; 8:28; 14:8; John 3:7; Acts 7:60; Romans 10:6; 1 Corinthians 16:11; 2 Corinthians 11:16; 2 Thessalonians 2:3 — (in the last three examples with the third person, contrary to Winer’s Grammar, 502 (467)); 1 Timothy 5:1; 2 Timothy 1:8; Revelation 6:6; 10:4 (mh grayhv, for emellon grafein precedes; but in John 19:21 mh grafe is used, because Pilate had already written); Revelation 11:2; 22:10, and very often. We have the imperative present and the aorist subjunctive together in Luke 10:4; Acts 18:9.

e. with the 2 person of the present subjunctive: mh sklhrunhte, Hebrews 3:8,15 (a rare construction though not wholly unknown to Greek writings (“ more than doubtful” (Liddell and Scott, under the word A. I. 2)); see Delitzsch on the latter passage, and Schaefer ad Greg. Corinth., p. 1005f; (Sophocles’ Lexicon, under the word mh. Others regard the above examples as subjunctive aorist; cf. 2 Kings 2:10; Isaiah 63:17; Jeremiah 17:23; 19:15, etc.)).

f. with the optative, in wishes: in that frequent formula mh genoito, Far be it! See ginomai, 2 a.; mh autoiv logisqeih, 2 Timothy 4:16 (Job 27:5).

II. As a conjunction, Latin ne with the subjunctive; 135

1. our “that, that not or lest” (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 56, 2 (Buttmann, sec. 139, 48f; Goodwin sec. 46)); after verbs of fearing, caution, etc.

a. with the subjunctive present, where one fears lest something now exists and at the same time indicates that he is ignorant whether it is so or not (Hermann on Sophocles Aj. 272): episkopountev, mh ... enoclh, Hebrews 12:15.

b. with the subjunctive aorist, of things which may occur immediately or very soon: preceded by an aorist, eulabhqeiv (L T Tr WH fobhqeiv) mh diaspasqh, Acts 23:10; by a present: foboumai, Acts 27:17; blepw, Matthew 24:4; Mark 13:5; Luke 21:8; Acts 13:40; 1 Corinthians 10:12; Galatians 5:15; Hebrews 12:25; skopew emauton, Galatians 6:1 (Buttmann, 243 (209) would refer this to 2 b. below; cf. Goodwin, p. 66); oJraw, Matthew 18:10; 1 Thessalonians 5:15; elliptically, oJra mh (namely, touto poihshv (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 64, 7 a.; Buttmann, 395 (338))): Revelation 19:10; 22:9.

c. with the indicative future (as being akin to the subjunctive (cf. grammatical references at the beginning)): foboumai, mh tapeinwsei me oJ Qeov mou, 2 Corinthians 12:20f (L text T Tr); add, Colossians 2:8.

2. “in order that not” (Latin eo consilio ne);

a. with the optative: twn stratiwtwn boulh egeneto, iJna touv desmwtav apokteinwsi, mh tiv ... diafugoi, Acts 27:42 Rec. (the more elegant Greek to express the thought and purpose of the soldiers; but the best todd. read diafugh, which G L T Tr WH have adopted).

b. with the subjunctive aorist: preceded by the present, Mark 13:36; 2 Corinthians 8:20 (cf. Goodwin sec. 43 Rem.); 12:6; Colossians 2:4 (where L T Tr WH iJna mhdeiv for R G mh tiv (— an oversight; in R G as well as in the recent critical editions the purpose is expressed by an inserted iJna)).

III. As an Interrogative particle it is used when a negative answer is expected, Latin num; (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 57, 3 b.; (Buttmann, 248 (213)));

1. in a direct question: Matthew 7:9f; 9:15; Mark 2:19; Luke 17:9; John 3:4; 4:12,33; 6:67,7:35,51f; Acts 7:28; Romans 3:3; 136 9:20; 1 Corinthians 1:13; 9:8f; 10:22; James 2:14 (1 WH); 3:12, etc.; mh gar (see gar, I.), John 7:41; mh ouk (where ouk belongs to the verb, and mh is interrogative), Romans 10:18f; 1 Corinthians 9:4f; mh gar ... ou, 1 Corinthians 11:22,

2. in an indirect question with the indicative (German ob etwa, ob wohl, “whether possibly, whether perchance”), where in admonishing another we intimate that possibly the case is as we fear (cf. Buttmann, sec. 139, 57; Winer’s Grammar, sec. 41 b. 4 a.): Luke 11:35, cf. Buttmann, 243 (209); Ast, Platonic Lexicon, ii., p. 334f; (Riddell, Plato’s Apology Digest of Idioms sections 137, 138).

IV. The particles ou mh in combination augment the force of the negation, and signify “not at all, in no wise, by no means”; (this formula arose from the fuller expressions ou deinon or deov or fobov, mh, which are still found sometimes in Greek authors, cf. Kühner, ii. sec. 516, 9, p. 773f; but so far was this origin of the phrase lost sight of that ou mh is used even of things not at all to be feared, but rather to be desired; so in the N.T. in Matthew 5:18,26; 18:3; Luke 18:17; 22:16; John 4:48; 20:25; 1 Thessalonians 5:3); cf. Matthiae, sec. 517; Kühner, ii., p. 775; Bernhardy (1829) p. 402ff; (Gildersleeve in the Amer. Jour. of Philol. for 1882, p. 202f: Goodwin sec. 89): Winer’s Grammar, sec. 56, 3 (Buttmann, 211 (183f)).

1. with the future indicative: ou mh estai soi touto, this shall never be unto thee, Matthew 16:22; add, Matthew 26:35; Luke 22:34 R G L; 10:19 (where Rst G WH marginal reading adikhsh); John 6:35 (here L Tr marginal reading peinasei, and L T Tr WH diyhsei); 13:38 R G; Mark 13:31 T Tr WH; Hebrews 10:17 L T Tr WH; in many passages enumerated by Winer’s Grammar, 506 (472); (cf. Buttmann, 212 (183)), the manuscripts vary between the indicative future and the subjunctive aorist In a question, ou mh poihsei thn ekdikhsin; Luke 18:7 R G.

2. with the aorist subjunctive (the use of which in the N.T. scarcely differs from that of the future; cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 56, 3; (Buttmann, sec. 139, 7)), in confident assertions: — subjunctive of the 1 aorist, Matthew 24:2; Mark 13:2; Luke 6:37; John 13:8; Hebrews 8:12; 1 Peter 2:6; Revelation 2:11; 7:16; 18:21,22,23; 21:27, etc.; 1 aorist middle subjunctive, John 8:52 (where Rec. 137 geusetai); thus these N.T. examples prove that Dawes made a great mistake in denying (in his Miscellanea Critica, p. 221ff (ed. (Th. Kidd) 2, p. 408f)) flint the first aorist subjunctive is used after ou mh; (cf. Goodwin in Transactions of American Philological Association for 1869-1870, pp. 4655; Liddell and Scott, under the phrase, ou mh, I. 1 b.; Buttmann, sec. 139, 8); — subjunctive of 2 aorist, Matthew 5:18,20, 26; Mark 10:15; Luke 1:15; 12:59; John 10:28; 11:26; 1 Corinthians 8:13; Hebrews 13:5; Revelation 3:3 (R G L Tr marginal reading WH text), and often. in questions: with 1 aorist, Luke 18:7 L T Tr WH; Revelation 15:4 (in L T Tr WH with the subjunctive aorist and the future); with 2 aorist, John 18:11. in declarations introduced by oJti: with 1 aorist, 1 Thessalonians 4:15; with 2 aorist, Matthew 24:34 (here R G T omit oJti); 26:29 (L T Tr WH omit oJti); Luke 13:35 (T WH omit; L brackets oJti); 22:16; John 11:56; in relative clauses: with 1 aorist, Matthew 16:28; Mark 9:1; Acts 13:41; Romans 4:8; with 2 aorist, Luke 18:30.

3. with the present subjunctive (as sometimes in Greek authors, cf. Winer’s Grammar, 507 (473)): oude ou mh se egkataleipw, Hebrews 13:5 Tdf. (for egkatalipw Rec., et al.) (cf. Buttmann, 213 (184)).
mhge, ei de mhge, see ge, 3 d.

mhdamwv (adverb from mhdamov, and this from mhde, and amov someone (perhaps allied with aJma, which see)) (from Aeschylus, Herodotus down), “by no means, not at all”: namely, touto genoito, in replies after an imperative (A.V. “Not so”), Acts 10:14; 11:8. (the Septuagint for hl;ylij;.)*

mhde (mh, which see, and de) (from Homer down), a negative disjunctive conjunction; (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 55, 6; Buttmann, sec. 149, 13);

1. used in continuing a negation or prohibition, “but not, and not, neither”; preceded by mh — either so that the two negatives have one verb in common: preceded by mh with a participle, Matthew 22:23; Mark 12:24; by mh with a present subjunctive, 1 Corinthians 5:8 (here L marginal reading present indicative); 1 John 3:18; by mh with imperative, Matthew 6:25; Luke 10:4; 12:22; 14:12; 1 John 2:15; by mh with an aorist subjunctive 2 person plural, Matthew 10:9f; by eiv 138 to mh, 2 Thessalonians 2:2 L T Tr WH; — or so that mhde has its own verb: preceded by oJv ean (an) mh, Matthew 10:14; Mark 6:11; by iJna mh, John 4:15; by oJpwv mh, Luke 16:26; with a participle after mh with a participle, Luke 12:47; 2 Corinthians 4:2; with an imperative after mh with imperative, John 14:27; Romans 6:12f; Hebrews 12:5; mhdeni epitiqei, followed by mhde with imperative 1 Timothy 5:22; with 2 person of the aorist subjunctive after mh with 2 person of the aorist subjunctive, Matthew 7:6; 23:9f; Luke 17:23; Colossians 2:21; 1 Peter 3:14; after mhde with an aorist subjunctive Mark 8:26 (T reads mh for the first mhde, T WH Tr marginal reading omit the second clause); after mhdena with an aorist subjunctive, Luke 3:14 (Tdf. repeats mhdena); mhde ... mhde with 1 person plural present subjunctive, 1 Corinthians 10:8f (see below); paraggellw followed by mh with inf ... mhde with an infinitive, Acts 4:18; 1 Timothy 1:4; 6:17; kalon to mh ... mhde with an infinitive Romans 14:21; with the genitive absolute after mhpw with the genitive absolute, Romans 9:11; with imperative after eiv to mh, 1 Corinthians 10:7; mhde is repeated several times in a negative exhortation after eiv to mh in 1 Corinthians 10:7-10.

2. “not even” (Latin ne ... quidem): with an infinitive after egraya, 1 Corinthians 5:11; after wJste, Mark 2:2; 3:20 (where R G T badly mhte (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 489f (456); Buttmann, pp. 367, 369)); with a present imperative, Ephesians 5:3; 2 Thessalonians 3:10.

mhdeiv, mhdemia, mhden (and mhqen, Acts 27:33 L T Tr WH — a form not infrequent from Aristotle onward (found as early as Buttmann, C. 378, cf. Meisterhans, Gr. d. Attic Inschr., p. 73); cf. Lob. ad Phryn., p. 181f; Winer’s Grammar, sec. 5, 1 d. 11; (Buttmann, 28 (25)); Kühner, sec. 187, 1 vol. 1:487f), (from mhde and eJiv) (fr. Homer down); it is used either in connection with a noun, “no, none, or absolutely, no one, not one, no man,” neuter “nothing,” and in the same constructions as mh; accordingly

a. with an imperative: mhdeiv being the person to whom something is forbidden, 1 Corinthians 3:18,21; 10:24; Galatians 6:17; Ephesians 5:6; Colossians 2:18; 1 Timothy 4:12; Titus 2:15; James 1:13; 1 John 3:7; neuter mhden, namely, estw (A.V. “have thou nothing to do with” etc.), Matthew 27:19; mhdeiv in the dative or the accusative depending on the imperative, Romans 13:8; 1 139 Timothy 5:22; mhden (accusative), Luke 3:13; 9:3; mhden fobou, Revelation 2:10 (here L Tr WH text mh).

b. mhdeiv with the optative: once in the N.T., Mark 11:14 (where Rec. oudeiv) (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 476 (443)).

c. with the 2 person of the aorist subjunctive, the mhdeiv depending on the verb; as, mhdeni eiphv, Matthew 8:4; 17:9; accusative, Luke 3:14; 10:4; mhden (accusative), Acts 16:28; kata mhdena tropon, 2 Thessalonians 2:3.

d. with the particles iJna and oJpwv (see mh, I. 3): with iJna, Matthew 16:20; Mark 5:43; 6:8; 7:36 9:9: Titus 3:13; Revelation 3:11; with oJpwv, Acts 8:24.

e. with an infinitive; [a]. with one that depends on another verb: — as on paraggellw, Luke 8:56; 9:21; Acts 23:22; deinumi, Acts 10:28; diatassomai, Acts 24:23; anaqematizw emauton, Acts 23:14; krinw (accusative with an infinitive), Acts 21:25 Rec.; eucomai, 2 Corinthians 13:7; boulomai (accusative with an infinitive), 1 Timothy 5:14; uJpomimnhskw tina, Titus 3:2, etc.; parakalw tina followed by to mh with the accusative and infinitive, 1 Thessalonians 3:3 L (stereotype edition) T Tr WH. [b]. with an infinitive depending on dia to: Acts 28:18; Hebrews 10:2.

f. with a participle (see mh, I. 5); in the dative, Acts 11:19; Romans 12:17; accusative mhdena, John 8:10; Acts 9:7; mhden, Acts 4:21; 27:33; 1 Corinthians 10:25, 27; 2 Corinthians 6:10; 2 Thessalonians 3:11; 1 Timothy 6:4; Titus 2:8; James 1:6; 3 John 1:7; mhdemian proskophn, 2 Corinthians 6:3; mhdemian ptohsin, 1 Peter 3:6; mhdemian aitian, Acts 28:18; anabolhn mhdemian, Acts 25:17.

g. noteworthy are — mhdeiv with a genitive, Acts 4:17; 24:23; mhden namely, toutwn, Revelation 2:10 (R G T WH marginal reading); ev mhdeni, “in nothing,” 1 Corinthians 1:7 (but carismati is expressed here); 2 Corinthians (6:3 (see h. below)); 7:9; Philippians 1:28; James 1:4. mhden einai, to be nothing i.e. of no account opposed to 140 einai ti, Galatians 6:3 (Sophocles Aj. 754; other examples from Greek authors see in Passow, ii., p. 231{b}; (Liddell and Scott, under the word II.: cf. Buttmann, sec. 139, 5)); mhden (accusative), “nothing i.e. not at all, in no respect”: Acts 10:20; 11:12, (Lucian, dial. deor. 2, 4; Tim. 43); as accusative of the object after verbs of harm, loss, damage, advantage, care (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 227 (313); Buttmann, sec. 131, 10): as, blaptein, Luke 4:35 (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 483 (450)); wfeleisqai, Mark 5:26; uJsterein, 2 Corinthians 11:5; merimnan, Philippians 4:6.

h. examples of a double negation, by which the denial is strengthened, where in Latin quisquam follows a negation (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 55, 9 b.): mhketi mhdeiv, Mark 11:14; Acts 4:17; mhdeni mhden, Mark 1:44 (L omits; Tr brackets mhden); Romans 13:8; mhdemian en mhdeni, 2 Corinthians 6:3; mh ... en mhdeni, Philippians 1:28; mh ... mhden, 2 Corinthians 13:7; mh ... mhdemian, 1 Peter 3:6; mh tiv ... kata mhdena tropon, 2 Thessalonians 2:3.

Mhdov, Mhdou, oJ, “a Mede,” a native or an inhabitant of Media, a well-known region of Asia whose chief city was Ecbatana (see B. D., under the word): Acts 2:9. (Cf. B. D. and Schaff-Herzog under the word Media.)*

mhketi (from mh and eti), adverb, employed in the same constructions as mh; “no longer; no more; not hereafter”:

a. with 3 person singular 2 aorist subjunctive, Matthew 21:19 R G Tr text; with 2 person singular Mark 9:25.

b. with 1 person plural present subjunctive, Romans 14:13.

c. with a present imperative: (Luke 8:49 L T Tr text WH); John 5:14; 8:11; Ephesians 4:28; 1 Timothy 5:23.

d. with the optative: Mark 11:14.

e. iJna mhketi: 2 Corinthians 5:15; Ephesians 4:14. 141

f. with an infinitive depending — on another verb: on bow (epibow), Acts 25:24; on apeilw, Acts 4:17; on legw kai marturomai, Ephesians 4:17; on eiv to, 1 Peter 4:2; on wJste, Mark 1:45; 2:2; tou mhketi douleuein, Romans 6:6.

g. with a participle: Acts 13:34 (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 65, 10); Romans 15:23; 1 Thessalonians 3:1.

h. ou mhketi (see mh, IV. 3): with 2 aorist subjunctive Matthew 21:19 L T Tr marginal reading WH.*

mhkov, mhkeov (mhkouv), to, from Homer down; the Septuagint very often for Ër,a;o “length”: Revelation 21:16; to platov kai mhkov kai baqov kai uJyov, language used in shadowing forth the greatness, extent, and number of the blessings received from Christ, Ephesians 3:18.*

mhkunw: (mhkov); from Herodotus and Pindar down; “to make long, to lengthen”; in the Bible twice of plants, equivalent to “to cause to grow, increase”: oJ efuteuse kuriov kai uJetov emhkunen (lDigæy]), Isaiah 44:14; hence, passive (others, middle) present mhkunomai; “to grow up”: Mark 4:27 (mhkunhtai (Tr marginal reading mhkunetai)).*

mhlwth, mhlwthv, hJ (from mhlon sheep, also a goat; as kamhlwth (‘camlet’) from kamhlov (cf. Lob. Paralip., p. 332)), “a sheepskin”: Hebrews 11:37, and thence in Clement of Rome, 1 Corinthians 17,1. For tr,D,aæ an outer robe, mantle, the Septuagint in 1 Kings 19:13,19; 2 Kings 2:8,13f, doubtless because these mantles were made of skins; hence, more closely tr,D,aæ r[;ce, a mantle of hair, Zechariah 13:4 (where the Septuagint derriv tricinh). In the Byzantine writings (Apoll. Dysk. 191, 9) mhloth denotes a monk’s garment.*
mhn ((from Homer down)), a particle of affirmation, “verily, certainly, truly” (Sap. 6:25); h mhn, see under h at the end.

mhn, genitive mhnov, oJ (with the Alexandrian LXX the accusative mhnan, Revelation 22:2 Lachmann; on which form see references under arshn, at the end); (from Homer down); 142

1. “a month”: Luke 1:24,26,36,56; 4:25; Acts 7:20; 18:11; 19:8; 20:3; 28:11; James 5:17; Revelation 9:5,10,15; 11:2; 13:5; 22:2.

2. “the time of new moon, new moon” (barbarous Latin novilunium: after the use of the Hebrew vd,jo, which denotes both a ‘month’ and a ‘new moon,’ as in Numbers 28:11; 29:1): Galatians 4:10 (Lightfoot compares Isaiah 66:23) (the first day of each month, when the new moon appeared, was a festival among the Hebrews; cf. Leviticus 23:24; Numbers 28:11; Psalm 80:4 (Psalm 81:4)); (others refer the passage to 1 (see Meyer at the passage)).*

mhnuw (cf. Curtius, sec. 429): 1 aorist emhnusa; 1 aorist passive participle feminine mhnuqeisa; as in Greek writings from Herodotus and Pindar down;

1. “to disclose or make known something secret”; in a forensic sense, “to inform, report”: followed by pou estin, John 11:57; tini ti, passive, Acts 23:30.

2. universally, “to declare, tell, make known”: 1 Corinthians 10:28.

3. “to indicate, intimate”: of a teacher; followed by oJti, Luke 20:37. (A.V. uniformly “show”.)*

mhpote (from mh and pote) (mh pote (separately) L WH (except Matthew 25:9, see below) Tr (except 2 Timothy 2:25)), differing from oupote as mh does from ou; (from Homer down). Accordingly it is:

1. a particle of Negation; “not ever, never”: epei mhpote iscuei, “since it is never of force,” because the writer thinks that the very idea of its having force is to be denied, Hebrews 9:17 (where WH text mh tote), on which see Winer’s Grammar, 480 (447), cf. Buttmann, 353 (304); but others refer, this passage to 3 a. below.

2. a prohibitory conjunction; “lest ever, lest at any time, lest haply,” (also written separately mh pote ((see at the beginning), especially when the component parts retain each its distinctive force; cf. Lipsius, Gram. Untersuch., p. 129f; Ellendt, Lex. Sophocles 2:107. In the N.T. use of this particle the notion of time usual to pote seems to recede before that of contingency, “lest perchance”)), so that it refers to the preceding verb and 143 indicates the purpose of the designated action (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 56, 2): with a subjunctive present Luke 12:58; with a subjunctive aorist, Matthew 4:6 and Luke 4:11, from Psalm 90:12 (Psalm 91:12) (where the Septuagint for ˆp,); Matthew 5:25 ((cf. below)); Matthew 7:6 (R G); 13:15 and Acts 28:27 (both from Isaiah 6:10, where the Septuagint for ˆp,); Matthew 13:29 (ou namely, qelw); Matthew 15:32; 27:64; Mark 4:12; Luke 14:12; with iJna prefixed, Luke 14:29; with a future indicative (see Buttmann, sec. 139, 7, cf. also, p. 368 (315) d.): (Matthew 7:6 L T Tr WH; (cf. 5:25)); Mark 14:2; (Luke 12:58 L T Tr WH). after verbs of fearing, taking care (Winer’s Grammar, as above; Buttmann, sec. 139, 48): with subjunctive aorist — so after prosecw, to take heed, lest etc., Luke 21:34; Hebrews 2:1 (Sir. 11:33); so that an antecedent foboumenoi or prosecontev must be mentally supplied, Acts 5:39; mhpote ouk arkesh, “lest perchance there be not enough” (so that ouk arkesh forms one idea, and foboumeqa must be supplied before mhpote), Matthew 25:9 R T WH marginal reading; but L Tr WH text, together with Meyer, et al., have correctly restored mhpote (namely, touto genesqw (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 64, 7 a.)) ou mh arkesh, i.e. “Not so! There will in no wise be enough” (see mh, IV. 2); cf. Bornemann in the Studien und Kritiken for 1843, p. 143f; (but all the editors above named remove the punctuation mark after mhpote; in which case it may be connected directly with the words which follow it and translated (with R.V.) ‘peradventure there will not be enough’; cf. Buttmann, sec. 148, 10, especially, p. 354 (304) note. For additional examples of mhpote in this sense (cf. Aristotle, eth. Nic. 10, 10, p. 1179a, 24; with indicative, ibid., pp. 1172{a}, 33; 1173{a} 22, etc.), see Sophocles’ Lexicon, under the word; Alexander Buttmann (1873) in his translation of Apoll. Dysk., index under the word; (cf. Liddell and Scott, under the word mh, Buttmann, 9)). after foboumai, with present subjunctive Hebrews 4:1; so that foboumenov must be supplied before it, Luke 14:8. after blepein with a future indicative (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 56, 2 b. [a].; Buttmann, 243 (209)), Hebrews 3:12.

3. a particle of interrogation accompanied with doubt (see mh, III.), “whether ever, whether at any time; whether perchance, whether haply,” (German doch nicht etwa; ob nicht etwa); 144

a. in a direct question introduced by epei, “for, else” (see epei, 2 under the end): so according to the not improbable interpretation of some (e.g. L WH marginal reading, Delitzsch) in Hebrews 9:17, see in 1 above. In the remaining N.T. passages so used that the inquirer, though he doubts and expects a negative answer, yet is inclined to believe what he doubtfully asks about; thus, in a direct question, in John 7:26.

b. in indirect questions; [a]. with the optative (where the words are regarded as the thought of someone (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 41 b. 4 c.; Buttmann, sec. 139, 60)): Luke 3:15. (See [^b].) [b]. with the subjunctive: 2 Timothy 2:25 (R G L (cf. Buttmann, 46 (40));. but T Tr WH text give the optative), where mhpote k.t.l. depend on the suppressed idea dialogizomenov (cf. Buttmann, sec. 139, 62 at the end; Winer’s Grammar, as above).*

mhpw (or mh pw, L Tr in Romans 9:11) (mh and pw) (from Homer down), adverb;

1. “not yet”: in construction with the accusative and infinitive, Hebrews 9:8; with a ptcp, mhpw gar gennhqentwn, though they were not yet born, Romans 9:11, where compare Fritzsche.

2. “lest in any way” (?): Acts 27:29 Lachmann*

mhpwv (G T, or mh pwv L Tr WH) (mh and pwv), (from Homer down);

1. a conjunction, “lest in any way, lest perchance”;

a. in final sentences, with an aorist subjunctive, preceded by a present 1 Corinthians 9:27; preceded by an aorist, 2 Corinthians 2:7; 9:4.

b. after verbs of fearing, taking heed: with an aorist subjunctive — after blepein, 1 Corinthians 8:9; after fobeisqai, Acts 27:29 R; 2 Corinthians 11:3; 12:20; with a perfect indicative, to indicate that what is feared has actually taken place (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 56, 2 b. [a].; Buttmann, 242 (209)), Galatians 4:11; with an aorist subjunctive, the 145 idea of fearing being suppressed, Romans 11:21 Rec. (Buttmann, sec. 148, 10; cf. Winer’s Grammar, 474 (442)).

2. an interrogative particle, “whether in any way, whether by any means”: in an indirect question, with an indicative present (of a thing still continuing) and aorist (of a thing already done), Galatians 2:2 (“I laid before them the gospel” etc., namely, inquiring, “whether haply” etc.; Paul expects a negative answer, by which lie wished his teaching concerning Christ to be approved by the apostles at Jerusalem, yet by no means because he himself had any doubt about its soundness, but that his adversaries might not misuse the authority of those apostles in assailing tiffs teaching, and thereby frustrate his past and present endeavors; cf. Holmann at the passage (Buttmann, 353 (303). Others, however, take trecw as a subjunctive, and render “lest haply I should be running” etc.; see Winer’s Grammar, 504f (470), cf. Ellicott at the passage)). with the indicative (of a thing perhaps already done, but which the writer wishes had not been done) and the aorist subjunctive (of a thing future and uncertain, which he desires God to avert) in one and the same sentence, 1 Thessalonians 3:5 (where mhpwv depends on gnwnai; cf. Schott, Lünemann (Ellicott), at the passage; (Buttmann, 353 (304); Winer’s Grammar, 505 (470))).*
mhrov, mhrou, oJ, “the thigh”: Revelation 19:16. (From Homer down; the Septuagint for Ërey;.)*

mhte (mh and the enclitic te) (from Homer down), a copulative conjunction of negation, “neither, nor” (differing from oute as mh does from ou. It differs from mhde; in that mhde separates different things, but mhte those which are of the same kind or which are parts of one whole; cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 55, 6; (Buttmann, sec. 149, 13 b.)): mhte ... mhte, “neither ... nor,” Luke 7:33 (T mh ... mhde); 9:3 (five times); Acts 23:12,21; 27:20; Hebrews 7:3; (but in Ephesians 4:27 for mh ... mhte we must with L T Tr WH substitute mh ... mhde). mh ... mhte ... mhte, Matthew 5:34-36 (four times); 1 Timothy 1:7; James 5:12; Revelation 7:3; iJna mh ... mhte ... mhte, Revelation 7:1; mhde ... mhte ... mhte, 2 Thessalonians 2:2 L T Tr WH; mh einai anastasin, mhde aggelon (for that is something other than anastasiv), mhte pneuma (because angels belong to the genus pneumata), Acts 23:8 R G; cf. Winer’s Grammar, 493 (409); (Buttmann, 367f (314f)).* 146

mhthr, genitive mhtrov, dative mhtri, accusative mhtera, hJ (from Homer down; from Sanskrit ma, ‘to measure’; but whether denoting the ‘moulder,’ or the ‘manager’ is debated; cf. Vanicek, p. 657; Curtius, sec. 472; (cf. metron)), Hebrew µae, “a mother”; properly: Matthew 1:18; 2:11, and often; tropically, of that which is like a mother: Matthew 12:49f; Mark 3:35; John 19:27; Romans 16:13, cf. 1 Timothy 5:2; a city is called hJ mhthr twn pornwn, that produces and harbors the harlots, Revelation 17:5; of a city where races of men (i.e. Christians) originated, Galatians 4:26 (here G T Tr WH omit; L brackets panton (on the origin of which cf. Lightfoot at the passage)).

mhti (so G T WH R (commonly), but mh ti L (except 1 Corinthians 6:3) Tr (except Matthew 26:22,25; Mark 4:21)) (mh and ti), “whether at all, whether perchance,” an interrogative expecting a negative answer; in a direct question (German doch nicht etwa? (in English generally untranslated; cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 57, 3 b.; Buttmann, 248 (213))): Matthew 7:16; 26:22,25; Mark 4:21; 14:19; Luke 6:39; John 7:31 (R G); 8:22; 18:35; 21:5 (here all texts mh ti (properly)); Acts 10:47; 2 Corinthians 12:18; James 3:11; mhti ara, 2 Corinthians 1:17; used by one asking doubtfully yet inclining to believe what he asks about (see mhpote, 3 a.): Matthew 12:23; John 4:29. ei mhti, see ei, III. 10. mhtige (or mhti ge) see in its place.*

mhtige (so G T WH; but mhti ge R L, mh ti ge Tr) (from mh, ti, ge), “to say nothing of, not to mention,” which according to the context is either

a. “much less”; or

b. “much more, much rather”; so once in the N.T., 1 Corinthians 6:3. Cf. Herm. ad Vig., p. 801f.*

mhtiv (so R G John 4:33), more correctly mh tiv;

1. prohibitive, “let no one” (cf. Buttmann, 31 (28)): (with 1 aorist subjunctive 1 Corinthians 16:11); with 2 aorist subjunctive, 2 Thessalonians 2:8.

2. interrogative (Lat: num quis?) “hath anyone” etc.: John 7:48; (2 Corinthians 12:17, cf. Buttmann, sec. 151, 7; Winer’s Grammar, 574 147 (534)); where one would gladly believe what he asks about doubtfully (see mhti, under the end): John 4:33.*
mhtra, mhtrav, hJ (mhthr), “the womb”: Luke 2:23 (on which see dianoigw, 1); Romans 4:19. (Herodotus, Plato, others; the Septuagint for µj,r., )*
mhtralwav (also mhtraloiav), L T Tr WH (see WH’s Appendix, p. 152) mhtrolwav, mhtrolou, oJ (mhthr, and aloiaw to thresh, smite), “a matricide”: 1 Timothy 1:9. (Aeschylus, Plato, Lucian, others.)*
mhtropoliv, mhtropolewv, hJ (mhthr and poliv), “a metropolis, chief city”; in the spurious subscription 1 Timothy 6:(22) at the end; (in this sense from Xenophon down).*

miainw; passive, 1 aorist subjunctive 3 person plural mianqwsin; perfect 3 person singular memiantai (unless it be better to take this form as a plural; cf. Krüger, sec. 33, 3 Anm. 9; Alexander Buttmann (1873) Gram. sec. 101 Anm. 7; Ausf. Spr. sec. 101 Anm. 13; Buttmann, 41 (36); (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 58, 6 b. [b].)), participle memiasmenov (Titus 1:15 R G) and meiammenov (ibid. L T Tr WH; also Sap. 7:25; Tobit 2:9; Josephus, b. j. 4, 5, 2 edition, Bekker; cf. Matthiae, i., p. 415; Krüger, sec. 40, under the word; Lob. ad Phryn., p. 35; Otto on Theophil. ad Autol. 1, 1, p. 2f; (Veitch, under the word)); from Homer down;

1. “to dye with another color, to stain”: elefanta foiniki, Homer Iliad 4, 141.

2. “to defile, pollute, sully, contaminate, soil” (the Septuagint often for aMef)i : in a physical and a moral sense, sarka (of licentiousness), Jude 1:8; in a moral sense, ton suneidhsin, ton noun, passive Titus 1:15; absolutely, “to defile with sin,” passive ibid. and in Hebrews 12:15; for ayfij’h,, Deuteronomy 24:6(4); in a ritual sense, of men, passive John 18:28 (Leviticus 22:5,8; Numbers 19:13,20; Tobit 2:9).* (Synonyms: miainw, molunw: according to Trench (N.T. Synonyms, sec. xxxi.) miainw “to stain” differs from molunw “to smear” not only in its primary and outward sense, but in the 148 circumstance that (like English “stain”) it may be used in good part, while molunw admits of no worthy reference.)

miasma, miasmatov, to (miainw), “that which defiles (cf. kauchma, 2); defilement” (Vulgate coinquinatio): tropically, miasmata tou kosmou, vices the foulness of which contaminates one in his contact with the ungodly mass of mankind, 2 Peter 2:20. (Tragg., Antiphanes, Demosthenes, Polybius, Josephus, Plutarch; the Septuagint, Leviticus 7:8 (18); Jeremiah 39:34 (Jeremiah 32:34); Judith 9:2; 1 Macc. 13:50.)*

miasmov, miasmou, oJ (miainw), “the act of defiling, defilement, pollution”: epiqumia miasmou, defiling lust (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 34, 3 b.), 2 Peter 2:10. (Sap. 14:26; 1 Macc. 4:43; Plutarch, mor., p. 393 c.; Test xii. Patr. (test. Leviticus 17; test. Benj. 8; Graecus Venetus (passim); Hermas, Past. sim. 5, 7, 2).)*

migma or (so L T) migma (on the accent cf. Lipsius, Gramm. Untersuch., pp. 32 and 34 (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 6, 1 e.; krima, at the beginning)), migmatov, to (megnumi), “that which has been produced by mixing, a mixture”: John 19:39 (WH text eJligma, which see). (Sir. 38:8; Aristotle, Plutarch, others.)*

mignumi and misgw: 1 aorist emixa; perfect passive participle memigmenov; from Homer down; “to mix, mingle”: ti tini, one thing with another, Revelation 8:7 Rec.; 15:2; also ti en tini (cf. Buttmann, sec. 133, 8), Revelation 8:7 G L T Tr WH; meta tinov, with a thing, Matthew 27:34; Luke 13:1 (on which see aJima, 2 a.). (Synonym: See kerannumi, at the end Compare: sunanamignumi.)*

mikrov, mikra, mikron, comparitive mikroterov, mikrotera, eron (from Homer down), the Septuagint for ˆfoq;, ˆf;q;, f[m], “small, little”; used

a. of size: Matthew 13:32; Mark 4:31; hence, of stature, th hJlikia, Luke 19:3; of length, James 3:5.

b. of space: neuter proelqwn (proselqwn, T Tr WH marginal reading in Matthew, Tr WH marginal reading in Mark (see prosercomai, a.)) mikron, having gone forward a little, Matthew 26:39; Mark 14:35 (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 32,6; Buttmann, sec. 131, 11f). 149

c. of age: less by birth, younger, Mark 15:40 (others take this of stature); oJi mikroi, “the little ones,” young children, Matthew 18:6,10,14; Mark 9:42; epo mikrou eJwv megalou (A.V. “from the least to the greatest”), Acts 8:10; Hebrews 8:11 (Jeremiah 6:13; 38:34 (Jeremiah 31:34)); mikrov te kai megav (both small and great) i.e. all, Acts 26:22; plural, Revelation 11:18; 13:16; 19:5,18; 20:12.

d. of time, “short, brief”: neuter — nominative, eti (or eti omitted) mikron (namely, estai) kai (yet) “a little while and” etc. i.e. shortly (this shall come to pass), John 14:19; 16:16f,19 ((cf. Exodus 17:4)); eti mikron oJson oJson (see oJsov, a.); without kai, Hebrews 10:37 (Isaiah 26:20); to mikron (Tr WH omits to), John 16:18; — mikron accusative (of duration), John 13:33 (Job 36:2); mikron cronon, John 7:33; 12:35; Revelation 6:11; 20:3; meta mikron, after a little while, Matthew 26:73; Mark 14:70, (pro mikrou, Sap. 15:8).

e. of quantity, i.e. number or amount: mikra zumh, 1 Corinthians 5:6; Galatians 5:9; of number, mikron poimion, Luke 12:32; of quantity, mikra dunamiv, Revelation 3:8; neuter mikron (ti), “a little,” 2 Corinthians 11:1,16.

f. of rank or influence: Matthew 10:42; Luke 9:48; 17:2; oJ mikroterov en th basileia twn ouranwn, he that is inferior to the other citizens of the kingdom of heaven in knowledge of the gospel (R.V. “but little in” etc.; cf. Winer’s Grammar, 244 (229); Buttmann, sec. 123, 13), Matthew 11:11; Luke 7:28.*

Milhtov, Milhtou, hJ, “Miletus,” a maritime city (now nearly ten miles from the coast (cf. Acts 20:38)) of Caria or Ionia, near the mouths of the Maeander and not far (about 35 miles south) from Ephesus. It was the mother of many (some eighty) colonies, and the birthplace of Thales, Anaximander, and other celebrated men: Acts 20:15,17; 2 Timothy 4:20. (Lewin, St. Paul, ii., 90f.)*

milion, miliou, to (a word of Latin origin (cf. Buttmann, 18 (16))), “a mile,” among the Romans the distance of a thousand paces or eight stadia (somewhat less than our mile): Matthew 5:41. (Polybius, Strabo, Plato.)* 150
mimeomai, mimoumai; (mimov (an actor, mimic)); “to imitate”: tina, anyone, 2 Thessalonians 3:7,9; ti, Hebrews 13:7; 3 John 1:11. (Pindar, Aeschylus, Herodotus, others.)*

mimhthv, mimhtou, oJ, “an imitator”: ginomai tinov (genitive of person), 1 Corinthians 4:16; 11:1; Ephesians 5:1; 1 Thessalonians 1:6; 2:14; Hebrews 6:12; with the genitive of the thing, 1 Peter 3:13 Rec. (where L T Tr WH zhlwtai). (Plato, Isocrates, others.)*

mimnhskw: (MNAW (allied with menw, manqanw; cf. Latin maneo, moneo, mentio, etc.; cf. Curtius, sec. 429)); “to remind”: Homer, Pindar, Theognis, Euripides, others; passive and middle, present mimnhskomai (Hebrews 2:6; 13:3; rare in Attic); 1 aorist emnhsqhn; perfect memnhmai; 1 future passive in a middle sense, mnhsqhsomai (Hebrews 10:17 L T Tr WH); the Septuagint for rkæz;; “to be recalled or to return to one’s mind, to remind oneself of, to remember”; emnhsqhn, with a passive significance (cf. Buttmann, 52 (46)), “to be recalled to mind, to be remembered, had in remembrance”: enwpion tinov, before, i.e., in the mind of one (see enwpion, 1 c.), Acts 10:31; Revelation 16:19 (passively also in Ezekiel 18:22; (Sir. 16:17 Rec.); and anamnhsqhnai, Numbers 10:9; <19A801>Psalm 108:16 (<19A916>Psalm 109:16)); — with a middle significance, followed by a genitive of the thing (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 30, 10 c.), “to remember a thing”: Matthew 26:75; Luke 24:8; Acts 11:16; 2 Peter 3:2; Jude 1:17; mnhsqhnai eleouv, to call to remembrance former love, Luke 1:54 (cf. Psalm 24:6 (Psalm 25:6)); thv diaqhkhv, Luke 1:72 (Genesis 9:15; Exodus 2:24; 1 Macc. 4:10; 2 Macc. 1:2); mh mnhsqhnai twn aJmartiwn tinov (A.V. “to remember no more”) i.e. to forgive, Hebrews 8:12; 10:17 (after the Hebrew; see Psalm 24:7 (Psalm 25:7); 78:8 (Psalm 79:8); Isaiah 43:25; and on the other hand, “to remember the sins of anyone” is said of one about to punish them, Jeremiah 14:10; 1 Macc. 5:4; 6:12); with genitive of a person, to remember for good, remember and care for: Luke 23:42; followed by oJti, Matthew 5:23; 27:63; Luke 16:25; John 2:17,22; 12:16; by wJv, Luke 24:6. perfect memnhmai, in the sense of a present (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 274 (257)), “to be mindful of”: with the genitive of the thing, 2 Timothy 1:4; panta mou memnhsqe, in all things ye are mindful of me, 1 Corinthians 11:2; present mimnhskomai, with the genitive of the 151 person, to remember one in order to care for him, Hebrews 2:2 (from Psalm 8:5); 13:3. (Compare: anamimnhskw, epanamimnhskw, uJpomimnhskw.)*

misew, misw; imperfect emisoun; future mishsw; 1 aorist emishsa; perfect memishka; passive, present participle misoumenov; perfect participle memishmenov (Revelation 18:2); the Septuagint for anec;; (from Homer down); “to hate, pursue with hatred, detest”; passive “to be hated, detested”: tina, Matthew 5:43 and Rec. in 44; 24:10; Luke 1:71; 6:22,27; 19:14; John 7:7; 15:18ff 23-25; 17:14; Titus 3:3; 1 John 2:9 (11); 3:13,15; 4:20; Revelation 17:16; passive, Matthew 10:22; 24:9; (Mark 13:13); Luke 21:17; ti: John 3:20; Revelation 7:15; Ephesians 5:29; Hebrews 1:9; Jude 1:23; Revelation 2:6 and Rec. in 15; passive Revelation 18:2. Not a few interpreters have attributed to misein in Genesis 29:31 (cf. Genesis 29:30); Deuteronomy 21:15f; Matthew 6:24; Luke 14:26; 16:13; (John 12:25); Romans 9:13, the signification “to love less, to postpone in love or esteem, to slight,” through oversight of the circumstance that ‘the Orientals, in accordance with their greater excitability, are accustomed both to feel and to profess “love and hate” where we Occidentals, with our cooler temperament, feel and express nothing more than “interest in, or disregard and indifference” to a thing’; Fritzsche, Commentary on Romans, ii., p. 304; cf. Rückert, Magazin f. Exegese u. Theologie des N.T., p. 27ff*

misqapodosia, misqapodosiav, hJ (misqov and apodidwmi; cf. the misqodosia of the Greek writings (Winer’s Grammar, 24)), “payment of wages due, recompense”: of reward, Hebrews 10:35; 11:20; of punishment, Hebrews 2:2. (Several times in ecclesiastical writings.)*

misqapodothv, misqapodothsou, oJ (misqov and apodidwmi; cf. the misqodothv of the Greek writings) (Vulgate remunerator); “one who pays wages, a rewarder”: Hebrews 11:6. (Several times in ecclesiastical writings.)*

misqiov, misqia, misqion, also of two terminations (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 11, 1) (misqov), “employed for hire, hired”: as a substantive (A.V. “hired servant”), Luke 15:17,19 (21 WH in brackets) 152 (the Septuagint for rk;c;, Leviticus 25:50; Job 7:1. Tobit 5:12; Sir. 7:20; 31:27; 37:11. Anth. 6, 283, 3 Plutarch).*

misqov, misqou, oJ (from Homer down), the Septuagint for rk;c,; also for tr,Koc]m,æ etc.;

1. “dues paid for work; wages, hire”: Romans 4:4 (kata ofeilhma); in a prov., Luke 10:7 and 1 Timothy 5:18; Matthew 20:8; James 5:4; Jude 1:11 (on which see ekcew, at the end); misqov adikiav, wages obtained by iniquity, Acts 1:18; 2 Peter 2:15 (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 30, 1 a.).

2. “reward”: used — of the fruit naturally resulting from toils and endeavors, John 4:36; 1 Corinthians 9:18; — of “divine recompense”:

a. in both senses, rewards and punishments: Revelation 22:12.

b. of the rewards which God bestows, or will bestow, upon good deeds and endeavors (on the correct theory about which cf. Weiss, Die Lehre Christi vom Lohn, in the Deutsche Zeitschr. für christl. Wissenschaft, 1853, p. 319ff; Mehlhorn, d. Lohnbegr. Jesu, in the Jahrbb. f. protest. Theol., 1876, p. 721ff; (cf. Beyer in Herzog xx, pp. 4-14)): Matthew 5:12; 6:2,5,16; 10:41f; Mark 9:41; Luke 6:23,35; 1 Corinthians 3:8,14; 2 John 1:8; Revelation 11:18; ecein misqon, “to have a reward,” is used of those for whom a reward is reserved by God, whom a divine reward awaits, Matthew 5:46; 1 Corinthians 9:17; with para tw patri uJmwn tw en toiv ouranoiv added, Matthew 6:1. c. of punishments: misqov adikiav, 2 Peter 2:13; thv dussebeiav, 2 Macc. 8:33.*

misqow: (misqov); 1 aorist middle emisqwsamhn; “to let out for hire; to hire” (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 38, 3): tina, Matthew 20:1,7. (Herodotus, Aristophanes, Xenophon, Plato, others; the Septuagint for rkæc,; Deuteronomy 23:4; 2 Chronicles 24:12.)*

misqwma, misqwmatov, to (misqow);

1. “the price for which anything is either let or hired” (Herodotus, Isocrates, Demosthenes, Aelian, others; of a harlot’s hire, Hosea 2:12; 153 Deuteronomy 23:18; Micah 1:7; Proverbs 19:13; Ezekiel 16:31-34, and in classical Greek (cf. Philo in Flac. sec. 16 at the end)).

2. “that which is either let or hired for a price,” as a house, dwelling, lodging ((cf. Lightfoot’s Commentary on Philip., p. 9 note 3)): Acts 28:30.*
misqwtov, misqwtou, oJ (misqow), “one hired, a hireling”: Mark 1:20; John 10:12f (Aristophanes, Plato, Demosthenes, others; the Septuagint for rk;c;.)*
Mitulhnh, Mitulhnhv, hJ, “Mitylene,” the chief maritime town of the island of Lesbos in the Aegean: Acts 20:14. (Lewin, St. Paul, ii. 84f.)*

Micahl, oJ (laek;ymi, i.e. ‘who like God?’), “Michael,” the name of an archangel, who was supposed to be the guardian angel of the Israelites (Daniel 12:1; 10:13,21): Jude 1:9; Revelation 12:7. (BB. DD. under the word.)*

mna, mnav, hJ, a word of Eastern origin (cf. Schrader, Keilinschriften as above with, p. 143), Arabic ..., Syriac ..., Hebrew hn,m; (from hn;m;, to appoint, mark out, count, etc.), Latin mina;

1. in the O.T. a weight, and an imaginary coin or money of account, equal to one hundred shekels: 1 Kings 10:17, cf. 2 Chronicles 9:16; 2 Esdr. 2:69, (otherwise in Ezekiel 45:12 (cf. Bible Educator, index under the word Maneh; Schrader in Riehm under the word Mine, p. 1000f)).

2. In Attic a weight and a sum of money equal to one hundred drachmae (see dracmh (and B. D. under the word Pound; especially Schrader in Riehm as above)): Luke 19:13,16,18,20,24f*
Mnaswn, Mnaswnov, oJ (MNAW), “Mnason,” a Christian of Cyprus: Acts 21:16. (The name was common also among the Greeks; (cf. Benseler’s Pape’s Eigennamen, under the word).)*

mneia, mneiav, hJ (mimnhskw), “remembrance, memory, mention”: epi pash th mneia uJmwn, as often as I remember you 154 (literally, ‘on all my remembrance’ etc. cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 18, 4), Philippians 1:3; poieisqai mneian tinov, to make mention of one, Romans 1:9; Ephesians 1:16; 1 Thessalonians 1:2; Philemon 1:4 (Plato, Phaedr., p. 254 a.; Diogenes Laërtius 8. 2, 66; the Septuagint <19B004> Psalm 110:4 (<19B104>Psalm 111:4)); ecein mneian tinov, to be mindful of one, 1 Thessalonians 3:6 (Sophocles, Aristophanes, Euripides, others); adialeipton ecein thn peri tinov mneian, 2 Timothy 1:3.*

mnhma, mnhmatov, to (mnaomai, perfect passive memnhmai);

1. “a monument or memorial” to perpetuate the memory of any person or thing (Homer, Pindar, Sophocles, others).

2. “a sepulchral monument” (Homer, Euripides, Xenophon, Plato, others).

3. “a sepulchre or tomb” (receptacle where a dead body is deposited (cf. Edersheim, Jesus the Messiah, ii., 316f)): Mark 5:3 G L T Tr WH; 5:5; (xv. 46 T WH); Luke 8:27; 23:53; 24:1; Acts 2:29; 7:16; Revelation 11:9 (Josephus, Antiquities 7, 1, 3; the Septuagint for rb,q,).*

mnhmeion, mnhmeiou, to;

1. “any visible object for preserving or recalling the memory of any person or thing; a memorial, monument” (Aeschylus, Pindar, Sophocles, and following); in Biblical Greek so in Sap. 10:7; specifically, “a sepulchral monument”: oikodomein mnhmeia, Luke 11:47; Josephus, Antiquities 13, 6, 5.

2. in the Scriptures “a sepulchre, tomb”: Matthew 23:29; 27:52,60; 28:8; Mark 5:2; 6:29; Luke 11:44; John 5:28; 11:17,31, and often in the Gospels; Acts 13:29; the Septuagint for rb,q,, Genesis 23:6,9; 50:5; Isaiah 22:16, etc.

mnhmh, mnhmhv, hJ (mnaomai); a. “memory, remembrance”; b. “mention”: mnhmhn poieisqai tinov, to remember a thing, call it to remembrance, 2 Peter 1:15; the same expression occurs in Greek writings from Herodotus down, but in the sense of Latin mentionem facere, “to make mention of” a thing.* 155

mnhmoneuw; imperfect 3 person plural emnhmoneuon; 1 aorist emnhmoneusa; (mnhmwn mindful); from Herodotus down; the Septuagint for rkæz;;

1. “to be mindful of, to remember, to call to mind”: absolutely, Mark 8:18; tinov, Luke 17:32; John 15:20; 16:4,21; Acts 20:35; 1 Thessalonians 1:3; (Hebrews 13:7); contextually equivalent to “to think of and feel for a person or thing”: with the genitive of the thing, Colossians 4:18; twn ptwcwn, Galatians 2:10 (see mimnhskw, at the end); with an accusative of the object “to hold in memory, keep in mind”: tina, 2 Timothy 2:8; ti, Matthew 16:9; 1 Thessalonians 2:9; ta adikhmata, of God as punishing them, Revelation 18:5 (see mimnhskw). Cf. Matthiae, sec. 347 Anm. 2; Winer’s Grammar, p. 205 (193); (Buttmann, sec. 132, 14). followed by oJti, Acts 20:31; Ephesians 2:11; 2 Thessalonians 2:5; followed by an indirect question, Revelation 2:5; 3:3.

2. “to make mention of”: tinov, Hebrews 11:15 (but others refer this to 1 above) (Plutarch, Themistius, 32; ti, Plato, de rep. 4, p. 441 d.; legg. 4,

p. 723 c.); peri tinov (as mnasqai in classic Greek, see Matthiae, sec. 341 Anm. 1), Hebrews 11:22; so in Latin memini de aliquo; cf. Ramshorn, Latin Gr. sec. 111 note 1; (Harpers’ Latin Dictionary, under the word memini, I. 3; cf. English “remember about,” etc.).*

mnhmosunon, mnhmosunou, to (mnhmwn), “a memorial (that by which the memory of any person or thing is preserved), a remembrance”: eiv mnhmosunon tinov, to perpetuate one’s memory, Matthew 26:13; Mark 14:9; aJi proseucai sou ... anebhsan eiv mnhmosunon enwpion tou Qeou (without the figure) have become known to God, so that he heeds and is about to help thee, Acts 10:4. (Herodotus, Aristophanes, Thucydides, Plutarch, others; the Septuagint for rk,z,, ˆwOrK;zi; also for hr;K;z]aæ, i.e. that part of a sacrifice which was burned on the altar together with the frankincense, that its fragrance might ascend to heaven and commend the offerer to God’s remembrance, Leviticus 2:9, 16; 5:12; Numbers 5:26; hence, euwdia eiv mnhmosunon, Sir. 45:16; and often in Siracid., 1 Macc., etc.)*

mnhsteuw: passive, perfect participle memnhsteumenov (R G) and emnhsteumenov (L T Tr WH) (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 12, 10; 156 Veitch, under the word; Tdf. Proleg., p. 121); 1 aorist participle mnhsteuqeiv; (mnhstov betrothed, espoused); from Homer down; the Septuagint for creae; tina (gunaika), “to woo her and ask her in marriage”; passive “to be promised in marriage, be betrothed”: tini, Matthew 1:18; Luke 1:27; 2:5.*

mogilalov (from mogov (others mogov, cf. Chandler sec. 366) one who has a hoarse, hollow voice, and lalov), “speaking with a harsh or thick voice”: Mark 7:32 Tdf. edition 2, Tr text; but the common reading mogilalov deserves the preference; cf. Fritzsche at the passage, p. 302f. (Etymologicum Magnum (under the word battarizein).)*
mogiv (mogov toil), from Homer down, “hardly, with difficulty”: Luke 9:39 (yet WH Tr marginal reading moliv, which see). (3 Macc. 7:6.)*

modiov, modiou, oJ, the Latin modius, a dry measure holding 16 sextarii (or one sixth of the Attic medimnus; commentary Nepos, Attic 2 (i.e. about a peck, A.V. “bushel”; cf. BB. DD. under the phrase, Weights and Measures)): Matthew 5:15; Mark 4:21; Luke 11:33.*

moicaliv, moicalidov, hJ (moicov), a word unknown to the earlier writers but found in Plutarch, Heliodorus, others; see Lob. ad Phryn., p. 452; (Winer’s Grammar, 24); the Septuagint for tp,a,nO (Ezekiel 16:38; 23:45) and tp,a,n;m] (Hosea 3:1; Proverbs 24:55 (30:20)); “an adulteress”;

a. properly: Romans 7:3; ofqalmoi mestoi moicalidov, eyes always on the watch for an adulteress, or from which adulterous desire beams forth, 2 Peter 2:14.

b. As the intimate alliance of God with the people of Israel was likened to a marriage, those who relapse into idolatry are said to commit adultery or play “the harlot” (Ezekiel 16:15ff; 23:43ff, etc.); hence, moicaliv is 157 figuratively equivalent to “faithless to God, unclean, apostate”: James 4:4 (where cf. Alford); as an adjective (cf. Matthiae, sec. 429, 4), genea ... moicaliv: Matthew 12:39; 16:4; Mark 8:38. (Cf. Clement of Alexandria, strom. vi. c. 16 sec. 146, p. 292, 5 edition Sylb.)*

moicaw, moicw: “to have unlawful intercourse with another’s wife, to commit adultery with”: tina. in Biblical Greek middle moicwmai, “to commit adultery”: of the man, Matthew 5:32b (yet WH brackets); 19:9 (yet not WH marginal reading), 9b (R G L Tr brackets WH marginal reading); ep’ authn, commits the sin of adultery “against her” (i.e., that has been put away), Mark 10:11; of the Woman, Matthew 5:32a (where L T Tr WH moiceuqhnai for moicasqai); Mark 10:12. (the Septuagint for ãaæn;, Jeremiah 3:8; 5:7; 9:2, etc.; in Greek writers, figuratively in the active, with thn qalassan, to usurp unlawful control over the sea, Xenophon, Hell. 1, 6, 15; to lecqen, to falsify, corrupt, Aelian n. a. 7, 39.)*

moiceia, moiceiav, hJ (moiceuw), “adultery”: John 8:3; Galatians 5:19 Rec.; plural (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 27, 3; Buttmann, sec. 123, 2): Matthew 15:19; Mark 7:21. (Jeremiah 13:27; Hosea 2:2; 4:2; (Andocides (405 B. C.), Lysias), Plato, Aeschines, Lucian, others.)*

moiceuw; future moiceusw; 1 aorist emoiceusa; passive, present participle moiceuomenh; 1 aorist infinitive moiceuqhnai; (moicov); from Aristophanes and Xenophon down; the Septuagint for ãaæn;; “to commit adultery”;

a. absolutely (“to be an adulterer”): Matthew 5:27; 19:18; Mark 10:19; Luke 16:18; 18:20; Romans 2:22; 13:9; James 2:11.

b. tina (gunaika), “to commit adultery with,” have unlawful intercourse with another’s wife: Matthew 5:28 (Deuteronomy 5:18; Leviticus 20:10; Aristophanes av. 558; Plato, rep. 2, p. 360 b.; Lucian, dial. deor. 6, 3; Aristaenet. epistles 1, 20; Aeschines dial. Socrates 2, 14); passive of the wife, “to suffer adultery, be debauched”: Matthew 5:32a L T Tr WH; (Matthew 19:9 WH marginal reading); John 8:4. By a Hebraism (see moicaliv, b.) tropically, meta tinov (gunaikov) moiceuein is used of those who at a woman’s solicitation are drawn away 158 to idolatry, i.e. to the eating of things sacrificed to idols, Revelation 2:22; cf. Jeremiah 3:9, etc.*

moicov, moicou, oJ, “an adulterer”: Luke 18:11; 1 Corinthians 6:9; Hebrews 13:4. Hebraistically (see moicaliv, b.) and figuratively, “faithless toward God, ungodly”: James 4:4 R G. (Sophocles, Aristophanes, Xenophon, Plutarch, and following; the Septuagint.)*

moliv (molov toil); an adverb used by post-Homeric writings indiscriminately with mogiv;

a. “with difficulty, hardly” (cf. Sap. 9:16, where meta ponou corresponds to it in the parallel member): (Luke 9:39 Tr marginal reading WH (others mogiv, which see)); Acts 14:18; 27:7f,16; 1 Peter 4:18.

b. “not easily,” i.e. “scarcely, very rarely”: Romans 5:7.*

Moloc, oJ (Hebrew Ël,mo, µKol]mi, also µK;l]m;æ cf. Gesenius, Thesaurus, ii., p. 794f), indeclinable, “Moloch,” name of the idol-god of the Ammonites, to which human victims, particularly young children, were offered in sacrifice. According to the description in the Jalkut ((Rashi (Vulgate Jarchi)) on Jeremiah 7:(31)), its image was a hollow brazen figure, with the head of an ox, and outstretched human arms. It was heated red-hot by fire from within, and the little ones placed in its arms to be slowly burned, while to prevent their parents from hearing their dying cries the sacrificing-priests beat drums (see ghnna): Acts 7:43 from Amos 5:26 the Septuagint, where Hebrew µk,k]m,æ which ought to have been translated basilewv uJmwn, i.e. of your idol. Cf. Winer’s RWB, under the word, Moloch; J. G. Müller in Herzog ix. 714f; Merx in Schenkel see 194f; (BB. DD. under the words Molech, Moloch; Winer’s Grammar, Robertson Smith in Encyc. Brit. edition 9, under the word; Baudissin, Jahve et Moloch etc. and especially in Herzog 2 vol. 10:168178).*

molunw: 1 aorist active emoluna; passive present molunomai; 1 aorist emolunqhn; from Aristophanes down; “to pollute, stain, contaminate, defile”; in the N.T. used only in symbolic and figurative discourse: ouk emolunan ta iJmatia autwn, of those who have kept 159 themselves pure from the defilement of sin, Revelation 3:4 (cf. Zechariah 3:3f); meta gunaikwn ouk emolunqhsan, who have not soiled themselves by fornication and adultery, Revelation 14:4; hJ suneidhsiv molunetai, of a conscience reproached (defiled) by sin, 1 Corinthians 8:7 (inexplebili quodam laedendi proposito conscientiam polluebat, Ammianus Marcellinus 15, 2; opposed to kaqara suneidhsiv, 1 Timothy 3:9; 2 Timothy 1:3; molunein thn yuchn, Sir. 21:28; but see miainw, 2). (Synonym: see miainw, at the end.)*

molusmov, molusmou, oJ (molunw), “defilement” (Vulgate inquinamentum); an action by which anything is defiled: with the genitive of the thing defiled, sarkov kai pneumatov, 2 Corinthians 7:1. (Jeremiah 23:15; 1 Esdr. 8:80; 2 Macc. 5:27; Plutarch, mor., p. 779 c.; (Josephus, contra Apion 1, 32, 2; 2, 24, 5; etc.); often in ecclesiastical writings.)*
momfh, momfhv, hJ (memfomai), “blame”: ecein momfhn prov tina, to have matter of complaint against anyone, Colossians 3:13. (Pindar, Tragg., others.)*

monh, monhv, hJ (menw) (from Herodotus down), “a staying, abiding, dwelling, abode”: John 14:2; monhn poiein (L T Tr WH poieisqai, as in Thucydides 1, 131; Josephus, Antiquities 8, 13, 7; 13, 2, 1), “to make an (one’s) abode,” para tini metaphorically, of God and Christ by their power and spirit exerting a most blessed influence on the souls of believers, John 14:23; see poiw, 1 c.*

monogenhv, monogenev (monov and genov) (Cicero, unigena; Vulgate (in Luke unicus, elsewhere) and in ecclesiastical writings unigenitus), “single of its kind, only” (A.V. “only-begotten”); used of only sons or daughters (viewed in relation to their parents), Hesiod theog. 426, 448; Herodotus 7, 221; Plato, Critias 113 d.; Josephus, Antiquities 1, 13, 1; 2, 7, 4; monogenev teknon patri, Aeschylus Ag. 898. So in the Scriptures: Hebrews 11:17; monogenh einai tini (to be one’s only son or daughter), Judges 11:34; Tobit 3:15; Luke 7:12; 8:42; 9:38; (cf. Westcott on Epistles of John, pp. 162ff). Hence, the expression oJ monogenhv uJiov tou Qeou and uJiov tou Qeou oJ monogonhv, John 3:16,18; 1:18 (see below); 1 John 4:9; monogenhv para patrov, John 1:14 (some take this generally, owing to the omission of the article (cf. Green, pp. 48f)), used of Christ, denotes “the only son of God” or one 160 who in the sense in which he himself is the son of God has no brethren. He is so spoken of by John not because oJ logov which was ensarkwqeiv in him was eternally generated by God the Father (the orthodox interpretation), or came forth from the being of God just before the beginning of the world (Subordinationism), but because by the incarnation (ensarkwsiv) of the logov in him he is of nature or essentially Son of God, and so in a very different sense from that in which men are made by him tekna tou Qeou (John 1:13). For since in the writings of John the title oJ iJuov tou Qeou is given only to the historic Christ so called, neither the Logos alone, nor Jesus alone, but oJ logov oJ ensarkwqeiv or Jesus through the logov united with God, is oJ monogenhv uJiov tou Qeou. The reading monogenhv Qeov (without the article before monogenhv) in John 1:18, — which is supported by no inconsiderable weight of ancient testimony, received into the text by Tregelles, and Westcott and Hort, defended with much learning by Dr. Hort (“On monogenhv Qeov in Scripture and Tradition” in his “Two Dissertations” Camb. and Lond. 1876), and seems not improbable to Harnack (in the Theol. Lit.-Zeit. for 1876, p. 541ff) (and Weiss (in Meyer 6te Aufl. at the passage)), but is foreign to John’s mode of thought and speech (John 3:16,18; 1 John 4:9), dissonant and harsh — appears to owe its origin to a dogmatic zeal which broke out soon after the early days of the church; (see articles on the reading by Prof. Abbot in the Bib. Sacr. for Oct. 1861 and in the Unitarian Revelation for June 1875 (in the latter copious references to other discussions of the same passage are given); see also Prof. Drummond in the Theol. Revelation for Oct. 1871). Further, see Grimm, Exgt. Hdbch. on Sap., p. 152f; (Westcott as above).*

monov, monh, monon, the Septuagint chiefly for dbæl] (from Homer down);

1. an adjective, “alone” (without a companion); a. with verbs: einai, eJuriskesqai, kataleipesqai, etc., Matthew 14:23; Mark 6:47; Luke 9:36; John 8:9; 1 Thessalonians 3:1; added to the pronouns egw, autov, ou, etc.: Matthew 18:15; Mark 9:2; Luke 24:18; Romans 11:3; 16:4, etc. b. it is joined with its noun to other verbs also, so that what is predicated may be declared to apply to some one person alone (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 131 (124) note): Matthew 4:10; Luke 4:8; 24:12 (T omits; L Tr brackets WH reject the verse); John 6:22; Hebrews 9:7; 2 Timothy 4:11; with a neg. followed by alla, 161 Matthew 4:4. oJ monov Qeov, he who alone is God: John 5:44; 17:3; Romans 16:27; oJ monov despothv, Jude 1:4. ouk ... ei mh monov: Matthew 12:4; 17:8; 24:36; Luke 6:4; oudeiv ... ei mh monov, Phil 4:15. equivalent to “forsaken, destitute of help,” Luke 10:40; John 8:16; 16:32, (Sap. 10:1).

2. Neuter monon as adverb, “alone, only, merely”: added to the object, Matthew 5:47; 10:42; Acts 18:25; Galatians 3:2; to the genitive Romans 3:29 (here WH marginal reading monwn); referring to an action expressed by a verb, Matthew 9:21; 14:36; Mark 5:36; Luke 8:50; Acts 8:16; 1 Corinthians 15:19; Galatians 1:23; 2:10. monon mh, Galatians 5:13; ou (mh) monon, Galatians 4:18; James 1:22; 2:24; followed by alla, Acts 19:26 (L alla kai; cf. Winer’s Grammar, 498 (464); Buttmann, 370 (317)); by alla pollw mallon, Philippians 2:12; by alla kai, Matthew 21:21; John 5:18; 11:52; 12:9; 13:9; 17:20; Acts 19:26 (Lachmann (see as above, especially Buttmann)); 21:13; 26:29; 27:10; Romans 1:32; 4:12,16, 23; 2 Corinthians 7:7, etc.; ou monon de alla kai: Acts 19:27; and often by Paul (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 583 (543)), Romans 5:3,11; 8:23; 9:10; 2 Corinthians 7:7; 8:19; Philippians 2:27 (here ou de monon etc.); 1 Timothy 5:13; (2 Timothy 4:8. kata monav (namely, cwrav), see katamonav).

monofqalmov, monofqalmon (monov, ofqalmov) (Vulgate luscus, Mark 9:47), “deprived of one eye, having one eye”: Matthew 18:9; Mark 9:47. (Herodotus, Apollod., Strabo, Diogenes Laërtius, others; (Lob. ad Phryn., p. 136; Bekker Anecd. 1:280; Rutherford, New Phryn., p. 209; Winer’s Grammar, 24).)*
monow, monw; (monov); from Homer down; “to make single or solitary; to leave alone, forsake”: perfect passive participle chra memonwmenh, i.e. without children, 1 Timothy 5:5, cf. 4.*

morfh, morfhv, hJ (from root signifying ‘to lay hold of’, ‘seize’ (cf. German Fassung); Fick, Part i., p. 174; Vanicek, p. 719), from Homer down, “the form by which a person or thing strikes the vision; the external appearance”: children are said to reflect yuchv te kai morfhv oJmoiothta (of their parents), 4 Macc. 15:3 (4); efanerwqh en eJtera morfh, Mark 16:12; en morfh Qeou uJparcwn, Philippians 2:6; morfhn doulou labwn, Philippians 2:7; — this whole passage (as I 162 have shown more fully in the Zeitschr. f. wissensch. f. protest. (God menei aei aJplwv en th autou morfh, Plato, de rep. 2, p. 381 c., and it is denied that God fantazesqai allote en allaiv ideaiv ... kai allattonta to autou eidov eiv pollav morfav ... kai thv eJautou ideav ekbainein, p. 380 d.; hJkist’ an pollav morfav iscoi oJ Qeov,

p. 381 b.; eJnov swmatov ousian metaschmatizein kai metacarattein eiv polutropouv morfav, Philo leg. ad Gaium sec. 11; ou gar wJsper to nomisma parakomma kai Qeou morfh ginetai, ibid. sec. 14 at the end; God ergoiv men kai carisin energhv kai pantov oJutinosoun fanerwterov, morfhn de kai megeqov hJmin afanestatov, Josephus, contra Apion 2, 22, 2.)* (Synonyms: morfh, schma: according to Lightfoot (see the thorough discussion in his ‘Detached Note’ on Philippians ii.) and Trench (N.T. moscopoiew, moscopoiw: 1 aorist emoscopoihsa; (moscov and poiew (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 26)); “to make (an image of) a calf”: Acts 7:41, for which Exodus 32:4 epoihse moscon. (Ecclesiastical writings.)*

mousikov, mousikh, mousikon (mousa (music, eloquence, etc.)); frequent in Greek writings; properly, “devoted to and skilled in the arts sacred to the muses; accomplished in the liberal arts”; specifically, “skilled in music; playing on musical instruments”; so Revelation 18:22 (R.V. “minstrels”).*

mocqov, mocqou, oJ, “hard and difficult labor, toil, travail; hardship, distress”: 2 Corinthians 11:27; 1 Thessalonians 2:9; 2 Thessalonians 3:8; see kopov, 3 b. (Hesiod scut. 306; Pindar, Tragg., Xenophon, others; the Septuagint chiefly for lm;[;.) (Synonym: see kopov, at the end.)* 164
muelov, muelou, oJ (enclosed within, from muw to close, shut), “marrow”: Hebrews 4:12. (From Homer down; the Septuagint Job 21:24.)*

muew, muw: perfect passive memuhmai; (from muw to close, shut ((cf. Latin mutus); Curtius, sec. 478));

a. “to initiate into the mysteries” (Herodotus, Aristophanes, Plato, Plutarch, others; 3 Macc. 2:30).

b. universally, “to teach fully, instruct; to accustom one to a thing; to give one an intimate acquaintance with a thing”: en panti kai en pasi memuhmai, to every condition and to all the several circumstances of life have I become accustomed; I have been so disciplined by experience that whatsoever be my lot I can endure, Philippians 4:12; (but others, instead of connecting en panti etc. here (as object) with memuhmai (a construction apparently without precedent; yet cf. muqov, muqou, oJ, from Homer down;

1. “a speech, word, saying”.

2. “a narrative, story”;

a. “a true narrative”.

b. “a fiction, a fable”; universally, “an invention, falsehood”: 2 Peter 1:16; the fictions of the Jewish theosophists and Gnostics, especially concerning the emanations and orders of the aeons, are called muqoi (A.V. “fables”) in 1 Timothy 1:4; 4:7; 2 Timothy 4:4; Titus 1:14. (Cf. Trench, sec. xc., and references under the word genalogia.)*

mukaomai, mukwmai; (from mu or mu, the sound which a cow utters (Latin mugio)), “to low, bellow,” properly, of horned cattle (Homer, Aeschylus, Euripides, Plato, others); “to roar,” of a lion, Revelation 10:3.* 165

mukthrizw: (mukthr the nose); present passive 3 person singular mukthrizetai; properly, “to turn up the nose or sneer at; to mock, deride”: tina, passive ou mukthrizetai, does not suffer himself to be mocked, Galatians 6:7. Clement of Rome, 1 Corinthians 39,1 (and Harnack’s note)). 1 Macc. 7:34; (1 Esdr. 1:49); Sextus Empiricus, adverb math. i. 211 (p. 648, 11 edition Bekker).) (Compare: ekmukthrizw.)* mulikov, mulikh, mulikon (mulh a mill), “belonging to a mill”: Mark 9:42 R G; Luke 17:2 L T Tr WH.*

mulinov, mulinh, mulinon;

2. equivalent to mulh, “a mill” ((Diodorus, Strabo, Plutarch)): Matthew 24:41 L T Tr WH; fwnh mulou, the noise made by a mill, Revelation 18:22.*
mulwn (not paroxytone; see Chandler sec. 596 cf. sec. 584), mulwnov, oJ, “place where a mill runs; mill-house”: Matthew 24:41 R G. (Euripides, Thucydides, Demosthenes, Aristotle, others.)*

D. under the word Myra; Lewin, St. Paul, ii., 186f): Acts 27:5.* 166

murizw: 1 aorist infinitive murisai; (muron); from Herodotus down; “to anoint”: Mark 14:8.*

Curtius, p. 714)), “ointment”: Matthew 26:7,9 Rec., 12; Mark 14:3-5; Luke 7:37f; 23:56; John 11:2; 12:3,5; Revelation 18:13; distinguished from elaion (which see and see Trench, Synonyms, sec. xxxviii.), Luke 7:46. ((From Aeschylus, Herodotus down); the Septuagint for ˆm,v,, fat, oil, Proverbs 27:9; for ˆm,v, bwOf, <19D202>Psalm 132:2 (133:2).)*

musthrion, musthriou, to (musthv (one initiated; from muew, which see)), in classical Greek “a hidden thing, secret, mystery”: musthrion sou mh kateiphv tw filw, Menander; plural generally “mysteries, religious secrets,” confided only to the initiated and not to be communicated by them to ordinary mortals; (cf. 1. “a hidden or secret thing, not obvious to the understanding”: 1 Corinthians 13:2; 14:2; (of the secret rites of the Gentiles, Sap. 14:15,23).

2. “a hidden purpose or counsel; secret will”: of men, tou basilewv, Tobit 12:7,11; thv boulhv autou, Judith 2:2; of God: musthria Qeou, the secret counsels which govern God in dealing with the righteous, which are hidden from ungodly and wicked men but plain to the godly, Sap. 2:22. In the N.T., God’s plan of providing salvation for men through Christ, which was once hidden but now is revealed: Romans 16:25; 1 Corinthians 2:7 (on this see en, I. 5 f.); Ephesians 3:9; Colossians 1:26f; with tou qelhmatov autou added, Ephesians 1:9; tou Qeou, which God formed, Colossians 2:2; (1 Corinthians 2:1 WH text); tou Cristou, respecting Christ, Colossians 4:3; tou euaggeliou, which is contained and announced in the gospel, Ephesians 6:19; etelesqh to musthrion tou Qeou, said of the consummation of this purpose, to be looked for when Christ returns, Revelation 10:7; ta musthria thv basileiav twn ouranwn or tou Qeou, the secret purposes relative to the kingdom of God, Matthew 13:11; Mark 4:11; Luke 8:10; used of certain single events decreed by God having reference to his kingdom or the salvation of men, Romans 11:25; 1 Corinthians 15:51; of God’s purpose to bless the Gentiles also with salvation through Christ (cf. Lightfoot on Colossians 1:26), Ephesians 3:3, cf. Ephesians 3:5; with tou Cristou added, Ephesians 3:4; oikonomoi musthriwn Qeou, the stewards of God’s mysteries, i.e. those intrusted with the announcement of God’s secret purposes to men, 1 Corinthians 4:1; used generally, of Christian truth as hidden from ungodly men: with the addition of thv pistewv, thv eusebeiav, which faith and godliness embrace and keep, 1 Timothy 3:9,16; to musthrion thv anomiav “the mystery of lawlessness,” the secret purpose formed by lawlessness, seems to be a tacit antithesis to God’s saving purpose, 2 Thessalonians 2:7. 168
