oJ, hJ, to, originally tov, th, to (as is evident from the forms toi, tai for oJi, aJi in Homer and the Ionic writings), corresponds to our definite article “the” (German der, die, das), which is properly a demonstrative pronoun, which we see in its full force in Homer, and of which we find certain indubitable traces also in all kinds of Greek prose, and hence also in the N.T.

I. As a demonstrative pronoun; Latin hic, hacc, hoc; German der, die, das, emphatic; cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 17, 1; Buttmann, 101f (89f);

1. in the words of the poet Aratus, tou gar kai genov esmen, quoted by Paul in Acts 17:28.

2. in prose, where it makes a partition or distributes into parts: oJ men ... oJ de, “that ... this, the one ... the other”: Matthew 13:23 R G Tr (here the division is threefold); Galatians 4:23 (here L WH Tr marginal reading brackets men); oJi men ... oJi de, Acts 28:24; Philippians 1:16f; oJi men ... oJ de, Hebrews 7:5f,20 (21), 23f; touv men ... touv de, Mark 12:5 R G; Ephesians 4:11; oJi men ... alloi de (Lclnn. oJi de) ... eJteroi de, Matthew 16:14 cf. John 7:12; tinev followed by oJi de, Acts 17:18; oJv (see oJv I.) men followed by oJ de, Romans 14:2; oJi de stands as though oJi men had preceded, Matthew 26:67; 28:17.

3. in narration, when either two persons or two parties are alternately placed in opposition to each other and the discourse turns from one to the other; oJ de, “but he, and he” (German er aber): Matthew 2:14; 4:4; 21:29f; Mark 1:45; 12:15; Luke 8:21,30,48; 22:10,34; John 9:38, and very often; plural, Matthew 2:5,9; 4:20; Mark 12:14 (R G L marginal reading), 16 (L brackets oJi de); Luke 7:4; 20:5,12; 22:9,38,71; Acts 4:21; 12:15, and often; oJi men oun, in the Acts alone: Acts 1:6; 5:41; 15:3,30; oJ men oun, 23:18; 28:5.

II. As the definite or prepositive article (to be distinguished from the postpositive article — as it is called when it has the force of a relative pronoun, like the German der, die, das, examples of which use are not found in the N.T.), whose use in the N.T. is explained at length by Winer’s Grammar, sections 18-20; Buttmann, 85 (74ff); (Green, p. 5ff). As in all 209 languages the article serves to distinguish things, persons, notions, more exactly, it is prefixed

1. to substantives that have no modifier; and

a. those that designate a person or a thing that is the only one of its kind; the article thus distinguishes the same from all other persons or things, as oJ hJliov, oJ ouranov, hJ gh, hJ qalassa, oJ Qeov, oJ logov (John 1:1f), oJ diabolov, to fwv, hJ skotia, hJ zwh, oJ qanatov, etc.

b. appellative names of persons and things definite enough in themselves, or made so by the context, or sufficiently well-known from history; thus, to the names of virtues and vices, as hJ dikaiosunh, hJ sofia), hJ dunamiv, hJ alhqeia, etc. oJ ercomenov, the well-known personage who is to come, i.e. the Messiah, Matthew 11:3; Luke 7:19; oJ profhthv, the (promised and expected) prophet, John 1:21; 7:40; hJ swthria, the salvation which all good men hope for, i.e. the Messianic salvation: hJ grafh, etc.; hJ nefelh, the cloud (well known from the O.T.), 1 Corinthians 10:1f; touv aggelouv, James 2:25; tw ektrwmati, 1 Corinthians 15:8. to designations of eminent personages: oJ uJiov tou Qeou, oJ uJiov tou anqrwpou (see uJiov); oJ didaskalov tou Israhl, John 3:10; cf. Fritzsche on Mark, p. 613. The article is applied to the repeated name of a person or thing already mentioned or indicated, and to which the reader is referred, as touv magouv, Matthew 2:7 cf. 1; oJi askoi, Matthew 9:17: oJi daimonev, Matthew 8:31 cf. Matthew 8:28; thn onon kai ton pwlon, Matthew 21:7, cf. Matthew 21:2, and countless other examples The article is used with names of things not yet spoken of, in order to show that definite things are referred to, to be distinguished from others of the same kind and easily to be known from the context; as ta brefh, the babes belonging to the people of that place, Luke 18:15; apo twn dendrwn, namely, which were there, Matthew 21:8; tw iJerei, to the priest whose duty it will be to examine thee, when thou comest, Matthew 8:4; Mark 1:44; Luke 5:14; to ploion, the ship which stood ready to carry them over, Matthew 8:23 (R G T, cf. Matthew 8:18); 9:1 (R G); 13:2 (R G); to orov, the mountain near the place in question (der an Ort u. Stelle befindliche Berg) (But some commentators still regard to orov as used here generically or Hebraistically like hJ oreinh, the mountain region or the highlands, in contrast with the low country (cf. the Septuagint Joshua 17:16; 20:7; Genesis 19:17,19, etc.); cf. Lightfoot ‘Fresh Revision’ etc., p. 111f; 210 Weiss, Matthäusevangelium, p. 129 note; and in Meyer’s Matthew 7te Aufl.), Matthew 5:1; Mark 3:13; Luke 9:28; John 6:3,15 (1 Macc. 9:38,40); hJ oikia, the house in which (Jesus) was wont to lodge, Matthew 9:10,28; 13:36; 17:25; uJpo ton modion, namely, that is in the house, Matthew 5:15; also epi thn lucnian, ibid.; en th fatnh, in the manger of the stable of the house where they were lodging, Luke 2:7 R G; oJ epainov, the praise of which he is worthy, 1 Corinthians 4:5; so everywhere in the doxologies: hJ doxa to kratov, 1 Peter 4:11; Revelation 5:13, etc.

c. The article prefixed to the plural often either includes all and every one of those who by the given name are distinguished from other things having a different name — as oJi asterev, Matthew 24:29; Mark 13:25; aJi alwtekev, Matthew 8:20; Luke 9:58, etc.; — or defines the class alone, and thus indicates that the whole class is represented by the individuals mentioned, however many and whosoever they may be; as in oJi Farisaioi, oJi grammateiv, oJi telwnai, oJi anqrwpoi people, the multitude (German die Leute); oJi aetoi, Matthew 24:28; toiv kusin, Matthew 7:6.

d. The article prefixed to the singular sometimes so defines only the class, that all and every one of those who bear the name are brought to mind; thus, oJ anqrwpov, Matthew 15:11; oJ eqnikov kai telwnhv, Matthew 18:17; oJ ergathv, Luke 10:7; 1 Timothy 5:18; oJ mesithv, Galatians 3:20; oJ klhronomov, Galatians 4:1; oJ dikaiov, Romans 1:17; Hebrews 10:38; ta shmeia tou apostolou, the signs required of anyone who claims to be an apostle, 2 Corinthians 12:12, and ether examples

e. The article is prefixed to the nominative often put for the vocative in addresses (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 29, 2; Buttmann, sec. 129 a. 5): caire oJ basileuv twn Ioudaiwn (properly, su oJ basileuv, thou who art the king), John 19:3; nai, oJ pathr, Matthew 11:26; age nun oJi plousioi, klausate, James 5:1; ourane kai oJi aJgioi, Revelation 18:20; add, Mark 5:41; 10:47; Luke 12:32; 18:11,13; John 8:10; 20:28; Acts 13:41; Romans 8:15; Ephesians 5:14,22,25; 6:1,4f; Revelation 12:12.

f. The Greeks employ the article, where we abstain from its use, before nouns denoting things that pertain to him who is the subject of discourse: 211 eipe or fhsi megalh th fwnh, Acts 14:10 (R G); 26:24 (Proverbs 26:25); gunh proseucomenh ... akatakaluptw th kefalh, 1 Corinthians 11:5; especially in the expression ecein ti, when the object and its adjective, or what is equivalent to an adjective, denotes a part of the body or something else which naturally belongs to anyone (as in French, il a les epaules larges); so, eJcein thn ceira xhran, Matthew 12:10 R G; Mark 3:1; to proswpon wJv anqrwpou ((Rec. anqrwpov)), Revelation 4:7; ta aisqhthria gegumnasmena, Hebrews 5:14; aparabaton thn iJerwsunhn, Hebrews 7:24; thn katoikhsin k.t.l., Mark 5:3; thn eiv eJautouv agaphn ektenh, 1 Peter 4:8. Cf. Grimm on 2 Macc. 3:25. the genitive of a person pronoun autou, uJmwn, is added to the substantive: Matthew 3:4; Mark 8:17; Revelation 2:18; 1 Peter 2:12, cf. Ephesians 1:18; cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 18, 2; (Buttmann, sec. 125,5).

g. Proper Names sometimes have the article and sometimes are anarthrous; cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 18, 5 and 6; Buttmann, sec. 124, 3 and 4; (Green, p. 28f); [a]. as respects names of Persons, the person without the article is simply named, but with the article is marked as either well known or as already mentioned; thus we find Ihsouv and oJ Ihsouv, Paulov and oJ Paulov, etc. Pilatov has the article everywhere in John’s Gospel and also in Mark’s Gospel, if Mark 15:43 (in R G L) be excepted (but T Tr WH insert the article there also); Titov is everywhere anarthrous. Indeclinable names of persons in the oblique cases almost always have the article, unless the case is made evident by a preposition: tw Iwshf, Mark 15:45; ton Iakwb kai ton Hsau, Hebrews 11:20, and many other examples, especially in the genealogies, Matthew 1:1ff; Luke 3:23; but where perspicuity does not require the article, it is omitted also in the oblique cases, as twn uJiwn Iwshf, Hebrews 11:21; twn uJiwn Emmwr, Acts 7:16; oJ Qeov Isaak, Matthew 22:32; Acts 7:32; oJtan oyhsqe Abraam kai Isaak ... kai pantav touv profhtav, Luke 13:28. The article is commonly omitted with personal proper names to which is added an apposition indicating the race, country, office, rank, surname, or something else, (cf. Matthiae, sec. 274): let the following suffice as examples: Abraam oJ pathr hJmwn, John 8:56; Romans 4:1; Iakwbon ton tou Zebedaiou kai Iwannhn ton adelfon autou, Matthew 4:21; Maria hJ Magdalhnh, Matthew 27:56, etc.; 212 Iwannhv oJ baptisthv, Matthew 3:1; HJrodhv oJ tetrarchv, Luke 9:7; Ihsouv oJ legomenov Cristov, Matthew 1:16; Saulov de oJ kai Paulov namely, kaloumenov, Acts 13:9; Simwnov tou leprou, Mark 14:3; Bartimaiov oJ tuflov, Mark 10:46 (R G); Zacariou tou apolomenou, Luke 11:51. But there are exceptions also to this usage oJ de HJrodhv oJ tetrarchv, Luke 3:19; ton Saoul, uJion Kiv, Acts 13:21; in the opening of the Epistles: Paulov apostolov, Romans 1:1; 1 Corinthians 1:1, etc. [b]. Proper names of countries and region s have the article far more frequently than those of cities and towns, for the reason that most names of countries, being derived from adjectives, get the force of substantives only by the addition of the article, as hJ Acaia (but cf. 2 Corinthians 9:2), hJ Galatia, hJ Galilaia, hJ Italia, hJ Ioudaia, hJ Makedonia (but cf. Romans 15:26; 1 Corinthians 16:5), etc. Only Aiguptov, if Acts 7:11 L T Tr WH be excepted, is everywhere anarthrous. The names of cities, especially when joined to prepositions, particularly en, eiv and ek, are without the article; but we find apo (R G ek) thv Rwmhv in Acts 18:2. [g]. Names of rivers and streams have the article in Matthew 3:13; Mark 1:5; Luke 4:1; 13:4; John 1:28; tou Kedrwn, John 18:1 G L Tr marginal reading

2. The article is prefixed to substantives expanded and more precisely defined by modifiers;

a. to nouns accompanied by a genitive of the pronouns mou, sou, hJmwn, uJmwn, autou, eJautwn, autwn: Matthew 1:21,25; 5:45; 6:10-12; 12:49; Mark 9:17; Luke 6:27; 10:7; 16:6; Acts 19:25 (L T Tr WH hJmin); Romans 4:19; 6:6, and in numberless other places; it is rarely omitted, as in Matthew 19:28; Luke 1:72; 2:32; 2 Corinthians 8:23; James 5:20, etc.; cf. Buttmann, sec. 127, 27.

b. The possessive pronouns emov, sov, hJmeterov, uJmeterov, joined to substantives (if John 4:34 be excepted) always take the article, and John generally puts them after the substantive (hJ krisiv hJ emh, John 5:30; oJ logov oJ sov, 17:17; koinwnia hJ hJmetera, 1 John 1:3; oJ kairov oJ uJmeterov, John 7:6), very rarely between the article and the substantive (toiv emoiv rhmasin, John 5:47; hJ emh didach, 7:16; thn shn lalian, 4:42), yet this is always done by the other N.T. writings, 213 Matthew 18:20; Mark 8:38; Luke 9:26; Acts 24:6 (Rec.); 26:5; Romans 3:7, etc.

c. When adjectives are added to substantives, either the adjective is placed between the article and the substantive — as to idion fortion, Galatians 6:5; oJ agaqov anqrwpov, Matthew 12:35; thn dikaian krisin, John 7:24; hJ agaqh meriv, Luke 10:42; to aJgion pneuma, Luke 12:10; Acts 1:8; hJ aiwniov zwh, John 17:3, and many other examples; — or the adjective preceded by an article is placed after the substantive with its article, as to pneuma to aJgion, Mark 3:29; John 14:26; Acts 1:16; Hebrews 3:7; 9:8; 10:15; hJ zwh aiwniov, 1 John 1:2; 2:25; oJ poimhn oJ kalov, John 10:11; thn pulhn thn sidhran, Acts 12:10, and other examples; — very rarely the adjective stands before a substantive which has the article, as in Acts (14:10 R G); 26:24; 1 Corinthians 11:5 (cf. Buttmann, sec. 125, 5; Winer’s Grammar, sec. 20, 1 c.). As to the adjectives of quantity, oJlov, pav, poluv, see each in its own place.

d. What has been said concerning adjectives holds true also of all other limitations added to substantives, as hJ kat’ ekloghn proqesiv, Romans 9:11; par’ emou diaqhkh, Romans 11:27; oJ logov oJ tou staurou, 1 Corinthians 1:18; hJ eiv Criston pistiv, Colossians 2:5; on the other hand, hJ pistiv uJmwn hJ prov ton Qeon, 1 Thessalonians 1:8; thv diakoniav thv eiv touv aJgiouv, 2 Corinthians 8:4; see many other examples of each usage in Winer’s Grammar, 131ff (124ff); (Buttmann, 91ff (80ff)).

e. The noun has the article before it when a demonstrative pronoun (oJutov, ekeinov) belonging to it either precedes or follows (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 18, 4; Buttmann, sec. 127, 29-31); as, oJ anqrwpov oJutov, John 9:24 (oJutov oJ anqrwpov, L Tr marginal reading WH); Acts 6:13; 22:26; oJ laov oJutov, Matthew 15:8; oJ uJiov sou oJutov, Luke 15:30; plural Luke 24:17, and numberless other examples; oJutov oJ anqrwpov, Luke 14:30; oJutov oJ laov, Mark 7:6 (oJ laov oJutov, L WH marginal reading); oJutov oJ uJiov mou, Luke 15:24; oJutov oJ telwnhv, Luke 18:11 (oJ telwnhv oJutov, L marginal reading); oJutov oJ logov, John 7:36 (oJ logov oJutov, L T Tr WH), and many other examples on ekeinov, see ekeinov, 2; on autov oJ etc., see autov (I. 1 b. etc.); on oJ autov etc., see autov, III. 214

3. The neuter article prefixed to adjectives changes them into substantives (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 34, 2; Buttmann, sec. 128, 1); as, to agaqon, to kalon (which see each in its place); to elatton, Hebrews 7:7; with a genitive added, to gnwston tou Qeou, Romans 1:19; to adunaton tou nomou, Romans 8:3; to asqenev tou Qeou, 1 Corinthians 1:25; authv, Hebrews 7:18; ta aorata tou Qeou, Romans 1:20; ta krupta thv aiscunhv, 2 Corinthians 4:2, etc.

4. The article with cardinal numerals: eJiv “one”; oJ eJiv the one (of two), see eJiv, 4 a.; but differently oJ eJiv in Romans 5:15,17, “the (that) one”. So also oJi duo (our “the twain”), Matthew 19:5; oJi deka the (those) ten, and oJi ennea, Luke 17:17; ekeinoi oJi deka (kai) oktw, Luke 13:4.

5. The article prefixed to participles

a. gives them the force of substantives (Winer’s Grammar, sections 18, 3; 45, 7; Buttmann, sections 129, 1 b.; 144, 9); as, oJ peirazwn, Matthew 4:3; 1 Thessalonians 3:5; oJ baptizwn, Mark 6:14 (for which Matthew 14:2 oJ baptisthv); oJ speirwn, Matthew 13:3; Luke 8:5; oJ oloqreuwn, Hebrews 11:28; oJi bastazontev, Luke 7:14; oJi boskontev, Matthew 8:33; Mark 5:14; oJi esqiontev, the eaters (convivae), Matthew 14:21; to ofeilomenon, Matthew 18:30,34; ta uJparconta (see uJparcw, 2).

b. the participle with the article must be resolved into “he who” (and a finite verb; cf. Buttmann, sec. 144, 9): Matthew 10:40; Luke 6:29; 11:23; John 15:23; 2 Corinthians 1:21; Philippians 2:13, and very often. pav oJ followed by a participle (Winer’s Grammar, 111 (106)), Matthew 5:22; 7:26; Luke 6:30 (T WH omit; L Tr marginal reading brackets article); 11:10; Romans 2:1; 1 Corinthians 16:16; Galatians 3:13, etc.; makariov oJ with a participle, Matthew 5:4 (5), 6, 10, etc.; ouai uJmin oJi with a preposition, Luke 6:25; the neuter to with a participle must be resolved into that which (with a finite verb), to gennwmenon, Luke 1:35; to gegennhmenon, John 3:6.

c. the article with participle is placed in apposition: Mark 3:22; Acts 17:24; Ephesians 3:20; 4:22,24; 2 Timothy 1:14; 1 Peter 1:21, etc.

6. The neuter to before infinitives 215

a. gives them the force of substantives (cf. Buttmann, 261ff (225ff) (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 44, 2 a.; 3 c.)); as, to kaqisai, Matthew 20:23; Mark 10:40; to qelein, Romans 7:18; 2 Corinthians 8:10; to poihsai, to epitelesai, 2 Corinthians 8:11, and other examples; touto krinate. to mh tiqenai k.t.l., Romans 14:13. On the infinite with the article depending on a preposition (anti tou, en tw, eiv to, etc.), see under each preposition in its place.

b. Much more frequent in the N.T. than in the earlier and more elegant Greek writings, especially in the writings of Luke and Paul (nowhere in John’s Gospel and Epistles), is the use of the genitive tou with an infinitive (and in the Septuagint far more frequent than in the N.T.), which is treated of at length by Fritzsche in an excursus at the end of his commentary on Matthew, p. 843ff; Winer’s Grammar, sec. 44, 4; Buttmann, 266ff (228ff). The examples fall under the following classes: tou with an infinitive is put [a.] after words which naturally require a genitive (of a noun also) after them; thus after axion, 1 Corinthians 16:4; elace, Luke 1:9 (1 Samuel 14:47); exaporoumai, 2 Corinthians 1:8. [b]. for the simple expletive (i.e. ‘complementary’) or (as it is commonly called) epexegetical infinite, which serves to fill out an incomplete idea expressed by a noun or a verb or a phrase (where in German zu is commonly used); thus after proqumia, 2 Corinthians 8:11; bradeiv, Luke 24:25; elpiv, Acts 27:20; 1 Corinthians 9:10 (not Rec.); ezhtei eukairian, Luke 22:6 (not L marginal reading); oJ kairov (namely, esti) tou arxasqai, to begin, 1 Peter 4:17 (kairon cein with the simple infinitive Hebrews 11:15); didonai thn exousian, Luke 10:19 (exousian ecein with simple infinitive, John 19:10; 1 Corinthians 9:4); ofeiletai esmen (equivalent to ofeilomen), Romans 8:12 (with an infinitive alone, Galatians 5:3); eJtoimon einai, Acts 23:15 (1 Macc. 3:58; 5:39; 13:31; with an infinitive alone, Luke 22:33); creian ecein, Hebrews 5:12; edwken ofqalmouv tou mh blepein kai wta tou mh akouein, that they should not see ... that they should not hear (cf. Buttmann, 267 (230)), Romans 11:8 (cein wta elsewhere always with a simple infinitive; see ouv, 2); eplhsqh oJ cronov tou tekein authn, at which she should be delivered (cf. Buttmann, the passage cited), Luke 1:57; eplhsqhsan hJmerai ... tou peritemein auton, that they should circumcise him (cf. Buttmann, the passage cited), Luke 2:21; after anendekton estin, Luke 17:1 (so 216 Buttmann, sec. 140, 15; (Winer’s Grammar, 328 (308) otherwise)); quite unusually after egeneto (cf. Buttmann, sec. 140, 16 [d.]; Winer’s Grammar, the passage cited), Acts 10:25 (Rec. omits the article). [g]. after verbs of deciding, entreating, exhorting, commanding, etc.: after krinein (see krinw, 4); egeneto gnwmh (gnwmhv T Tr WH (see ginomai, 5 e. a.)), Acts 20:3; to proswpon esthrixen, Luke 9:51; suntiqesqai, Acts 23:20 (with an infinitive alone, Luke 22:5); proseucesqai, James 5:17; parakalein, Acts 21:12; entellesqai, Luke 4:10; epistellein, Acts 15:20 (with an infinitive alone, Acts 21:25 (R G T, but L Tr text WH here epesteilamen; Buttmann, 270 (232))); kataneuein, Luke 5:7. [d]. after verbs of hindering, restraining, removing (which naturally require the genitive), and according to the well-known pleonasm with mh before the infinitive (see mh, I. 4 a.; Buttmann, sec. 148, 13; Winer’s Grammar, 325 (305)); thus, after katecw tina, Luke 4:42; kratoumai, Luke 24:16; kwluw, Acts 10:47; uJpostellomai, Acts 20:20,27; pauw, 1 Peter 3:10; katapauw, Acts 14:18; without mh before the infinitive after egkoptomai, Romans 15:22. [e]. tou with an infinitive is added as a somewhat loose epexegesis: Luke 21:22; Acts 9:15; 13:47; Philippians 3:21; eiv akaqarsian tou atimazesqai ta swmata autwn, to the uncleanness of their bodies being dishonored, Romans 1:24 (cf. Buttmann, sec. 140, 14); Winer’s Grammar, 325f (305f). [z.] it takes the place of an entire final clause, “in order that” (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 44, 4 b.; Buttmann, sec. 140, 17); especially after verbs implying motion: Matthew 2:13; 3:13; 13:3; 24:45; Mark 4:3 (where L T WH omit; Tr brackets tou); Luke 1:77,79; 2:24,27; 5:1 (R G L text Tr marginal reading); 8:5; 12:42 (here L omits; Tr brackets tou); 22:31; 24:29; Acts 3:2; 20:30; 26:18; Romans 6:6; 11:10; Galatians 3:10; Philippians 3:10; Hebrews 10:7,9; 11:5. hJ. used of result “so that”: Acts 7:19; Romans 7:3; after poiw, “to cause that, make to,” Acts 3:12; (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 326 (306); Buttmann, sec. 140, 16 [d].).

7. The article with adverbs (Buttmann, sec. 125, 10f; Winer’s Grammar, sec. 18, 3), 217

a. gives them the force of substantives; as, to peran, the region beyond; ta anw, ta katw, to nun, ta emprosqen, ta opisw, etc.; see these words in their proper places.

b. is used when they stand adjectivally, as hJ anw IJerousalhm, oJ tote kosmov, oJ esw anqrwpov, oJ nun aiwn, etc., on which see these several words. c. the neuter to is used in the accusative absolute, especially in specifications of time: both with adverbs of time, to palin, 2 Corinthians 13:2; ta nun or tanun, and with neuter adjectives used adverbially, as to loipon, to proteron (John 6:62; Galatians 4:13); to prwton (John 10:40; 12:16; 19:39); to pleiston (1 Corinthians 14:2;); see these words themselves.

8. The article before prepositions with their cases is very often so used that wn, ontev, onta, must be supplied in thought (cf. Buttmann, sec. 125, 9; Winer’s Grammar, sec. 18, 3); thus, oJi apo Italiav, apo Qessalonikhv, Acts 17:13; Hebrews 13:24 (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 66, 6); oJ en tini, Matthew 6:9; Romans 8:1; neuter ta prov, Mark 2:2; oJi ek tinov, Romans 2:8; 4:14,16; Philippians 4:22 etc.; oJi para tinov, Mark 3:21 (see para, I.e.). ta peri tinov, Luke 24:19; Acts 24:10; Philippians 1:27; (add, ta (T Tr WH to) peri emou, Luke 22:37), etc. (see peri, I. b. [b.]); ta peri tina, Philippians 2:23 (see peri, II. b.); oJi meta tinov, those with one, his companions, Matthew 12:3; oJi peri tina, and many other examples which are given under the several prepositions. the neuter to in the accusative absolute in adverbial expressions (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 230 (216); Buttmann, sections 125, 12; 131, 9): to kaq’ hJmeran, “daily, day by day,” Luke 11:3; 19:47; Acts 17:11 (R G WH brackets); to kaqolou, “at all,” Acts 4:18 (L T WH omit to); besides, in to kata sarka, as respects human origin, Romans 9:5 (on the force of the article here see Abbot in the Journal of the Society for Biblical Literature, etc. for 1883, p. 108); ta kat’ eme, as respects what relates to me, my state, my affairs, Colossians 4:7; Ephesians 6:21; to ex uJmwn, as far as depends on you, Romans 12:18; to ef’ uJmin, as far as respects you, if I regard you, Romans 16:19 R G; ta prov (ton) Qeon, the accusative absolute, as respects the things pertaining to God, i.e. in things pertaining to God, Romans 15:17; Hebrews 2:17; 5:1 (iJerei ta prov touv Qeouv, strathgw de ta prov touv anqrwpouv, Xenophon, resp. Laced. 13, 11; cf. Fritzsche, Ep. ad Romans, iii., p. 262f); to ek 218 merouv namely, on, that which has been granted us in part, that which is imperfect, 1 Corinthians 13:10.

9. The article, in all genders, when placed before the genitive of substantives indicates “kinship, affinity, or some kind of connection, association or fellowship, or in general that which in some way pertains to a person or thing” (cf Winer’s Grammar, sec. 30, 3; Buttmann, sec. 125, 7);

a. the masculine and the feminine article: Iakwbov oJ tou Zebedaiou, oJ tou Alfaiou, the son, Matthew 10:2 (3), 3; Maria hJ tou Iakwbou, the mother, Mark 16:1 (T omits; Tr brackets tou); Luke 24:10 (L T Tr WH); Emmor tou Sucem, of Hamor, the father of Shechem, Acts 7:16 R G; hJ tou Ouriou, the wife, Matthew 1:6; oJi Clohv, either the kinsfolk, or friends, or domestics, or work-people, or slaves, of Chloe, 1 Corinthians 1:11; also oJi Aristoboulou, oJi Narkissou, Romans 16:10f; oJi tou Cristou, the followers of Christ (A.V. “they that are Christ’s”), 1 Corinthians 15:23 G L T Tr WH; Galatians 5:24; oJi twn Farisaiwn, the disciples of the Pharisees, Mark 2:18a Rec., 18b R G L; Kaisareia hJ Filippou, the city of Philip, Mark 8:27.

b. to and ta tinov: as ta tou Qeou, the cause or interests, the purposes, of God, opposed to ta twn anqrwpwn, Matthew 16:23; Mark 8:33; in the same sense ta tou kuriou, opposed to ta tou kosmou, 1 Corinthians 7:32-34; ta thv sarkov, ta tou pneumatov, Romans 8:5; ta uJmwn, your possessions, 2 Corinthians 12:14; zhtein to or ta tinov, 1 Corinthians 10:24; 13:5; Philippians 2:21; ta thv eirhnhv, thv oikodomhv, which make for, Romans 14:19; ta thv asqeneiav mou, which pertain to my weakness, 2 Corinthians 11:30; ta Kaisarov, ta tou Qeou, due to Caesar, due to God, Matthew 22:21; Mark 12:17; Luke 20:25; ta tou nhpiou, the things wont to be thought, said, done, by a child, 1 Corinthians 13:11; ta tinov, the house of one (ta Lukwnov, Theocritus, 2, 76; (eiv ta tou adelfou, Lysias

c. Eratosthenes sec. 12, p. 195); cf. en toiv patrikoiv, in her father’s house, Sir. 42:10; (Chrysost. hom. 52:(on Genesis 26:16), vol. iv. part ii. col. 458, Migne edition; Genesis 41:51; Esther 7:9, (Hebrew tyiBæ); Job 18:19 (Hebrew rWgm;))); with the name of a deity, “the 219 temple” (ta tou Diov, Josephus, contra Apion 1, 18, 2; also to tou Diov, Lycurgus, adverb, Leocr., p. 231 ((orat. Attic, p. 167, 15))), Luke 2:49 (see other examples in Lob. ad Phryn., p. 100). ta tou nomou, the precepts of the (Mosaic) law, Romans 2:14; to thv paroimiav, the (saying) of (that which is said in) the proverb, 2 Peter 2:22; ta twn daimonizomenwn, what the possessed had done and experienced, Matthew 8:33; to thv sukhv, what has been done to the fig-tree, Matthew 21:21.

10. The neuter to is put

a. before entire sentences, and sums them up into one conception (Buttmann, sec. 125, 13; Winer’s Grammar, 109 (103f)): eipen autw to Ei dunasai pisteusai, said to him this: ‘If thou canst believe,’ Mark 9:23 (but L T Tr WH to Ei dunh ‘If thou canst!’); cf. Bleek at the passage; (Riddell, The Apology etc. Digest of Idioms sec. 19 [g].). before the sayings and precepts of the O.T. quoted in the New: to Ou foneuseiv, the precept, ‘Thou shalt not kill’, Matthew 19:18; add, Luke 22:37 (where Lachmann oJti for to); Romans 13:9; (1 Corinthians 4:6 L T Tr WH); Galatians 5:14. before indirect questions: to tiv etc., to ti etc., to pwv etc., Luke 1:62; 9:46; 19:48; 22:2,4,23f; Acts 4:21; 22:30; Romans 8:26; 1 Thessalonians 4:1; cf. Matthiae, sec. 280; Krüger, sec. 50, 6, 10; Passow, ii., p. 395b; (Liddell and Scott, under the word, B. I. 3f).

b. before single words which are explained as parts of some discourse or statement (references as above): to Agar, the name Agar, Galatians 4:25 (T L text WH marginal reading omit; Tr brackets Agar); to ‘anebh’, this word anebh, Ephesians 4:9 (cf. Lightfoot on Galatians, the passage cited); to eti aJpax, Hebrews 12:27; cf. Matthiae, 2, p. 731f, 11. We find the unusual expression ouai (apparently because the interjection was to the writer a substitute for the term hJ plhgh or hJ qliyiv (Winer’s Grammar, 179 (169))), misery, calamity (A.V. “the Woe”), in Revelation 9:12; 11:14.

III. Since it is the business, not of the lexicographer, but of the grammarian, to exhibit the instances in which the article is omitted in the N.T. where according to the laws of our language it would have been expected, we refer those interested in this matter to the Grammars of Winer (sec. 19) and Alex. Buttmann (sec. 124, 8) (cf. also Green, chapter 220 ii. sec. iii.; Middleton, The Doctrine of the Greek Article (edited by Rose), pp. 41ff, 94f; and, particularly with reference to Granville Sharp’s doctrine (Remarks on the uses of the Def. Art. in the Greek Text of the N.T., 3rd edition 1803), a tract by C. Winstanley (A Vindication etc.) republished at Cambr. 1819), and only add the following remarks:

1. More or less frequently the article is lacking before appellatives of persons or things of which only one of the kind exists, so that the article is not needed to distinguish the individual from others of the same kind, as hJliov, gh, Qeov, Cristov, pneuma aJgion, zwh aiwniov, qanatov, nekroi (of the whole assembly of the dead (see nekrov, 1 b., p. 423b)); and also of those persons and things which the connection of discourse clearly shows to be well-defined, as nomov (the Mosaic law (see nomov, 2,

p. 428a)), kuriov, pathr, uJiov, anhr (husband), gunh (wife), etc.

2. Prepositions which with their cases designate a state and condition, or a place, or a mode of acting, usually have an anarthrous noun after them; as, eiv fulakhn, en fulakh, eiv aera, ek pistewv, kata sarka, ep’ elpidi, par’ elpida, ap’ agorav, ap’ agrou, an agrw, eiv oJdon, en hJmeraiv HJrwdou, eiv hJmeran apolutrwsewv, and numberless other examples.

ogdwv, ogdh, ogdon (from Homer down), “the eighth”: Luke 1:59; Acts 7:8; Revelation 17:11; 21:20; “our who has seven other companions, who with others is the eighth,” 2 Peter 2:5; so dekatov, “with nine others,” 2 Macc. 5:27; cf. Matthiae, sec. 469, 9; Viger. edition, Herm., p. 72f and 720f; Winer’s Grammar, sec. 37, 2; (Buttmann, 30 (26)).*

ogkov, oggdou, oJ (apparently from EGKW, enegkein, equivalent to fortov, see Buttmann, Lexil. i. 288ff (Fishlake’s translation, p. 151f), “whatever is prominent, protuberance, bulk, mass,” hence), “a burden, weight, encumbrance”: Hebrews 12:1. (In many other uses in Greek writings of all ages.)* (Synonyms: ogkov, barov, fortion: barov refers to “weight,” o. to “bulk,” and either may be oppressive (contra Tittmann); Barov “a load” in so far as it is heavy, fortion “a burden” in so far as it 221 is borne; hence, the fortion may be either ‘heavy’ (Matthew 23:4; Sir. 21:16), or ‘light’ (Matthew 11:30).)

oJde, hJdh, tode (from the old demonstrative pronoun oJ, hJ, to, and the enclitic de) (from Homer down), “this one here,” Latin hicce, haecce, hocce; a. it refers to what precedes: Luke 10:39 and Rec. in 16:25; tade panta, 2 Corinthians 12:19 Griesbach; to what follows: neuter plural tade, “these” (viz. “the following”) “things, as follows, thus,” introducing words spoken, Acts 15:23 R G; tade legei etc., Acts 21:11; Revelation 2:1,8,12,18; 3:1,7,14. b. eiv thnde thn polin (where we say “into this or that city”) (the writer not knowing what particular city the speakers he introduces would name), James 4:13 (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 162 (153), who adduces as similar thnde thn hJmeran, Plutarch, symp. 1, 6, 1; (but see Lünemann’s addition to Winer’s and especially Buttmann, sec. 127, 2)).*

oJdeuw; (oJdov); “to travel, journey”: Luke 10:33. (Homer Iliad 11,569; Xenophon, an. 7, 8, 8; Josephus, Antiquities 19, 4, 2; b. j. 3, 6,3; Herodian, 7, 3, 9 (4 edition, Bekker); Plutarch, others; Tobit 6:6.) (Compare: diodeuw, sunodeuw.)*

oJdhgew, oJdhgw; future oJdhghsw; 1 aorist subjunctive 3 person singular oJdhghsh; (oJdhgov, which see); the Septuagint chiefly for hj;n;, also for Ëyrid]hi, Ëylwho, etc.; a. properly, “to be a guide, lead on one’s way, to guide”: tina, Matthew 15:14; Luke 6:39; tina epi ti, Revelation 7:17; (Aeschylus, Euripides, Diodorus, Alciphron, Babrius, others). b. tropically, “to be a guide or teacher; to give guidance to”: tina, Acts 8:31 (Plutarch, mor. 954 b.); eiv thn alhqeian, John 16:13 (R G L Tr WH text (see below)) (oJdhghson me epi thn alhqeian sou kai didaxon me, Psalm 24:5 (25:5) (followed by eiv and prov in the Teaching of the Apostles, chapter 3)); followed by en, with the dative of the thing in which one gives guidance, instruction or assistance to another, en th alhqeia, John 16:13 T WH marginal reading (see above) (oJdhghson me en th oJdw sou kai poreusomai en th alhqeia sou, Psalm 85:11 (Psalm 86:11); cf. <19B803>Psalm 118:35 (<19B935>Psalm 119:35); Sap. 9:11; 10:17).*

oJdhgov, oJdhgou, oJ (oJdov and hJgeomait; cf. corhgov), “a leader of the way, a guide”; 222

a. properly: Acts 1:16 (Polybius 5, 5, 15; Plutarch, Alex. 27; 1 Macc. 4:2; 2 Macc. 5:15).

b. in figurative and sententious discourse oJdhgov tuflwn, i.e. like one who is literally so called, namely “a teacher of the ignorant and unexperienced,” Romans 2:19; plural, tufloi ... oJdhgoi tuflwn, i.e. like blind guides in the literal sense, in that, while themselves destitute of a knowledge of the truth, they offer themselves to others as teachers, Matthew 15:14; 23:16,24.*

oJdoiporew, oJdoiporw; (oJdoiporov a wayfarer, traveller); “to travel, journey”: Acts 10:9. (Herodotus, Sophocles, Xenophon, Aelian

v. h. 10, 4; Herodian, 7, 9, 1, others.)*

oJdoiporia, oJdoiporiav, hJ (oJdoiporov), “a journey, journeying”: John 4:6; 2 Corinthians 11:26. (Sap. 13:18; 18:3; 1 Macc. 6:41; Herodotus, Xenophon, Diodorus 5, 29; Herodian, others.)* oJdopoiew, oJdopoiw; in Greek writings from Xenophon down, “to make a road; to level, make passable, smooth, open, a way”; and so also in the Septuagint: wJdopoihse tribon th orgh autou, for slep,i Psalm 77:50 (78:50); for llæs;, to construct a lever way by casting up an embankment, Job 30:12; Psalm 67:5 (Psalm 68:5); for hN;pi, Psalm 79:10 (Psalm 80:10); for hN;pi Ër,d,, Isaiah 62:10; — and so, at least apparently, in Mark 2:23 L Tr marginal reading WH marginal reading (see poiew, I. 1 a. and c.) (with oJdon added, Xenophon, anab. 4, 8, 8).*

oJdov, oJdou, hJ (apparently from the root, ED, to go (Latin adire, accedere), allied with Latin solum; Curtius, sec. 281); the Septuagint numberless times for Ër,d,, less frequently for jræao; (from Homer down); “a way”;

1. properly,

a. “a travelled way, road”: Matthew 2:12; 7:13f; 13:4,19; Mark 4:4,15; 10:46; Luke 8:5,12; 10:31; 18:35; 19:36; Acts 8:26; 9:17; James 2:25, etc.; kata thn oJdon (as ye pass along the way (see kata,

II. 1 a.)) “by the way, on the way,” Luke 10:4; Acts 8:36; 25:3; 26:13; sabbatou oJdov (A.V. “a sabbath-day’s journey”) the distance that 223 one is allowed to travel on the sabbath, Acts 1:12 (see sabbaton, 1 a.). hJ oJdov with a genitive of the object, the way leading to a place (the Hebrew Ër,d, also is construed with a genitive, cf. Geseuius, Lehrgeb., p. 676 (Gr. sec. 112, 2; cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 30, 2)): eqnwn, Matthew 10:5; twn aJgiwn into the holy place, Hebrews 9:8, cf. 10:20, where the grace of God is symbolized by a way, cf. zaw, II. b. (tou xulou, Gcn. 3:24; Aiguptou ... Assuriwn, Jeremiah 2:18; ghv Filistieim, Exodus 13:17; tou Sina, Judith 5:14; Latin via mortis, Tibull. 1, 10, 4; cf. Kühner, ii., p. 286, 4). in imitation of the Hebrew Ër,d,, the accusative of which takes on almost the nature of a preposition, “in the way to, toward” (cf. Gesenius, Thesaurus, i., p. 352{a}), we find oJdon qalasshv in Matthew 4:15 from Isaiah 8:23 (Isaiah 9:1) (so oJdon (thv qalasshv, 1 Kings 18:43); ghv autwn, 1 Kings 8:48; 2 Chronicles 6:38; oJdon dusmwn hJliou, Deuteronomy 11:30; moreover, once with the accusative, oJdon qalassan eruqran, Numbers 14:25; (Deuteronomy 2:1); cf. Thiersch, De Alex. Pentateuchi versione, p. 145f; (Buttmann, sec. 131, 12)), with a genitive of the subject, “the way in which one walks”: en taiv oJdoiv autwn, Romans 3:16; eJtoimazein thn oJdon twn basilewn, Revelation 16:12; in metaphorical phrases, kateuqenein thn oJdon tinov, to remove the hindrances to the journey, 1 Thessalonians 3:11; eJtoimazein (and euqunein, John 1:23; kataskeuazein, Matthew 11:10; Mark 1:2; Luke 7:27) thn oJdon tou kuriou, see eJtoimazw.

b. “a traveller’s way, journey, travelling”: en th oJdw, on the journey, on the road, Matthew 5:25; 15:32; 20:17; Mark 8:27; 9:33; 10:32,52; Luke 12:58; 24:32,35; Acts 9:27; ex oJdou, from a journey, Luke 11:6; airein or ktasqai ti eiv oJdon, Matthew 10:10; Mark 6:8, and eiv thn oJdon, Luke 9:3; poreuomai thn oJdon, to make a journey (Xenophon, Cyril 5, 2, 22), with autou added (A.V. “to go on one’s way”), to continue the journey undertaken, Acts 8:39; oJdov hJmerav, a journey requiring a (single) day for its completion, used also, like our “a day’s journey, as a measure of distance,” Luke 2:41 (Genesis 30:36; 31:23; Exodus 3:18; Judith 2:21; 1 Macc. 5:24; 7:45; aopecein pampollwn hJmerwn oJdon, Xenophon, Cyril 1, 1, 3, cf. Herodotus 4, 101 (Winer’s Grammar, 188 (177))); on the phrase oJdon poiein, Mark 2:23 see poiew, I. 1 a. and c.

2. Metaphorically, 224

a. according to the familiar figure of speech, especially frequent in Hebrew (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 32) and not unknown to the Greeks, by which an action is spoken of as a “proceeding” (cf. the German Wandel), oJdov denotes a course of conduct, “a way (i.e. manner) of thinking, feeling, deciding”: a person is said oJdon deiknunai tini, who shows him how to obtain a thing, what helps he must use, 1 Corinthians 12:31; with a genitive of the object, i.e. of the thing to be obtained, eirhnhv, Romans 3:17; zwhv, Acts 2:28; swthriav, Acts 16:17; with a genitive of the subjunctive, thv dikaiosunhv, the way which hJ dikaiosunh points out and which is accustomed to characterize hJ dikaiosunh, so in Matthew 21:32 (on which see dikaiosunh, 1 b., p. 149{a} bottom); used of the Christian religion, 2 Peter 2:21; likewise thv alhqeiav, 2 Peter 2:2; with the genitive of the person deciding and acting, James 5:20; tou Kain, Jude 1:11; tou Balaam, 2 Peter 2:15; en pasaiv taiv oJdoiv autou, in all his purposes and actions, James 1:8; tav oJdouv mou en Cristw, the methods which I as Christ’s minister and apostle follow in the discharge of my office, 1 Corinthians 4:17; those are said poreuesqai taiv oJdoiv autwn (“to walk in their own ways”) who take the course which pleases them, even though it be a perverse one, Acts 14:16 (on the dative see poreuw, under the end); aJi oJdoi tou Qeou or kuriou, the purposes and ordinances of God, his ways of dealing with men, Acts 13:10; Romans 11:33; Revelation 15:3 (Hosea 14:9; Psalm 94:10 (Psalm 95:10); 144:17 (<19E517>Psalm 145:17); Sir. 39:24; Tobit 3:2, etc.). hJ oJdov tou Qeou, the course of thought, feeling, action, prescribed and approved by God: Matthew 22:16; Mark 12:14; Luke 20:21; used of the Christian religion, Acts 18:26; also hJ oJdov tou kuriou, Acts 18:25; oJdov used generally of a method of knowing and worshipping God, Acts 22:4; 24:14; hJ oJdov simply, of the Christian religion (cf. Buttmann, 163 (142)), Acts 9:2; 19:9,23; 24:22.

b. in the saying of Christ, egw eimi hJ oJdov “I am the way” by which one passes, i.e. with whom all who seek approach to God must enter into closest fellowship, John 14:6. (On the omission of oJdov in certain formulas and phrases (Luke 5:19; 19:4), see Winer’s Grammar, 590f (549f); Buttmann, sec. 123, 8; Bos, Ellipses etc. (edited by Schaefer), p. 331f.) 225

odouv (according to Etymologicum Magnum 615, 21 (Pollux 6, 38) from edw, Latin edere, etc., cf. Curtius, sec. 289; others from the root, da, to divide, cf. daiw, daknw; (Latin dens); Fick i., p. 100), odontov, oJ, from Homer down; the Septuagint for ˆve; “a tooth”: Matthew 5:38; Mark 9:18; Acts 7:54; plural Revelation 9:8; oJ brugmov twn odontwn, see brugmov.*

odunaw, odunw: present indicative passive odunwmai; present indicative middle 2 person singular odunasai (see katakaucaomai), participle odunwmenov; (odunh); “to cause intense pain”; passive “to be in anguish, be tormented”: Luke 16:24f; middle “to torment or distress oneself” (A.V. “to sorrow”), Luke 2:48; epi tini, Acts 20:38. (Aristophanes, Sophocles, Euripides, Plato, others; the Septuagint.)*
odunh (perhaps allied with edw; “consuming” grief; cf. Latin curae edaces), odunhv, hJ, “pain, sorrow”: Romans 9:2; 1 Timothy 6:10. (From Homer down; the Septuagint.)*

odurmov, odurmou, oJ (oduromai to wail, lament (see klaiw, at the end)), “a wailing, lamentation, mourning”: Matthew 2:18 (from Jeremiah 38:15 (Jeremiah 31:15) for µyriWrm]Tæ); 2 Corinthians 7:7. (2 Macc. 11:6; Aeschylus, Euripides, Plato, Josephus, Plutarch, Aelian

v. h. 14, 22.)*

Oziav (L T Tr WH Ozeiav (cf. Tdf. Proleg., p. 84; WH’s Appendix, p. 155, and see ei, i)), Oziou (but cf. Buttmann, 18 (16)), oJ, (hY;Z[u and WhY;Z[u, strength of Jehovah, or my strength is Jehovah), “Ozias or Uzziah,” son of Amaziah, king of Judah (circa) B. C. 811-759 (2 Kings 15:30ff): Matthew 1:8f, where the Evangelist ought to have preserved this order: Iwram, Ocoziav, Iwav, Amaziav, Oziav. He seems therefore to have confounded Ocoziav and Oziav; see another example of (apparent) confusion under Ieconiav. (But Matthew has simply omitted three links; such omissions were not uncommon, cf. e.g. 1 Chronicles 6:3ff and Ezra 7:1ff See the commentators.)*

ozw; (from root od, cf. Latin and English “odor” etc.; Curtius, sec. 288); from Homer down; “to give out an odor (either good or bad), to smell, emit a smell”: of a decaying corpse, John 11:39; cf. Exodus 8:14.* 226

oJqen (from the relative pronoun oJ and the enclitic qen which denotes motion from a place) (from Homer down), adverb, “from which; whence”; it is used

a. of the place from which: Matthew 12:44; Luke 11:24; Acts 14:26; 28:13; by attraction for ekeiqen oJpou etc., Matthew 25:24,26; cf. Buttmann, sec. 143, 12; (Winer’s Grammar, 159 (150)).

b. of the source from which a thing is known, “from which, whereby”: 1 John 2:18.

c. of the cause from which, “for which reason, wherefore, on which account” (A.V. “whereupon” (in the first two instances)): Matthew 14:7; Acts 26:19; Hebrews 2:17; 3:1; 7:25; 8:3; 9:18; 11:19; often in the last three books of Macc.*
oqonh, oqonhv, hJ (from Homer down); a. “linen” (i.e. fine white linen for women’s clothing; cf. Vanicek, Fremdwörter, under the word). b. “linen cloth” (sheet or sail); so Acts 10:11; 11:5.*

oqonion, oqoniou, to (diminutive of oqonh, which see), “a piece of linen, small linen cloth”: plural strips of linen cloth for swathing the dead, Luke 24:12 (T omits; L Tr brackets WH reject the verse); John 19:40; 20:5-7. (In Greek writings of ships’ sails made of linen, bandages for wounds, and other articles; the Septuagint for ˆydis;, Judges 14:13; for ht,v]pi or tv,pe, Hosea 2:5(7),9(11).)*

oikeiov, oikeia, oikeion (oikov), from Hesiod down, “belonging to a house or family, domestic, intimate”: belonging to one’s household, “related by blood, kindred,” 1 Timothy 5:8; oikeioi tou Qeou, belonging to God’s household, i.e. to the theocracy, Ephesians 2:19; in a wider sense, with a genitive of the thing, “belonging to, devoted to, adherents of” a thing, oJi oikeioi thv pistewv, professors of the (Christian) faith, Galatians 6:10 (but others associate this passage with that from Ephesians as above; see Lightfoot at the passage); so oikeiov filosofiav, Strabo 1, p. 13 b. (1, 17 edition Sieben.); gewgrafiav, p. 25 a. (1, 34 edition Sieben.); oligarciav, Diodorus 13, 91; turannidov, 227 19, 70. (The Septuagint for raev], related by blood; dwOD, 1 Samuel 10:14ff; hr;a}v,æ consanguinity, Leviticus 18:17; oikeiov tou spermatov for rc;B;, Isaiah 58:7.)* oiketeia (others, oiketeia, cf. Chandler sec. 99ff), oiketeiav, hJ (oikethv, which see), “household i.e. body of servants” (Macrobius, Appuleius (160 A. D.) famulitium, German Dienerschaft): Matthew 24:45 L T Tr WH. (Strabo, Lucian, Inscriptions; plural Josephus, Antiquities 12, 2, 3),*

oikethv, oiketou, oJ (oikew), from (Aeschylus and) Herodotus down, Latin domesticus, i.e. one who lives in the same house with another, spoken of all who are under the authority of one and the same householder, Sir. 4:30; 6:11, especially “a servant, domestic”; so in Luke 16:13; Acts 10:7; Romans 14:4; 1 Peter 2:18; the Septuagint for db,[., See more fully on the word, Meyer on Romans, the passage cited (where he remarks that oikethv is a more restricted term than doulov, designating a “house-servant,” one holding closer relations to the family than other slaves; cf. diakonov at the end, Schmidt, chapter 162.)*

oikew, oikw; (oikov); from Homer down; the Septuagint for bvæy;, a few times for ˆkæv;; Latin habito (transitive), “to dwell in”: ti (Herodotus and often in Attic), 1 Timothy 6:16; (intransitive, “to dwell”), meta tinov, with one (of the husband and wife), 1 Corinthians 7:12f; tropically, (en tini, to be fixed and operative in one’s soul: of sin, Romans 7:17f,20; of the Holy Spirit, Romans 8:(9),11; 1 Corinthians 3:16. (Compare: enoikew, katoikew, enkatoikew, paroikew, perioikew, sunoikew.)*

oikhma, oikhmatov, to, from (Pindar and) Herodotus down, “a dwelling-place, habitation”; euphemistically “a prison” (R.V. “cell”), Acts 12:7, as in Thucydides 4, 47f; Demosthenes, Lucian, Tox. 29; Plutarch, Agis 19; Aelian v. h. 6, 1.*

oikhthrion, oikhthriou, to (oikhthr), “a dwelling-place, habitation”: Jude 1:6; of the body as the dwelling-place of the spirit, 2 Corinthians 5:2 (2 Macc. 11:2; 3 Macc. 2:15; (Josephus, contra Apion 1, 20, 7); Euripides, Plutarch, Cebes (399 B. C.) tab. 17).* 228

oikia, oikiav, hJ (oikov), the Septuagint for tyiBæ (from Herodotus down), “a house”; a. properly, an inhabited edifice, a dwelling: Matthew 2:11; 7:24-27; Mark 1:29; Luke 15:8; John 12:3; Acts 4:34; 1 Corinthians 11:22; 2 Timothy 2:20, and often; oJi en th oikia namely, ontev, Matthew 5:15; oJi ek thv oikiav with the genitive of person, Philippians 4:22; hJ oikia tou (patrov mou) Qeou, i.e. heaven,. John 14:2; of the body as the habitation of the soul, 2 Corinthians 5:1. b. “the inmates of a house, the family”: Matthew 12:25; hJ oikia tinov, the household, the family of anyone, John 4:53; 1 Corinthians 16:15 (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 58, 4; Buttmann, sec. 129, 8 a.);. universally, for persons dwelling in the house, Matthew 10:13. c. “property, wealth, goods” (cf. Latin res familiaris): tinov, Matthew 23:14 (13) Rec. (cf. Wetstein (1752) at the passage); Mark 12:40; Luke 20:47; so oikov in Homer (as Odyssey 2, 237 katedousi biaiwv oikon Odusshov, cf. 4, 318), in Herodotus 3, 53 and in Attic; Hebrew tyiBæ, Genesis 45:18 (the Septuagint ta uJparconta); Esther 8:1 (the Septuagint oJsa uJphrcen). Not found in Revelation (Synonym: see oikov, at the end)
oikodespotew, oikodespotw; (oikodespothv); “to be master (or head) of a house; to rule a household, manage family affairs”: 1 Timothy 5:14. (A later Greek word; see Lob. ad Phryn., p. 373.)*

oikodespothv, oikodespotou, oJ (oikov, despothv), “master of a house, householder”: Matthew 10:25; 13:27; 20:11; 24:43; Mark 14:14; Luke 12:39; 13:25; 14:21; anqrwpov oikodespothv (see anqrwpov, 4 a.), Matthew 13:52; 20:1; 21:33; oikodespothv thv oikiav, Luke 22:11, on this pleonasm cf. Bornemann, Schol. at the passage; Winer’s Grammar, sec. 65, 2. (Alexis, a comic poet of the IV. century B. C. quoted in Pollux 10, 4, 21; Josephus, contra Apion 2, 11, 3; Plutarch, quaest. Romans 30; Ignatius ad Ephesians 6. Lob. ad Phryn., p. 313 shows that the earlier Greeks said oikou or oikiav despothv.)* 229

oikodomew, oikodomw; imperfect wkodomoun; future oikodomhsw; 1 aorist wkodomhsa (oikodomhsa Tr WH in Acts 7:47; see Tdf. at the passage; Proleg., p. 120; WH’s Appendix, p. 161; Lob. ad Phryn., p. 153; Winer’s Grammar, sec. 12, 4; Buttmann, 34 (30)); passive (present oikodomoumai (infinitive [oikodomeisthai], Luke 6:48 Treg.); perfect infinitive oikodomhsqai (Luke 6:48 T WH)); pluperfect 3 person singular wkodomhto; 1 aorist wkodomhqhn (oikodomhqhn, T WH in John 2:20); 1 future oikodomhqhsomai; (oikodomov, which see); from Herodotus down; the Septuagint for hn;B;; “to build a house. erect a building”;

a. properly, [a]. “to build” (up from the foundation): absolutely, Luke 11:48 G T WH Tr text 14:30; 17:28; oJi oikodomountev, a substantive, “the builders” (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 45, 7; Buttmann, sec. 144, 11), Matthew 21:42; Mark 12:10; Luke 20:17; Acts 4:11 Rec.; 1 Peter 2:7, from <19B702>Psalm 117:22 (Psalm 118); ep’ allotrion qemelion, to build upon a foundation laid by others, i.e. (without a figure) to carry on instruction begun by others, Romans 15:20; oikodomein ti, Galatians 2:18; purgon, Matthew 21:33; Mark 12:1; Luke 14:28; apoqhkav, Luke 12:18; naon, Mark 14:58; passive John 2:20 (on the aorist cf. 2 Esdr. 5:16); oikon, passive, 1 Peter 2:5 ((here T epoikon), cf. Winer’s Grammar, 603 (561), and add oikourgein ta kata ton oikon, Clement of Rome, 1 Corinthians 1, 3); (oikian, Luke 6:48 (cf. Winer’s Grammar, the passage cited)); sunagwghn or oikon tini, for the use of or in honor of one, Luke 7:5; Acts 7:47,49 (Genesis 8:20; Ezekiel 16:24); oikian epi ti, Matthew 7:24,26; Luke 6:49; polin ep’ orouv, Luke 4:29. [b]. contextually equivalent to “to restore by building, to rebuild, repair”: ti, Matthew 23:29; 26:61; 27:40; Mark 15:29; Luke 11:47 and R (L brackets Tr marginal reading) in 48.

b. metaphorically, [a]. equivalent to “to found”: epi tauth th petra oikodomhsw mou thn ekklhsian, i.e. by reason of the strength of thy faith thou shalt be my principal support in the establishment of my church, Matthew 16:18. 230 [b]. Since both a Christian church and individual Christians are likened to a building or temple in which God or the Holy Spirit dwells (1 Corinthians 3:9,16ff; 2 Corinthians 6:16; Ephesians 2:21), the erection of which temple will not be completely finished till the return of Christ from heaven, those who, by action, instruction, exhortation, comfort, promote the Christian wisdom of others and help them to live a correspondent life are regarded as taking part in the erection of that building, and hence, are said oikodomein, i.e. (dropping the figure) “to promote growth in Christian wisdom, affection, grace, virtue, holiness, blessedness”: absolutely, Acts 20:32 L T Tr WH; 1 Corinthians 8:1; 10:23; tina, 14:4; 1 Thessalonians 5:11; passive “to grow in wisdom, piety,” etc., Acts 9:31; 1 Corinthians 14:17; universally, “to give one strength and courage, dispose to”: eiv thn pistin, Polycarp, edition Philip. 3, 2 (yet here “to be built up into” (in) etc.); even to do what is wrong (A.V. “embolden”), eiv to ta eidwloquta esqiein, 1 Corinthians 8:10 (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 39, 3 N. 3). This metaphorical use of the verb Paul, in the opinion of Fritzsche (Ep. ad Romans, iii., p. 205f), did not derive from the figure, of building a temple, but from the O.T., where “hn;B; and sræh; with an accusative of the person (to build one up and to pull one down) denote “to bless and to ruin”; to prosper and to injure, anyone”; cf. Psalm 27:5 (Psalm 28:5); Jeremiah 24:6; 40:7 (Jeremiah 33:7). (Compare: anoikodomew, epoikodomew, sunoikodomew.)*

oikodomh, oikodomhv, hJ (oikov, and demw to build), a later Greek word, condemned by Phryn., yet used by Aristotle, Theophrastus, ((but both these thought to be doubtful)), Diodorus (1, 46), Philo (vit. Moys. i. sec. 40; de monarch. ii. sec. 2), Josephus, Plutarch, the Septuagint, and many others, for oikodomhma and oikodomhsiv; cf. Lob. ad Phryn., p. 481ff, cf. p. 421; (Winer’s Grammar, 24);

1. (the act of) “building, building up,” equivalent to to oikodomein; as, twn teicewn, 1 Macc. 16:23; tou oikou tou Qeou, 1 Chronicles 26:27; in the N.T. metaphorically, “edifying, edification, i.e. the act of one who promotes another’s growth in Christian wisdom, piety, holiness, happiness” (see oikodomew, b. b. (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 35 (34))): Romans 14:19; 15:2; (1 Corinthians 14:26); 2 Corinthians 10:8 (see below); 13:10; Ephesians 4:29; with a genitive of the person whose growth is furthered, uJmwn, 2 Corinthians 12:19 (cf. 10:8); eJautou 231 (Tdf. autou), Ephesians 4:16; tou swmatov tou Cristou, Ephesians 4:12; thv ekklhsiav, 1 Corinthians 14:12; equivalent to to oikodomoun, what contributes to edification, or augments wisdom, etc. lalein, labein, oikodomhn, 1 Corinthians 14:3,5.

2. equivalent to oikodomhma, “a building” (i.e. thing built, edifice): Mark 13:1f; tou iJerou, Matthew 24:1; used of the heavenly body, the abode of the soul after death, 2 Corinthians 5:1; tropically, of “a body of Christians, a Christian church” (see oikodomew, b. b.), Ephesians 2:21 (cf. pav, I. 1 c.); with a genitive of the owner or occupant, Qeou, 1 Corinthians 3:9.*

oikodomia, oikodomiav, hJ (oikodomew) (the act of) “buliding, erection” (Thucydides, Plato, Polybius, Plutarch, Lucian, etc.; but never in the Septuagint); metaphorically, oikodomian Qeou thn en pistei, the increase which God desires in faith (see oikodomh), 1 Timothy 1:4 Rec.bez elz; but see oikonomia. Not infrequent oikonomia and oikodomia are confounded in the manuscripts; see Grimm on 4 Maccabees, p. 365, cf. Hilgenfeld, the Epistle of Barnabas, p. 28; (D’Orville, Chariton 8, 1, p. 599).*

oikonomew, oikonomw; (oikonomov); “to be a steward; to manage the affairs of a household”: absolutely, Luke 16:2. (Univ. “to manage, dispense, order, regulate”: Sophocles, Xenophon, Plato, Polybius, Josephus, Plutarch, others; 2 Macc. 3:14.)*

oikonomia, oikonomiav, hJ (oikonomew), from Xenophon, and Plato down, “the management of a household or of household affairs; specifically, the management, oversight, administration, of others’ property; the office of a manager or overseer, stewardship”: Luke 16:24; hence, the word is transferred by Paul in a theocratic sense to the office (duty) intrusted to him by God (the lord and master) of proclaiming to men the blessings of the gospel, 1 Corinthians 9:17; hJ, oikonomia tou Qeou, “the office of administrator (stewardship) intrusted by God,” Colossians 1:25. universally, “administration, dispensation,” which in a theocratic sense is ascribed to God himself as providing for man’s 232 salvation: aJitinev ... hJ oikonomian Qeou thn en pistei, which furnish matter for disputes rather than the (knowledge of the) dispensation of the things by which God has provided for and prepared salvation, which salvation must be embraced by faith, 1 Timothy 1:4 L T Tr WH; hJn proeqeto ... kairwn, which good will he purposed to show with a view to (that) dispensation (of his) by which the times (namely, of infancy and immaturity cf. Galatians 4:1-4) were to be fulfilled, Ephesians 1:9f; hJ oikonomia thv caritov tou Qeou thv doqeishv moi, that dispensation (or arrangement) by which the grace of God was granted me, Ephesians 3:2; hJ oikonomia tou musthriou, the dispensation by which he carried out his secret purpose, Ephesians 3:9 G L T Tr WH.*

oikonomov, oikonomou, oJ (oikov, nemw (‘to dispense, manage’); Hesychius oJ thn oikon nemomenov), “the manager of a household or of household affairs; especially a steward, manager, superintendent” (whether free-born, or, as was usually the case, a freedman or slave) to whom the head of the house or proprietor has intrusted the management of his affairs, the care of receipts and expenditures, and the duty of dealing out the proper portion to every servant and even to the children not yet of age: Luke 12:42; 1 Corinthians 4:2; Galatians 4:2; “the manager of a farm or landed estate, an overseer” (A.V. “steward”): Luke 16:1,3,8; oJ oikonomov thv polewv, “the superintendent of the city’s finances, the treasurer of the city” (Vulgate arcarius civitatis): Romans 16:23 (of the treasurers or quaestors of kings, Esth. 8:9; 1 Esdr. 4:49; Josephus, Antiquities 12, 4, 7; 11, 6, 12; 8, 6, 4). Metaphorically, the apostles and other Christian teachers (see oikonomia) are called oikonomouv musthriwn tou Qeou, as those to whom the counsels of God have been committed to be made known to men: 1 Corinthians 4:1; a bishop (or overseer) is called oikonomov Qeou, of God as the head and master of the Christian theocracy (see oikov, 2), Titus 1:7; and any and every Christian who rightly uses the gifts intrusted to him by God for the good of his brethren, belongs to the class called kaloi oikonomoi poikilhv caritov Qeou, 1 Peter 4:10. (Aeschylus, Xenophon, Plato, Aristotle, others; for l[æ tyiBæ the Septuagint 1 Kings 4:6; 16:9, etc.)*

oikov, oikou, oJ (cf. Latin vicus, English ending “-wich”; Curtius, sec. 95), from Homer down; the Septuagint in numberless places for tyiBæ, also for lk;yhæ, a palace, lh,ao, a tent, etc.; 233

1. “a house”;

a. strictly, “an inhabited house” (differing thus from domov the building): Acts 2:2; 19:16; tinov, Matthew 9:6f; Mark 2:11; 5:38; Luke 1:23,40,56; 8:39,41, etc.; ercesqai eiv oikon, to come into a house (domurn venire), Mark 3:20 (19); eiv ton oikon, into the (i.e. “his or their”) house, “home,” Luke 7:10; 15:6; en tw oikw, in the (her) house, John 11:20; en oikw, at home, 1 Corinthians 11:34; 14:35; oJi eiv ton oikon(see eiv, C. 2), Luke 9:61; kat’ oikon, opposed to en tw iJerw, in a household assembly, “in private” (R.V. “at home”; see kata, II. 1 d.), Acts 2:46; 5:42; kat’ oikouv, opposed to dhmosia, in private houses (A.V. “from house to house”; see kata, II. 3 a.), Acts 20:20; kata touv oikouv eisporeuomenov, entering house after house, Acts 8:3; hJ kat’ oikon tinov ekklhsia, see ekklhsia, 4 b. aa.

b. “any building whatever”: emporiou, John 2:16; proseuchv, Matthew 21:13; Mark 11:17; Luke 19:46; tou basilewv, tou arcierewv, “the palace of” etc., Matthew 11:8; Luke 22:54 (here T Tr WH oikia); tou Qeou, the house where God was regarded as present — of the tabernacle, Matthew 12:4; Mark 2:26; Luke 6:4; of the temple at Jerusalem, Matthew 21:13; Mark 11:17; Luke 19:46; John 2:16f, (Isaiah 56:5, 7); cf. Luke 11:51; Acts 7:47,49; of the heavenly sanctuary, Hebrews 10:21 (oikov aJgiov Qeou, of heaven, Deuteronomy 26:15; Baruch 2:16); a body of Christians (a church), as pervaded by the Spirit and power of God, is called oikov pneumatikov, 1 Peter 2:5.

c. “any dwelling-place”: of the human body as the abode of demons that possess it, Matthew 12:44; Luke 11:24; (used in Greek authors also of tents and huts, and later, of the nests, stalls, lairs, of animals). universally, “the place where one has fixed his residence,” one’s “settled abode, domicile”: oikov uJmwn, of the city of Jerusalem, Matthew 23:38; Luke 13:35.

2. by metonymy, “the inmates of a house, all the persons forming one family, a household”: Luke 10:5; 11:17 (al: refer this to 1, and take epi either locally (see epi, C. I. 1), or of succession (see epi, C. I. 2 c.)); 19:9; Acts 7:10; 10:2; 11:14; 16:31; 18:8; 1 Corinthians 1:16; 1 Timothy 3:4f; 5:4; 2 Timothy 1:16; 4:19; Hebrews 11:7; plural, 1 Timothy 3:12; Titus 1:11 (so also Genesis 7:1; 47:12, and often in 234 Greek authors); metaphorically, and in a theocratic sense oJ oikov tou Qeou, “the family of God,” of the Christian church, 1 Timothy 3:15; 1 Peter 4:17; of the church of the Old and New Testament, Hebrews 3:2,5f (Numbers 12:7).

3. “stock, race, descendants” of one (A.V. “house”): oJ oikov Dauid, Luke 1:27,69; 2:4 (1 Kings 12:16); oikov Israhl, Matthew 10:6; 15:24; Luke 1:33; Acts 2:36; 7:42; ((oJ oikov Iakwb), 46 L T Tr marginal reading); Hebrews 8:8,10 (Jeremiah 38:31 (Jeremiah 31:31); Exodus 6:14; 12:3; 19:3; 1 Samuel 2:30; (cf. oJ sebastov oikov, Philo in Flac. sec. 4)). The word is not found in the Apocalypse. (Synonyms: oikov, oikia: in Attic (and especially legal) usage, oikov denotes one’s “household establishment, one’s entire property,” oikia, “the dwelling itself”; and in prose oikov is not used in the sense of oikia. In the sense of “family” oikov and oikia are alike employed; Schmidt vol. ii., chapter 80. In relation to distinctions (real or supposed) between oikov and oikia the following passages are of interest (cf. Valckenaer on Herodotus 7, 224): Xenophon, oecon. 1, 5 oikov de dh ti dokei hJmin keinai; ara oJper oikia, h kai oJsa tiv exw thv oikiav kekthtai, panta tou oikou tauta estin ... panta tou okou einai oJsa tiv kekthtai. Aristotle, polit. 1, 2, p. 1252{b}, 9ff, ek men oun toutwn twn duo koinwniwn (viz. of a man with wife and servant) oikia prwth, kai orqwv HJsiodov eipe poihsav “oikon men prootista] gunaika te boun t’ arothra.” ... hJ men oun eiv pasan hJmeran sunesthkuia koinwnia kata fusin oikov estin. ibid. 3, p. 1253{b}, 2ff, pasa poliv ek oikiwn sugkeitai. Oikiav de merh, ek wJn auqiv oikia sunistatai. Oikia de teleiov ek doulwn kai eleuqerwn ... prwta de kai elacista merh oikiav despothv kai doulov kai posiv kai alocov. Pathr kai tekna, etc. Plutarch, de audiend. poetis sec. 6 kai gar Oikon pote men thn oikian kalousin, “Oikon ev uJyorofon.” pote de thn ousian, “esqietai moi oikov.” (see oikia, c.) Hesychius’ Lexicon, under the words oikia, oikoi, under the word oikov. oligh oikia ... kai merov ti thv oikiav ... kai ta en th oikia. In the N.T., although the words appear at times to be used with some discrimination (e.g. Luke 10:5,6,7; Acts 16:31,32,34; cf. John 14:2), yet other passages seem to show that no distinction can be insisted upon: e.g. Matthew 9:23; Mark 5:38; Luke 7:36,37; Acts 10:17,(22,32); 17:5; 19:16; 21:8; 11:11,12,13; 16:15; (1 Corinthians 1:16; 16:15).) 235

oikoumenh, oikoumenhv, hJ (feminine of the present passive participle from oikew (namely, gh; cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 64, 5; Buttmann, sec. 123, 8));

1. “the inhabited earth”;

a. in Greek writings often “the portion of the earth inhabited by the Greeks,” in distinction from the lands of the barbarians, cf. Passow, ii., p. 415a; (Liddell and Scott, under the word, I.).

b. in the Greek authors who wrote about Roman affairs (like the Latin orbis terrarum) equivalent to “the Roman empire”: so pasa hJ oikoumenh contextually equivalent to all the subjects of this empire, Luke 2:1.

c. “the whole inhabited earth, the world” (so in (Hyperides, Eux. 42 (“probably” Liddell and Scott)) the Septuagint for lbeTe and er,a), : Luke 4:5; 21:26; Acts 24:5; Romans 10:18; Revelation 16:14; Hebrews 1:6 (pasa hJ oikoumenh, Josephus, b. j. 7, 3, 3); oJlh hJ oikoumenh, Matthew 24:14; Acts 11:28 (in the same sense Josephus, Antiquities 8, 13, 4 pasa hJ oikoumenh; cf. Bleek, Erklär. d. drei ersten Evv. i., p. 68); by metonymy, “the inhabitants of the earth, men”: Acts 17:6,31 (Psalm 9:9); 19:27; hJ oikoumenh oJlh, all mankind, Revelation 3:10; 12:9.

2. “the universe, the world”: Sap. 1:7 (alternating there with ta panta); hJ oikoumenh mellousa, that consummate state of all things which will exist after Christ’s return from heaven, Hebrews 2:5 (where the word alternates with panta and ta panta, Hebrews 2:8, which there is taken in an absolute sense).*
oikourgov, oikourgon (oikov, ERGW (cf. ergon), cf. ampelourgov, gewrgov, etc.), “caring for the house, working at home”: Titus 2:5 L T Tr WH; see the following word. Not found elsewhere.*

oikteirw; future (as if from oikteirew, a form which does not exist) as in the Septuagint oikteirhsw, for the earlier oikteirw, see Lob. ad Phryn., p. 741; (Veitch, under the word; Winer’s Grammar, 88 (84); Buttmann, 64 (56)); (from oiktov pity, and this from the interjection oi, “Oh!”); “to pity, have compassion on”: tina, Romans 9:15 (from Exodus 33:19. Homer, Tragg., Aristophanes, Xenophon, Plato, Demosthenes, Lucian, Plutarch, Aelian; the Septuagint for ˆnæj; and µjær)i . (Synonym: see elhw, at the end.)*

oiktirmov, oiktirmou, oJ (oikteirw), the Septuagint for µymij}ræ) (the viscera, which were thought to be the seat of compassion (see splagcnon, b.)), “compassion, pity, mercy”: splagcna oiktirmou (Rec. oiktirmwn), bowels in which compassion resides, “a heart of compassion,” Colossians 3:12; in the Scriptures mostly plural (conformably to the Hebrew µymij}ræ), “emotions, longings, manifestations of pity” (English “compassions”) (cf. Buttmann, sec. 132, 10; Winer’s Grammar, 237 (222))), the father of mercies i.e. most merciful, 2 Corinthians 1:3; joined with splagcna, Philippians 2:1. (Pindar, Pythagoras 1, 164.) (Synonym: see elhw, at the end.)*

oiktirmwn, oiktirmon, genitive oiktirmonov (okteirw), “merciful”: Luke 6:36; James 5:11. (Theocritus, 15, 75; Anth. 7, 359, 1 (Epigr. Anth. Pal. Append. 223, 5); the Septuagint for µWjræ.) (“In classic Greek only a poetic term for the more common elhemwn.” Schmidt iii., p. 580.)*

oinopothv, oinopotou, oJ (oinov, and pothv a drinker), “a winebibber, given to wine”: Matthew 11:19; Luke 7:34. (Proverbs 23:20; Polybius 20, 8, 2; Anacreon (530 B. C.) fragment 98; Anthol. 7, 28, 2.)* 237

oinov, oinou, oJ (from Homer down), the Septuagint for ˆyyæ, also for vwryTi (must, new wine), rm,j,, etc.; “wine”;

a. properly: Matthew 9:17; (xxvii. 34 L text T Tr WH); Mark 15:23; Luke 1:15; John 2:3; Romans 14:21; Ephesians 5:18; 1 Timothy 5:23; Revelation 17:2, etc.; oinw prosecein, 1 Timothy 3:8; douleuein, Titus 2:3.

b. metaphorically: oinov tou qumou (see qumov, 2), fiery wine, which God in his wrath is represented as mixing and giving to those whom he is about to punish by their own folly and madness, Revelation 14:10; 16:19; 19:15; with thv porneiav added (cf. oinoflugia, oinoflugiav, hJ (oinoflugew, and this from oinoflux, which is compounded of oinov and fluw, to bubble up, overflow), “drunkenness” (A.V. “wine-bibbing”): 1 Peter 4:3. (Xenophon, oec. 1, 22; Aristotle, eth. Nic. 3, 6, 15; Polybius 2, 19, 4; Philo, vita Moys. iii., sec. 22 (for other examples see Siegfried, Philo etc.,

p. 102); Aelian v. h. 3, 14.) (Cf. Trench, sec. lxi.)*

oJiov, oJia, oJion (from Homer down), relative pronoun (correlative to the demonstrative toiov and toioutov), “what sort of, what manner of, such as” (Latin qualis): oJiov ... toioutov, 1 Corinthians 15:48; 2 Corinthians 10:11; ton auton ... oJion, Philippians 1:30; with the pronoun toioutov suppressed, Matthew 24:21; Mark 9:3; 13:19 (here however the antecedent demonstrative is merely attracted into the relative clause or perhaps repeated for rhetorical emphasis, cf. 238 Buttmann, sec. 143, 8; Winer’s Grammar, 148 (140); see toioutov, b.); 2 Corinthians 12:20; 2 Timothy 3:11; Revelation 16:18; oJiwdhpotoun noshmati, of what kind of disease soever, John 5:4 Lachmann (cf. Lob. ad Phryn., p. 373f); in indirect question, Luke 9:55 (Rec.); 1 Thessalonians 1:5. ouc oJion de oJti ekpeptwken, concisely for ou toion estin oJion oJti ekpeptwken, “but the thing (state of the case) is not such as this, that the word of God hat fallen to the ground, i.e. the word of God hath by no means come to nought” (A.V. “but not as though the word of God hath” etc.), Romans 9:6; cf. oknew, oknw: 1 aorist wknhsa; (oknov (perhaps allied with the frequent. cunc-tari (cf. Curtius, p. 708)) delay); from Homer down; “to feel loath, to be slow; to delay, hesitate”: followed by an infinitive Acts 9:38. (Numbers 22:16; Judges 18:9, etc.)*

oknhrov, oknhra, oknhron (oknew), “sluggish, slothful, backward”: Matthew 25:26; with a dative of respect (cf. oligopistov, oligopistou, oJ, hJ (oligov and pistiv), “of little faith, trusting too little”: Matthew 6:30; 8:26; 14:31; 16:8; Luke 12:28. (Not found in secular authors)*

[g].); prov oligon, for a little time, James 4:14; simply oligon, adverbially: of time, “a short time, a (little) while,” Mark 6:31; 1 Peter 1:6; 5:10; Revelation 17:10; of space, “a little” (further), Mark 1:19; Luke 5:3. plural oliga, a few things: (Luke 10:41 WH); Revelation 2:14, 20 (Rec.); ep’ oliga ((see at the beginning and) epi, C. I. 2 e.), Matthew 25:21,23; di’ oligwn, briefly, in few words, grafein, 1 Peter 5:12 (see dia, A. III. 3) (rhqhnai, Plato, Phil., p. 31 d.; legg. 6, p. 778 c.).*
oligoyucov, oligoyucon (oligov, yuch), “faint-hearted”: 1 Thessalonians 5:14. (Proverbs 14:29; 18:14; Isaiah 57:15, etc.; Artemidorus Daldianus, oneir. 3, 5.)*

oligwrew, oligwrw; (oligwrov, and this from oligov and wra care); “to care little for, regard lightly, make small account of”: tinov (see Matthiae, sec. 348; (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 30, 10 d.)), Hebrews 12:5 from Proverbs 3:11. Havercamp’s Josephus, ii., p. 321)). Ethically, “free from sin, faultless” (R.V. “entire”): 1 Thessalonians 5:23; plural, connected with teleioi and with the addition of en mhdeni leipomenoi, James 1:4; “complete in all respects, consummate,” dikaiosunh, Sap. 15:3; eusebeia, 4 Macc. 15:17. (Plato, Polybius, Lcian, Epictetus, others; the Septuagint for µlæv], Deuteronomy 27:6; µymiT;, Leviticus 23:15; Ezekiel 15:5.)* (Synonyms: oJloklhrov, teleiov (cf. Trench, sec. xxii.): ‘in the oJloklhrov no grace which ought to be in a Christian man is deficient; in the teleiov no grace is merely in its weak imperfect beginnings, but all have reached a certain ripeness and maturity.’)

ololuzw; an onomatopoetic verb (cf. the similar oimwzein, aiazein, alalazein, pipizein, kokkuzein, tizein. oJlov, oJlh, oJlon, the Septuagint for lK; (from Pindar (Homer) down), “whole” (all): with an anarthrous substantive five (six) times in the N.T., viz. oJlon anqrwpon, John 7:23; eniauton oJlon, Acts 11:26; oJlh IJerousalhm, 21:31; dietian oJlhn, 28:30; oJlouv oikouv, Titus 1:11; (to which add, di’ oJlhv nuktov, Luke 5:5 L T Tr WH). usually placed before a substantive which has the article: oJlh hJ Galilaia, Matthew 4:23; oJlh hJ Suria, 24; kaq’ oJlhn thn polin, Luke 8:39; oJlon to swma, Matthew 5:29f; 6:22f; Luke 11:34; 1 Corinthians 12:17; James 3:2, etc.; (oJlh hJ ekklhsia, Romans 16: 23 L T Tr WH); oJlhn thn hJmeran, Matthew 20:6; Romans 8:36; oJlov oJ nomov, Matthew 22:40; Galatians 5:3; James 2:10; en oJlh th kardia sou, Matthew 22:37; ex oJlhv thv kardiav sou, Mark 12:30, and many other examples it is placed after a substantive which has the article (Winer’s Grammar, 131 (124) note; Buttmann, sec. 125, 6): hJ poliv oJlh, Mark 1:33; Acts 19:29 (Rec.); 21:30 — (the distinction which Krüger, sec. 50,11, 7 makes, viz. that hJ oJlh poliv denotes the whole city as opposed to its parts, but that oJlh hJ poliv and hJ poliv hJ oJlh denotes the whole city in opposed to other ideas, as the country, the fields, etc., does not hold good at least for the N.T. where even in hJ poliv oJlh the city is opposed only to its parts); add the following examples: Matthew 16:26; 26:59; Luke 9:25; 11:36a; John 4:53; Romans 16:23 (R G); 1 John 5:19; Revelation 3:10; 6:12 G L T Tr WH; 12:9; 16:14. oJlotelhv, oJlotelev (oJlov, telov), “perfect, complete in all respects”: 1 Thessalonians 5:23. (Plutarch, plac. philos. 5, 21; (Field, Hexapla, Leviticus 6:23; Psalm 50:21); ecclesiastical writings.)*

Olumpav (perhaps contracted from Olumpiodwrov, Winer’s Grammar, 103 (97); cf. Fick, Gr. Personennamen, pp. 63f, 201), Olumpa (Buttmann, 20 (18)), oJ, “Olympas,” a certain Christian: Romans 16:15.* 243

(Hesiod from 14; Herodotus 1, 193; Dioscorid. 1, 185; Theophrastus, caus. plant. 5, 9, 12; the Septuagint cant. 2:13.)*

oJlwv (oJlov), adverb, “wholly, altogether” (Latin omnino), (with a neg. “at all”): Matthew 5:34 (with which compare Xenophon, mem. 1, 2, 35); 1 Corinthians 5:1 (R.V. “actually”); 6:7; 15:29. ((Plato, Isocrates, others.))*

ombrov, ombrou, oJ (Latin imber) “a shower,” i.e. a violent rain, accompanied by high wind with thunder and lightning: Luke 12:54. (Deuteronomy 32:2; Sap. 16:16; in Greek writings from Homer down.)* omeiromai (or omeirw, see below) equivalent to iJmeiromai; “to desire, long for, yearn after” (A.V. “to be affectionately desirous”): tinov, 1 Thessalonians 2:8, G L T Tr WH (but the last read omeiromenoi, cf. their Appendix, p. 144 and Lob. Pathol. Element. 1:72), on the authority of all the uncial and many cursive manuscripts, for Rec. iJmeiromenoi. The word is unknown to the Greek writers, but the commentators at the passage recognize it, as do Hesychius, Phavorinus, and Photius, and interpret it by epiqumein. It is found in Psalm 62:2 Symmachus, and according to some manuscripts in Job 3:21. According to the conjecture of Fritzsche, Commentary on Mark, p. 792, it is composed of oJmou and eirein, just as Photius (p. 331, 8 edition Porson) explains it oJmou hJrmosqai (so Theophylact (cf. Tdf.’s note)). But there is this objection, that all the verbs compounded with oJmou govern the dative, not the genitive. Since Nicander, ther. verse 402, uses meiromai for iJmeiromai, some suppose that the original form is meiromai, to which, after the analogy of kellw and okellw), either iJ or oJ is for euphony prefixed in iJmeiromai and oJmeiromai But as iJmeiromai is derived from iJmerov, we must suppose that Nicander dropped the iJsyllable to suit the meter. Accordingly, oJmeiresqai seems not to differ at all from iJmeiresqai, and its form must be attributed to a vulgar pronunciation. Cf. (WH’s Appendix, p. 152); Winer’s Grammar, 101 (95); (Buttmann, 64 (56); Ellicott on 1 Thessalonians, the passage cited; (Kuenen and Cobet, N.T. Vat., p. ciii.)).* 244

(cf. µvi hwO;hy]), “the name of God” in the N.T. is used for all those qualities which to his worshippers are summed up in that name, and by which God makes himself known to men; it is therefore equivalent to his “divinity,” Latin numen (not his nature or essence as it is in itself), “the divine majesty and perfections,” so far forth as these are apprehended, named, magnified (cf. Winer, Lex. Hebrew et Chald., p. 993; Oehler in Herzog x., p. 196ff; Wittichen in Schenkel iv., p. 282ff); so in the phrases aJgion to onoma autou namely, estin, Luke 1:49; aJgiazein to onoma tou Qeou, Matthew 6:9; Luke 11:2; oJmologein tw onomati autou, Hebrews 13:15; yallein, Romans 15:9; doxazein, John 12:28; (Revelation 15:4); faneroun, gnwrizein, John 17:6,26; fobeisqai to onoma tou Qeou, Revelation 11:18; 15:4 (G L T Tr WH); diaggellein, Romans 9:17; apaggellein, Hebrews 2:12; blasfhmein, Romans 2:24; 1 Timothy 6:1; Revelation 13:6; 16:9; agaphn endeiknusqai eiv to onoma tou Qeou, Hebrews 6:10; thrhson autouv en tw onomati sou, wJ (by attraction for oJ (cf. Buttmann, sec. 143, 8, p. 286; Winer’s Grammar, sec. 24, 1; Rec. incorrectly oJuv)) dedwkav moi, keep them consecrated and united to thy name (character), which thou didst commit to me to declare and manifest (cf. verse 6), John 17:11; (cf. uJper tou aJgiou onomatov sou, oJu kateskhnwsav en taiv kardiaiv hJmwn, ‘Teaching’ etc., chapter 10, 2). After the analogy of the preceding expression, “the name of 255 Christ” (Ihsou, Ihsou Cristou, tou kuriou Ihsou, tou kuriou hJmwn, etc.) is used in the N.T. of all those things which, in hearing or recalling that name, we are bidden to recognize in Jesus and to profess; accordingly, of “his Messianic dignity, divine authority, memorable sufferings, in a word the peculiar services and blessings conferred by him on men,” so far forth as these are believed, confessed, commemorated (cf. Westcott on the Epistles of John, p. 232): hence, the phrases euaggelizesqai ta peri tou onomatou Ihsou Cristou, Acts 8:12; megalunein to onoma Acts 19:17; tw onomati (Rec. en tw onomati) autou elpizein, Matthew 12:21 (Buttmann, 156 (153)); pisteuein, 1 John 3:23; pisteuousin eiv to onoma, John 1:12; 2:23; 3:18; 1 John 5:13a (Rec., 13b); pistiv tou onoma, Acts 3:16; oJ onomazwn to onoma kuriou, whoever nameth the name of the Lord namely, as his Lord (see onomazw, a.), 2 Timothy 2:19; kratein, to hold fast i.e. persevere in professing, Revelation 2:13; ouk arneisqai, Revelation 3:8; to onoma Ihsou endoxazetai en uJmin, 2 Thessalonians 1:12; bastazein to onoma enwpion eqnwn (see bastazw, 3), Acts 9:15; to do or to suffer anything epi tw onomati Cristou, see epi, B. 2 a. [b.], p. 232b. The phrase en tw onomati Cristou is used in various senses:

a. “by the command and authority of Christ”: see examples just above.

b. “in the use of the name of Christ” i.e. the power of his name being invoked for assistance, Mark 9:38 Relz L T Tr WH (see f. below); Luke 10:17; Acts 3:6; 4:10; 16:18; James 5:14; universally, en poiw onomati epoihsate touto; Acts 4:7.

c. “through the power of Christ’s name,” pervading and governing their souls, Mark 16:17.

d. “in acknowledging, embracing, professing, the name of Christ”: swqhnai, Acts 4:12; dikaiwqhnai, 1 Corinthians 6:11; zwhn ecein, John 20:31; “in professing and proclaiming the name of Christ,” parrhsiazesqai, Acts 9:27,28 (29).

e. “relying or resting on the name of Christ, rooted (so to speak) in his name, i.e. mindful of Christ”: poiein ti, Colossians 3:17; eucaristein, Ephesians 5:20; aitein ti, i.e. (for substance) “to ask a thing, as prompted by the mind of Christ and in reliance on the bond which unites us to him,” John 14:13f; 15:16; 16:24,(26), and R G L in 23; cf. 256 Ebrard, Gebet im Namen Jesu, in Herzog iv. 692ff. God is said to do a thing en onomati Cristou, “regardful of the name of Christ,” i.e. moved by the name of Christ, for Christ’s sake, didonai the thing asked, John 16:23 T Tr WH; pempein to pneuma to aJgion John 14:26f. en onomati Cristou (A.V. “for the name of Christ”) (German auf Grund Namens Christi), i.e. because one calls himself or is called by the name of Christ: oneidizesqai, 1 Peter 4:14 (equivalent to wJv Cristianov, 16). The simple dative tw onomati Cristou signifies “by the power of Christ’s name,” pervading and prompting souls, Matthew 7:22; so also tw onomati tou kuriou (i.e. “of God”) lalein, of the prophets, James 5:10 R G; tw onomati sou, by uttering thy name as a spell, Mark 9:38 R^st^bez G (see b. above). eiv to onoma tou Cristou sunagesqai is used of those who come together to deliberate concerning any matter relating to Christ’s cause (German auf den Namen), “with the mind directed unto, having regard unto, his name,” Matthew 18:20. eJneken tou onomatou (A.V. “for my name’s sake”), i.e. “on account of professing my name,” Matthew 19:29; also dia to onoma mou, autou, etc.: Matthew 10:22; 24:9; Mark 13:13; Luke 21:17; John 15:21; 1 John 2:12; Revelation 2:3. dia tou onomatov tou kuriou parakalein tina, to beseech one by employing Christ’s name as a motive or incentive (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 381 (357)), 1 Corinthians 1:10; by embracing and avowing “his name,” afesin aJmartiwn labein, Acts 10:43. uJper tou onomatov autou, equivalent to for defending, spreading, strengthening, the authority of Christ, Acts 5:41 (see below); 9:16; 15:26; 21:13; Romans 1:5; 3 John 1:7; — (but according to the better texts in Acts 5:41; 3 John 1:7, to onoma is used absolutely, “the Name,” namely, kuriou, of the Lord Jesus; so the Vaticanus manuscript James 5:14; cf. Leviticus 24:11,16; Lightfoot on Ignatius ad Ephesians 3, 1; Buttmann, 163 (142) note; Winer’s Grammar, 594 (553). So Lightfoot in Philippians 2:9; (see 1 above)). prov to onoma Ihsou tou Nazwraiou ... enantia praxai, Acts 26:9.

3. In imitation of the Hebrew twOmve (Numbers 1:2,18,20; 3:40,43; 26:53), the plural onomata is used equivalent to “persons reckoned up by name”: Acts 1:15; Revelation 3:4; 11:13.

4. Like the Latin nomen, equivalent to “the cause or reason named”: en tw onomati toutw, in this cause, i.e. on this account, namely, because he 257 suffers as a Christian, 1 Peter 4:16 L T Tr WH (others, more simply, take onoma here as referring to Cristianov preceding); en onomati, oJti (as in Syriac ...) Cristou este, in this name, i.e. “for this reason,” because ye are Christ’s (disciples), Mark 9:41.

onomazw; 1 aorist wnomasa; passive, present onomazomai; 1 aorist wnomasqhn; (onoma); from Homer down; “to name” (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 615 (572));

a. to onoma, “to name i.e. to utter”: passive Ephesians 1:21; tou kuriou (Rec. Cristou), the name of the Lord (Christ) namely, as his Lord, 2 Timothy 2:19 (the Septuagint for hwO;hy] µvi hwO;hy], “to make mention of the name of Jehovah” in praise, said of his worshippers, Isaiah 26:13; Amos 6:10); to onoma Ihsou epi tina, Acts 19:13, see epi, C. I. 1 c., p. 234{b} middle

c. tina or ti, “to utter the name of a person or thing”: oJpou wnomasqh Cristov, of the lands into which the knowledge of Christ has been carried, Romans 15:20 (1 Macc. 3:9); onomazesqai of things which are called by their own name because they are present or exist (as opposed to those which are unheard of), 1 Corinthians 5:1 Rec.; Ephesians 5:3. (Compare: eponomazw.)*
onov, onou, oJ, hJ (from Homer down), the Septuagint for rwOmj} and ˆwOta;, “an ass”: Luke 14:5 Rec.; Matthew 21:5; John 12:15; — oJ, Luke 13:15; hJ, Matthew 21:2,7.*
