Anm. 3; Kühner, sec. 335 Anm. 2), adverb, “truly, in reality, in point of fact,” as opposed to what is pretended, fictitious, false, conjectural: Mark 11:32 (see ecw, I. 1 f.); Luke 23:47; 24:34; John 8:36; 1 Corinthians 14:25; Galatians 3:21 and Rec. in 2 Peter 2:18; oJ, hJ, to ontwv followed by a noun, “that which is truly etc., that which is indeed” (ta ontwv agata h kala, P’lat. Phaedr., 258

p. 260 a.; thn ontwv kai alhqwv filian, Plato, Clit., p. 409 e.; oJi ontwv basileiv, Josephus, Antiquities 15, 3, 5): as hJ ontwv (Rec. aiwniov) zwh, 1 Timothy 6:19; hJ ontwv chra, a widow that is a widow indeed, not improperly called a widow (as parqenov hJ legomenh chra, i.e., a virgin that has taken a vow of celibacy, in Ignatius ad Smyrn. 13 (cf. (Euripides, Aristophanes, Xenophon, Plato, and following; the Septuagint for µn;m]au, Numbers 22:37; for ˆkea;, Jeremiah 3:23; for Ëaæ, Jeremiah 10:19.)*

oxov, oxeov (oxouv), to (oxuv), “vinegar” (Aeschylus, Hippocrates, Aristophanes, Xenophon, and following; for xm,j,o Ruth 2:14; Numbers 6:3, etc.); used in the N.T. for Latin posca, i.e. the mixture of sour wine or vinegar and water which the Roman soldiers were accustomed to drink: Matthew 27:34 R L marginal reading, 48; Mark 15:36; Luke 23:36; John 19:29f.*

oxuv, oxeia, oxu (allied with Latin acer, acus, etc.; cf. Curtius, sec. 2);

1. “sharp” (from Homer down): romfaia, drepanon, Revelation 1:16; 2:12; 14:14,17f; 19:15 (Isaiah 5:28; Psalm 56 (Psalm 57:5)).

2. “swift, quick” (so from Herodotus 5, 9 down; cf. wkuv fleet): Romans 3:15 (Amos 2:15; Proverbs 22:29).*

oph, ophv, hJ (perhaps from oy (root op (see oJraw); cf. Curtius, sec. 627)), properly, “through which one can see” (Pollux (2, 53, p. 179) oph, di’ hJv estin idein, cf. German Luke, Loch (?)), “an opening, aperture” (used of “a window,” Song of Solomon 5:4): of fissures in the earth, James 3:11 (Exodus 33:22); of caves in rocks or mountains, Hebrews 11:38 (here R.V. “holes”); Obadiah 1:3. (Of various other kinds of holes and openings, in Aristophanes, Aristotle, others.)*

opisqen (see opisw), adverb of place, “from behind, on the back, behind, after”: Matthew 9:20; Mark 5:21; Luke 8:44; Revelation 4:6; 5:1 (on which see grafw, 3). As a preposition it is joined with the genitive (like emprosqen, exwqen, etc. (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 54, 6; Buttmann, sec. 146, 1)): Matthew 15:23; Luke 23:26; 259 (Revelation 1:10 WH marginal reading). (From Homer down; the Septuagint for yræj}aæ, sometimes for rwOja;.)*

opisw ((perhaps) from hJ opiv; and this from eJpw, eJpomai, to follow (but cf. Vanicek, p. 530)), adverb of place and time, from Homer down; the Septuagint for rjæaæ, rwOja; and especially for yræj}aæ; (at the) “back, behind, after”;

1. adverbially of place: eJstanai, Luke 7:38; epistreyai opisw, back, Matthew 24:18 (uJpostrefein opisw, Josephus, Antiquities 6, 1, 3); ta opisw, “the things that are behind,” Philippians 3:13 (14); eiv ta opisw apercesqai, “to go backward,” Vulgate abire retrorsum, John 18:6; “to return home,” of those who grow recreant to Christ’s teaching and cease to follow him, John 6:66; strefesqai, to turn oneself back, John 20:14; epistrefein, to return back to places left, Mark 13:16; Luke 17:31; uJpostreyai eiv ta opisw, tropically, of those who return to the manner of thinking and living already abandoned, 2 Peter 2:21 Lachmann; blepein (Vulgate (aspicere or) respicere retro (A.V. “to look back”)), Luke 9:62.

2. By a usage unknown to Greek authors, as a preposition with the genitive (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 54, 6; Buttmann, sec. 146, 1); a. of place: Revelation 1:10 (WH marginal reading opisqen); 12:15 (Numbers 25:8; Song of Solomon 2:9); ia phrases resembling the Hebrew (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 30; Buttmann, as above and 172 (150)): opisw tinov ercesqai to follow anyone as a guide, to be his disciple or follower, Matthew 16:24; Luke 9:23; Mark 8:34 R L Tr marginal reading WH; (cf. Luke 14:27); also akolouqein, Mark 8:34 G T Tr text; Matthew 10:38 (see akolouqew, 2 at the end); poreuesqai, to join oneself to one as an attendant and follower, Luke 21:8 (Sir. 46:10); to seek something one lusts after, 2 Peter 2:10 (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 594 (553); Buttmann, 184 (160)); apercomai opisw tinov, to go off in order to follow one, to join one’s party, Mark 1:20; John 12:19; to run after a thing which one lusts for (cf. Buttmann, as above), eJterav sarkov, Jude 1:7; deute episw mou (see deute, 1), Matthew 4:19; Mark 1:17; apostellein tina opisw tinov, Luke 19:14; afistanai, apospan, tina opisw autou, to draw one away to (join) his party, Acts 5:37; 20:30; ektrepesqai, to turn out of the right path, turn aside from rectitude, 1 Timothy 5:15; by a pregnant construction, 260 after qaumazein, “to wonder after” i.e. to be drawn away by admiration to follow one (Buttmann, 185 (160f)), Revelation 13:3 (pav oJ laov exesth opisw autou, 1 Samuel 13:7); uJpage opisw mou (A.V. “get thee behind me”), out of my sight: Luke 4:8 R L brackets; Matthew 4:10 (G L brackets); 16:23; Mark 8:33. b. of time, “after”: ercesqai opisw tinov, to make his public appearance after (subsequently to) one, Matthew 3:11; Mark 1:7; John 1:15,27,30 (opisw tou sabbatou, Nehemiah 13:19).*

oJplizw: (1 aorist middle imperative 2 person plural oJplisasqe); (oJplon); from Homer down; “to arm, furnish with arms”; universally, “to provide”; middle ti, “to furnish oneself with a thing” (as with arms); metaphorically, thn authn ennoian oJplisasqe (A.V. “arm yourselves with” i.e.) take on the same mind, 1 Peter 4:1 (qrasov, Sophocles Electr. 995). (Compare: kaqsplizw.)*

oJplon (allied to eJpw, Latin sequor, socius, etc.; Curtius, sec. 621), oJplou, to, as in classical Greek from Homer down, “any tool or implement” for preparing a thing (like the Latin arma); hence,

1. plural “arms” used in warfare, “weapons”: John 18:3; 2 Corinthians 10:4; metaphorically, thv dikaiosunhv, which hJ dikaiosunh furnishes, 2 Corinthians 6:7; tou fwtov, adapted to the light, such as light demands, Romans 13:12 (here L marginal reading erga).

2. “an instrument”: oJpla adikiav, for committing unrighteousness, opposed to oJpla dikaiosunhv, for practising righteousness, Romans 6:13.*

oJpoiov, oJpoia, oJpoion (poiov with the relative oJ), (from Homer down), “of what sort or quality, what manner of”: 1 Corinthians 3:13; Galatians 2:6; 1 Thessalonians 1:9; James 1:24; preceded by toioutov (such as), Acts 26:29.*
oJpote (pote with the relative oJ) (from Homer down), “when” (cf. Buttmann, sec. 139, 34; Winer’s Grammar, sec. 41 b. 3): Luke 6:3 R G T (where L Tr WH oJte).*

oJpou (from pou and the relative oJ) (from Homer down), “where”; 261

1. adverb of place,

a. “in which place, where”; [a]. in relative sentences with the indicative it is used to refer to a preceding noun of place; as, epi thv ghv, oJpou etc. Matthew 6:19; add, Matthew 6:20; 13:5; 28:6; Mark 6:55; 9:44,46 (which verses T WH omit; Tr brackets), 48; Luke 12:33; John 1:28; 4:20,46; 6:23; 7:42; 10:40; 11:30; 12:1; 18:1,20; 19:18,20,41; 20:12; Acts 17:1; Revelation 11:8; 20:10. it refers to ekei or ekeise to be mentally supplied in what precedes or follows: Matthew 25:24,26; Mark 2:4; 4:15; 5:40; 13:14; John 3:8; 6:62; 7:34; 11:32; 14:3; 17:24; 20:19; Romans 15:20; Hebrews 9:16; 10:18; Revelation 2:13. it refers to ekei expressed in what follows: Matthew 6:21; Luke 12:34; 17:37; John 12:26; James 3:16. in imitation of the Hebrew rv,a} µv; (Genesis 13:3; Ecclesiastes 9:10, etc.): oJpou ekei, Revelation 12:6 (G T Tr WH), 14 (see ekei, a.); oJpou ... ep’ autwn, Revelation 17:9. oJpou also refers to men, so that it is equivalent to “with (among) whom, in whose house”: Matthew 26:57; (add, Revelation 2:13; cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 54, 7 at the end); “in which state” (viz. of the renewed man), Colossians 3:11. it is loosely connected with the thought to which it refers, so that it is equivalent to “wherein” (A.V. “whereas”), 2 Peter 2:11 (in the same sense in indirect question, Xenophon, mem. 3, 5, 1). oJpou an, “wherever” — with imperfect indicative (see an, II. 1), Mark 6:56 (Tdf. ean); with aorist subjunctive (Latin future perfect), Mark 9:18 (where L T Tr WH oJpou ean); Mark 14:9 (here too T WH oJpou ean); also oJpou ean (see ean, II.), Matthew 26:13; Mark 6:10; 14:14a (in both of the last two passages, L Tr oJpou an); with subjunctive present Matthew 24:28. [b]. in indirect questions (yet cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 57, 2 at the end), with subjunctive aorist: Mark 14:14b; Luke 22:11.

b. joined to verbs signifying motion into a place instead of oJpoi, “into which place, whither” (see ekei, b.): followed by the indicative, John 8:21f; 13:33,36; 14:4; 21:18; (James 3:4 T Tr WH (see below)); oJpou an, “where (whither) soever,” with indicative present, Revelation 14:4 L Tr WH (cf. below), cf. Buttmann, sec. 139, 30; with subjunctive present, Luke 9:57 R G T WH (others, oJpou ean, see below); James 3:4 (R 262 G L); Revelation 14:4 R G T (see above); oJpou ean, with subjunctive present, Matthew 8:19, and L Tr in Luke 9:57.

2. It gets the force of a conditional particle “if” (“in case that, in so far as” (A.V. “whereas” (cf. 2 Peter 2:11 above))): 1 Corinthians 3:3 (Clement of Rome, 1 Corinthians 43, 1, and often in Greek writings; cf. Grimm on 4 Macc. 2:14; Meyer on 1 Corinthians 3:3; (Müller on the Epistle of Barnabas 16, 63).*
optanw (OPTW): “to look at, behold”; middle present participle optanomenov; “to allow oneself to be seen, to appear”: tini, Acts 1:3. (1 Kings 8:8; Tobit 12:19; (Graecus Venetus, Exodus 34:24).)*

optasia, optasiav, hJ (optazw);

1. “the act of exhibiting oneself to view”: optasiai kuriou, 2 Corinthians 12:1 (A.V. “visions”; cf. Meyer at the passage) (en hJmeraiv optasiav mou, Additions to Esther 4:1. 44 (13); (cf. Malachi 3:2); hJliov en optasia, coming into view, Sir. 43:2).

2. “a sight, a vision,” an appearance presented to one whether asleep or awake: ouraniw optasia, Acts 26:19; eJwrakenai optasian, Luke 1:22; with the genitive of apposition aggelwn, Luke 24:23. A later form for oyiv (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 24), Anthol. 6, 210, 6; for ha,r]m,æ (Theodotion) Daniel 9:23; 10:1,7f.*
optov, opth, opton (optaw (to roast, cook)), “cooked, broiled”: Luke 24:42. (Exodus 12:8,9; in classical Greek from Homer down.)*

opwra, opwrav, hJ (derived by some from opiv (cf. opisw), eJtomai, and wJra; hence, the time that follows the wJra (Curtius, sec. 522); by others from opov (cf. our “sap”) juice, and wJra, i.e. the time of juicy fruits, the time when fruits become ripe), from Homer down;

1. “the season which succeeds qerov, from the rising of Sirius to that of Arcturus,” i.e. late summer, early autumn, our dog-days (the year being divided into seven seasons as follows: ear, qerov, opwra, fqinopwron, sporhtov, ceimwn, futalia). 263

2. “ripe fruits” (of trees): sou thv epiqumiav thv yuchv for wJn hJ yuch sou epiqumei, Revelation 18:14. (Jeremiah 47:10 (40:10), and often in Greek writings.)*

oJpwv (from pwv and the relative oJ), with the indicative, a relative adverb but, like the Latin ut, assuming also the nature of a conjunction (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 449 (418f)).

I. As an adverb; “as, in what manner, how”; once so in the N.T. in an indirect question, with the indicative: ouk egnwv, oJpwv k.t.l., Luke 24:20, where cf. Bornemann, Scholia etc.

II. A conjunction, Latin ut, answering to the German dass, that; in classical Greek with the optative, and subjunctive, and future indicative; cf. especially Klotz ad Devar. ii. 2, p. 681ff But the distinction observed between these constructions by the more elegant Greek writings is quite neglected in the N.T., and if we except Matthew 26:59 L T Tr (oJpwv qanatwsousin) (1 Corinthians 1:29 Rec.elz), only the subjunctive follows this particle (for in Mark 5:23, for oJpwv ... zhsetai, L text T Tr WH have correctly restored iJna ... zhsh); cf. Winer’s Grammar, 289 (271); Buttmann, 233f (201f); (214 (185)).

1. It denotes the purpose or end, “in order that; with the design or to the end that; that”;

a. without an — after the present, Matthew 6:2,16; Philemon 1:6; Hebrews 9:15; after este to be supplied, 1 Peter 2:9; after the perfect, Acts 9:17; Hebrews 2:9; oJpwv mh, Luke 16:26; after the imperfect, Matthew 26:59 (R G (see above)); Acts 9:24; after the aorist, Acts 9:2,12; 25:26; Romans 9:17; Galatians 1:4; oJpwv mh, Acts 20:16; 1 Corinthians 1:29; after the pluperfect, John 11:57; after the future, Matthew 23:35; and Rec. in Acts 24:26; after an aorist subjunctive by which something is asked for, Mark 5:23 Rec.; after imperatives, Matthew 2:8; 5:16,45; 6:4; Acts 23:15,23; 2 Corinthians 8:11; oJpwv mh, Matthew 6:18; after clauses with iJna and the aorist subjunctive, Luke 16:28; 2 Corinthians 8:14; 2 Thessalonians 1:12. Noteworthy is the phrase oJpwv plhroqh, i.e. “that according to God’s purpose it might be brought to pass or might be proved by the event,” of O.T. prophecies and types (see iJna, II. 3 at the end): Matthew 2:23; 8:17; 12:17 (where L T Tr WH iJna); 13:35. 264

b. oJpwv an, “that, if it be possible,” Matthew 6:5 R G; “that, if what I have just said shall come to pass,” Luke 2:35; Acts 3:20 (19) (R.V. “that so”); 15:17; Romans 3:4 (Buttmann, 234 (201)); examples from the Septuagint are given in Winer’s Grammar, sec. 42, 6.

2. As in the Greek writings also (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 338 (317); (Buttmann, sec. 139, 41)), oJpwv with the subjunctive is used after verbs of praying, entreating, asking, exhorting, to denote what one wishes to be done: Matthew 8:34 (here L iJna); 9:38; Luke 7:3; 10:2; 11:37; Acts 8:15,24; 9:2; 23:20; 25:3; James 5:16; after a verb of deliberating: Matthew 12:14; 22:15; Mark 3:6 (from which examples it is easy to see how the use noted in II. arises from the original adverbial force of the particle; for sumboulion edidoun ... oJpwv auton apoleswsin, “they took counsel to destroy him” is equivalent to “how they might destroy him,” and also to to this end that they might destroy him; cf. Kühner, sec. 552 Anm. 3, ii., p. 892).*

oJrama, oJramatov, to (oJraw), “that which is seen, a sight, spectacle”: Acts 7:31; Matthew 17:9; “a sight divinely granted in an ecstasy or in sleep, a vision,” Acts 10:17,19; di’ oJramatov, Acts 18:9; en oJramati, Acts 9:10,12 (RG); 10:3; oJrama blepein, Acts 12:9; idein, Acts 11:5; 16:10. (Xenophon, Aristotle, Plato, Aelian v. h. 2, 3 (others, eikwn); the Septuagint several times for ha,r]m,æ ˆwOzj;, Chaldean aw;z]j, etc.; see optasia.)*

oJrasiv, oJrasewv, hJ (oJraw);

1. “the act of seeing”: ommatwn crhsiv eiv oJrasin, Sap. 15:15; “the sense of sight,” Aristotle, de anima 3, 2; Diodorus 1, 59; Plutarch, mor., p. 440f; plural “the eyes,” ekkoptein tav oJraseiv, Diodorus 2, 6.

2. “appearance, visible form”: Revelation 4:3 (Numbers 24:4; Ezekiel 1:5,26,28; Sir. 41:20, etc.).

3. “a vision,” i.e. an appearance divinely granted in an ecstasy: Revelation 9:17; oJraseiv oyontai, Acts 2:17 from Joel 2:28. (The Septuagint chiefly for ha,r]mæ and ˆwOzj;.)*
oJratov, oJrath, oJraton (oJraw), “visible, open to view”: neuter plural substantively, Colossians 1:16. (Xenophon, Plato, Theocritus, Philo; the Septuagint)* 265

orgh, orghv, hJ (from orgaw to teem, denoting an internal motion, especially that of plants and fruits swelling with juice (Curtius, sec. 152); cf. Latin turgere alicui for irasci alicui in Plautus Cas. 2, 5, 17; Most. 3, 2, 10; cf. German arg, Aerger), in Greek writings from Hesiod down “the natural disposition, temper, character; movement or agitation of soul, impulse, desire, any violent emotion,” but especially (and chiefly in Attic) “anger”. In Biblical Greek “anger, wrath, indignation” (on the distinction between it and qumov, see qumov, 1): Ephesians 4:31; Colossians 3:8; James 1:19f; met’ orghv, indignant (A.V. “with anger”), Mark 3:5; cwriv orghv, 1 Timothy 2:8; “anger exhibited in punishing,” hence, used for the “punishment” itself (Demosthenes or. in middle sec. 43): of the punishments inflicted by magistrates, Romans 13:4; dia thn orghn, i.e. because disobedience is visited with punishment, Romans 13:5. The orgh attributed to God in the N.T. is “that in God which stands opposed to man’s disobedience, obduracy” (especially in resisting the gospel) “and sin, and manifests itself in punishing the same”: John 3:36; Romans 1:18; 4:15; 9:22a; Hebrews 3:11; 4:3; Revelation 14:10; 16:19; 19:15; absolutely, hJ orgh, Romans 12:19 (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 594 (553)); skeuh orghv, “vessels into which wrath will be poured” (at the last day), explained by the addition kathrtismena eiv apwleian, Romans 9:22b; hJ mellousa orgh, which at the last day will be exhibited in penalties, Matthew 3:7; Luke 3:7 (others understand in these two passages the (national) judgments immediately impending to be referred to — at least primarily); also hJ orgh hJ ercomenh, 1 Thessalonians 1:10; hJmera orghv, the day on which the wrath of God will be made manifest in the punishment of the wicked (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 30, 2 a.), Romans 2:5; and hJ hJmera hJ megalh thv orghv autou (Revelation 6:17; see hJmera, 3 at the end); ercetai hJ orgh tou Qeou epi tina, the wrath of God cometh upon one in the infliction of penalty (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 40, 2 a.), Ephesians 5:6; Colossians 3:6 (T Tr WH omit; L brackets epi etc.); efqase (efqaken L text WH marginal reading) ep’ autouv hJ orgh, 1 Thessalonians 2:16; so hJ orgh passes over into the notion of retribution and “punishment,” Luke 21:23; Romans (Romans 2:8); 3:5; 5:9; Revelation 11:18; tekna orghv, men exposed to divine punishment, Ephesians 2:3; eiv orghn, “unto wrath,” i.e. to undergo punishment in misery, 1 Thessalonians 5:9. orgh is attributed to Christ also when he comes as Messianic judge, Revelation 6:16. (The Septuagint for hr;b][,, 269 “wrath, outburst of anger,” µ[æzæ, hk;je, ˆwOrj;, ãx,q,, etc.; but chiefly for ãaæ.) Cf. Ferd. Weber, Vom Zorne Gottes. Erlang. 1862; Ritschl, Die christl. Lehre v. d. Rechtfertigung u. Versöhnung, ii., p. 118ff.*

orgizw: passive, present orgizomai; 1 aorist wrgisqhn; (orgh); from Sophocles, Euripides, and Thucydides down; “to provoke, arouse to anger”; passive “to be provoked to anger, be angry, be wroth” (the Septuagint for hr;j,; ãxæq;, also for hr;j; ãaæ etc.): absolutely, Matthew 18:34; 22:7; Luke 14:21; 15:28; Ephesians 4:26 (Buttmann, 290 (250); cf. Winer’s Grammar, sections 43, 2; 55, 7); Revelation 11:18; tini, Matthew 5:22; epi tini, Revelation 12:17 (L omits epi) as in 1 Kings 11:9; (Andocides (405 B. C.) 5, 10); Isocrates, p. 230 c.; (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 232 (218)). (Compare: prwrgizw.)*

orgilov, orgilh, orgilon (orgh), “prone to anger, irascible” (A.V. “soon angry”): Titus 1:7. (Proverbs 22:24; 29:22; Xenophon, de re equ. 9, 7; Plato (e.g. de rep. 411 b.); Aristotle (e.g. eth. Nic. 2, 7, 10); others.)*

orguia, orguiav, hJ (oregw to stretch out), the distance across the breast front the tip of one middle finger to the tip of the other when the arms are outstretched; five or six feet, “a fathom”: Acts 27:28. (Homer, Herodotus, Xenophon, others.)*

oregw: (cf. Latin rego, German recken, strecken, reichen (English “reach”; Curtius, sec. 153)); from Homer down; “to stretch forth,” as ceira, Homer, Iliad 15, 371, etc.; present middle (cf. Winer’s Grammar, p. 252 (237) note), “to stretch oneself out in order to touch or to grasp something, to reach after or desire something”: with a genitive of the thing, 1 Timothy 3:1; Hebrews 11:16; filarguriav, to give oneself up to the love of money (not quite accurately since filarguriav is itself the orexiv; (cf. Ellicott at the passage)), 1 Timothy 6:10.*

oreinov, oreinh, oreinon (orov), “mountainous, hilly”; hJ oreinh (WH orinh, see Iota) namely, cwra (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 591 (550)) (which is added in Herodotus 1, 110; Xenophon, Cyril 1, 3, 3), “the mountain-district, hill-country”: Luke 1:39,65 (Aristotle, h. a. 5, 28, 4; the Septuagint for rhæ, Genesis 14:10; Deuteronomy 11:11; Joshua 2:16, etc.).* 270

orexiv, orexewv, hJ (oregomai, which see), “desire, longing, craving,” for; “eager desire, lust, appetite”: of lust, Romans 1:27. It is used both in a good and a bad sense, as well of natural and lawful and even of proper cravings (of the appetite for food, Sap. 16:2f; Plutarch, mor., p. 635 c.; others; episthmhv, Plato, de fin., p. 414 b.), as also of corrupt and unlawful desires, Sir. 18:30; 23:6; alogoi and logistikai orexeiv are contrasted in Aristotle, rhet. 1, 10, 7. (Cf. Trench, sec. lxxxvii.)*

orqopodew, orqopodw; (orqopouv with straight feet, going straight; and this from orqov and pouv); “to walk in a straight course”; metaphorically, “to act uprightly,” Galatians 2:14 (cf. prov, I. 3 f.). Not found elsewhere; (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 26; 102 (96)).*

orqov, orqh, orqon (ORW, ornumi (to stir up, set in motion; according to others, from the root, to lift up; cf. Fick iii., p. 775; Vanicek,

p. 928; Curtius, p. 348)), “straight, erect”; i.e.

a. “upright”: anasthqi, Acts 14:10; so with sthnai in 1 Esdr. 9:46, and in Greek writings, especially Homer

b. opposed to skoliov, “straight” i.e. not crooked: trociai, Hebrews 12:13 (for yv;y;, Proverbs 12:15 etc.; (Pindar, Theognis, others)).*

orqotomew, orqotomw; (orqotomov cutting straight, and this from orqov and temnw);

1. “to cut straight”: tav oJdouv, to cut straight ways, i.e. to proceed by straight paths, hold a straight course, equivalent to to do right (for rVeyi), Proverbs 3:6; 11:5 (viam secare, Vergil Aen. 6, 899).

2. dropping the idea of cutting, “to make straight and smooth”; Vulgate recte tracto, “to handle aright”: ton logon thv alhqeiav, i.e. to teach the truth correctly and directly, 2 Timothy 2:15; ton alhqh logon, Eustathius, opuscc., p. 115, 41. (Not found elsewhere (except in ecclesiastical writings (Winer’s Grammar, 26); e.g. constt. apost. 7, 31 en tw tou kuriou dogmasin; cf. Suicer ii. 508f). Cf. kainotomew, “to cut new veins” in mining; dropping the notion of cutting, “to make something new, introduce new things, make innovations or changes,” etc.)*

orqrizw: 3 person singular imperfect wrqrizen; (orqrov); not found in secular authors ((cf. Winer’s Grammar, 26; 33; 91 (87)); Moeris 271 (p. 272, Pierson edition) orqreuei attikwv, orqrizei eJllhnikwv); the Septuagint often for µyKiv]hi; (cf. Grimm on 1 Macc. 4:52 and on Sap. 6:14); “to rise early in the morning”: prov tina, to rise early in the morning in order to betake oneself to one, to resort to one early in the morning, (Vulgate manico ad aliquem), Luke 21:38, where see Meyer.*

orqrinov, orqrinh orqrinon (from orqrov; cf. hJmerinov, eJsperinov, opwrinov, prwinov a poetic (Anth.) and later form for orqriov (see Lob. ad Phryn., p. 51; Sturz, De dial. Maced. et Alex., p. 186; (Winer’s Grammar, 25)), “early”: Revelation 22:16 Rec.; Luke 24:22 L T Tr WH. (Hosea 6:4; Sap. 11:23 (22).)*

orqriov, orqria, orqrion (from orqrov, which see; cf. oyiov prwiov), “early; rising at the first dawn or very early in the morning”: Luke 24:22 R G (Job 29:7; 3 Macc. 5:10, 23). Cf. the preceding word. (Homer (h. Merc. 143), Theognis, others.)*

orqrov, orqrou, oJ (from ORW, ornumi to stir up, rouse; cf. Latin orior, ortus), from Hesiod down; the Septuagint for rjivæ dawn, and several times for rq,Bo; “daybreak, dawn”: orqrou baqeov or baqewv (see baqewv and baquv (on the genitive cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 30, 11; Buttmann, sec. 132, 26)), at early dawn, Luke 24:1; orqrou, at daybreak, at dawn, early in the morning, John 8:2 (Hesiod, Works, 575; the Septuagint Jeremiah 25:4; 33:5 (Jeremiah 26:5) 5, etc.); uJpo ton orqron, Acts 5:21 (Dio Cassius, 76, 17).*
orqwv (orqov), adverb, “rightly”: Mark 7:35; Luke 7:43; 10:28; 20:21. (Aeschylus and Herodotus down.)*

oJrizw; 1 aorist wJrisa; passive, perfect participle wJrismenov; 1 aorist participle oJrisqeiv; (from oJrov a boundary, limit); from (Aeschylus and) Herodotus down; “to define”; i.e.

1. “to mark out the boundaries or limits” (of any place or thing): Herodotus, Xenophon, Thucydides, others; Numbers 34:6; Joshua 13:27.

2. “to determine, appoint”: with an accusative of the thing, hJmeran, Hebrews 4:7; kairouv, Acts 17:26 (numerous examples from 272 Greek authors are given in Bleek, Hebrew-Br. 2:1, p. 538f); passive wJrismenov, ‘determinate,’ settled, Acts 2:23; to wJrismenon, “that which hath been determined,” according to “appointment, decree,” Luke 22:22; with an accusative of person Acts 17:31 (wJ by attraction for oJn (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 24, 1; Buttmann, sec. 143, 8)); passive with a predicate nominative, Romans 1:4 (for although Christ was the Son of God before his resurrection, yet he was openly appointed (A.V. “declared”) such among men by this transcendent and crowning event); oJrizw, “to ordain, determine, appoint,” Acts 10:42; followed by an infinitive Acts 11:29 (Sophocles from 19 d. (i.e. Aegeus (539), viii., p. 8, Brunck edition)). (Compare: aforizw, apodiorizw, prwrizw.)*

oJrion, oJriou, to (from oJrov (boundary)) (fr. Sophocles down), “a bound, limit,” in the N.T. always in plural (like Latin fines) “boundaries” (R.V. “borders”), equivalent to “region, district, land, territory”: Matthew 2:16; 4:13; 8:34; 15:22,39; 19:1; Mark 5:17; 7:24 L T Tr WH,31; 10:1; Acts 13:50. (the Septuagint very often for lWbG]; several times for hl;WbG].)*

oJrkizw; (oJrkov);

1. “to force to take an oath, to administer an oath to”: Xenophon, conviv. 4, 10; Demosthenes, Polybius; cf. Lob. ad Phryn., p. 361.

2. “to adjure” (“solemnly implore”), with two accusative of person, viz. of the one who is adjured and of the one by whom he is adjured (cf. Matthiae, sec. 413, 10; (Buttmann, 147 (128))): 1 Thessalonians 5:27 R G (see enorkizw); Mark 5:7; Acts 19:13. (the Septuagint for [yæBiv]hi, tina followed by kata with the genitive, 1 Kings 2:42 (1 Kings 3:42); 2 Chronicles 36:13; en, Nehemiah 13:25.) (Compare: enorkizw, exorkizw.)*

oJrkov, oJrkou, oJ (from ergw, eirgw; equivalent to eJrkov an enclosure, confinement; hence, Latin orcus) (from Homer down), the Septuagint for h[;Wbv], “an oath”: Matthew 14:7,9; 26:72; Mark 6:26; Luke 1:73 (Winer’s Grammar, 628 (583); Buttmann, sec. 144, 13); Acts 2:30 (Winer’s Grammar, 226 (212); 603 (561)); Hebrews 273 6:16f; James 5:12; by metonymy, “that which has been pledged or promised with an oath”; plural “vows,” Matthew 5:33 ((cf. Wünsche ad loc.)).*

oJrkwmosia, oJrkwmosiav, hJ (oJrkwmatew (oJrkov and omnumi); cf. apwmosia, antwmosia), “affirmation made on oath, the taking of an oath, an oath”: Hebrews 7:20(21),21,28. (Ezekiel 17:18; 1 Esdr. 8:90 (92); Josephus, Antiquities 16, 6, 2. Cf. Delitzsch, Commentary on Hebrew, the passage cited.)*

oJrmaw, oJrmw: 1 aorist wJrmhsa; (from oJrmh);

1. transitive, “to set in rapid motion, stir up, incite, urge on”; so from Homer down.

2. intransitive, “to start forward impetuously, to rush” (so from Homer down): eiv ti, Matthew 8:32; Mark 5:13; Luke 8:33; Acts 19:29; epi tina, Acts 7:57.*

oJrmh, oJrmhv, hJ (from the root, sar, to go, flow; Fick i., p. 227; Curtius, sec. 502), from Homer down, “a violent motion, impulse”: James 3:4; “a hostile movement, onset, assault,” Acts 14:5 (cf. Trench, sec. lxxxvii.).*

oJrmhma, oJrmhmatov, to (oJrmaw), “a rush, impulse”: Revelation 18:21 (here A.V. “violence”). (For hr;b][, outburst of wrath, Amos 1:11; Hab. 3:8, cf. Schleusner, Thesaurus iv., p. 123; “an enterprise, venture,” Homer, Iliad 2, 356, 590, although interpreters differ about its meaning there (cf. Ebeling, Lex. Homer or Liddell and Scott, v.); “that to which one is impelled or hurried away by impulse” (rather, “incitement, stimulus”), Plutarch, mor. (de virt. mor. sec. 12), p. 452c.)*
orneon, orneou, to, “a bird”: Revelation 18:2; 19:17, 21. (The Septuagint; Homer, Thucydides, Xenophon, Plato; Josephus, Antiquities 3, 1, 5.)*

ornix (so manuscripts a D), equivalent to orniv (which see): Luke 13:34 Tdf. The nominative is not found in secular writings, but the trisyllabic forms ornicov, ornici for orniqov, etc., are used in Doric; (Photius (edited by Porson, p. 348, 22) Iwnev ornix ... kai Dwrieiv ornix. Cf. Curtius, p. 495).* 274 orniv, orniqov, oJ, hJ (OROO, ornumi, (see orqrov));

1. “a bird”; so from Homer down.

2. specifically, “a cock, a hen”: Matthew 23:37; Luke 13:34 (Tdf. ornix, which see); (so Aeschylus Eum. 866; Xenophon, an. 4, 5, 25; Theocritus, Polybius 12, 26, 1; (others)).*

oJroqesia, oJroqesiav, hJ (from oJroqethv; and this from oJrov (a boundary; see oJrion), and tiqhmi); a. properly, “a setting of boundaries, laying down limits”. b. “a definite limit”; plural “bounds,” Acts 17:26. (Ecclesiastical writings; (Winer’s Grammar, 25).)*

orov, orouv, to (ORW, ornumi (i.e. a rising; see orqroi])) (from Homer down), the Septuagint for rhæ, “a mountain”: Matthew 5:14; Luke 3:5; Revelation 6:14, and often; to orov, the mountain nearest the place spoken of, the mountain near by (but see oJ, II. 1 b.), Matthew 5:1; Mark 3:13; Luke 9:28; John 6:3,15; plural orh, Matthew 18:12; 24:16; Mark 5:5; Revelation 6:16, etc.; genitive plural orewn (on this uncontracted form, used also in Attic, cf. Alexander Buttmann (1873) Gram. sec. 49 note 3; Winer’s Grammar, sec. 9, 2 c.; (Buttmann, 14 (13); Dindorf in Fleckeisen’s Jahrb. for 1869, p. 83)), Revelation 6:15; orh meqistanein a proverb. phrase, used also by rabbinical writings, “to remove mountains,” i.e. “to accomplish most difficult, stupendous, incredible things”: 1 Corinthians 13:2, cf. Matthew 17:20; 21:21; Mark 11:23.

orussw: 1 aorist wruxa; from Homer down; the Septuagint for rpæj,; hr;K,; etc.; “to dig”: to make ti by digging, Mark 12:1; ti en tini, Matthew 21:33; equivalent to to make a pit, en th gh, Matthew 25:18 (here T Tr WH wruxen ghn). (Compare: diorussw, exorussw.)*

orfanov, orfanh, orfanon (ORFOS, Latin orbus; (Curtius, sec. 404)), from Homer, Odyssey 20, 68 down, the Septuagint for µwOty;; “bereft” (of a father, of parents), James 1:27 (A.V. “fatherless”); of those bereft of a teacher, guide, guardian, John 14:18 (Lamentations 5:3).* 275

orceomai, orcoumai: 1 aorist wrchsamhn; (from corov, by transposition orcov; cf. aJrpw, aJrpazw, and Latin rapio, morfh and Latin forma; (but these supposed transpositions are extremely doubtful, cf. Curtius, sec. 189; Fick 4:207, 167. Some connect orceomai with the root, argh, ‘to put in rapid motion’; cf. Vanicek, p. 59)); “to dance”: Matthew 11:17; 14:6; Mark 6:22; Luke 7:32. (From Homer down; the Septuagint for dqær;, 1 Chronicles 15:29; Ecclus. 3:4; 2 Samuel 6:21.)*

oJv, hJ, oJ, the postpositive article, which has the force of:

I. a demonstrative pronoun, “this, that” (Latin hic, haec, hoc; German emphatic der, die, das); in the N.T. only in the following instances: oJv de, “but he” (German er aber), John 5:11 L Tr WH; (Mark 15:23 T Tr text WH; cf. Buttmann, sec. 126, 2); in distributions and distinctions: oJv men ... oJv de, “this ... that, one ... another, the one ... the other,” Matthew 21:35; 22:5 L T Tr WH; 25:15; Luke 23:33; Acts 27:44; Romans 14:5; 1 Corinthians 7:7 R G; 11:21; 2 Corinthians 2:16; Jude 1:22; oJ men ... oJ de, “the one ... the other,” Romans 9:21; (oJ men ... oJ de ... oJ de, “some ... some ... some,” Matthew 13:23 L T WH); oJ de ... oJ de ... oJ de, “some ... some ... some,” Matthew 13:8; wJ (masculine) men ... allw (de) ... eJterw de (but L T Tr WH omit this de) k.t.l., 1 Corinthians 12:8-10 oJ men ... allo de (L text T Tr WH kai allo), Mark 4:4; with a variation of the construction also in the following passages: oJ men ... kai eJteron, Luke 8:5; oJuv men with the omission of oJuv de by anacoluthon, 1 Corinthians 12:28; oJv men ... oJ de asqenwn etc. “one man ... but he that is weak” etc. Romans 14:2. On this use of the pronoun, chiefly by later writers from Demosth. down, cf. Matthiae, sec. 289 Anm. 7; Kühner, sec. 518, 4 b. ii., p. 780; (Jelf, sec. 816, 3 b.); Alexander Buttmann (1873) Gram. sec. 126, 3; Buttmann, 101 (89); Winer’s Grammar, 105 (100); Fritzsche on Mark, p. 507.

II. a relative pronoun “who, which, what”;

1. in the common construction, according to which the relative agrees as respects its gender with the noun or pronoun which is its antecedent, but as respects case is governed by its own verb, or by a substantive, or by a preposition: oJ asthr oJn eidon, Matthew 2:9; oJ ... Ioudaiov oJu oJ epainov k.t.l., Romans 2:29; oJutov peri oJu egw akouw toiauta, Luke 9:9; apo thv hJmerav, af’ hJv, Acts 20:18; Qeov di’ oJu, ex 276 oJu, 1 Corinthians 8:6, and numberless other examples it refers to a more remote noun in 1 Corinthians 1:8, where the antecedent of oJv is not the nearest noun Ihsou Cristou, but tw Qew in 4; yet cf. Winer’s Grammar, 157 (149); as in this passage, so very often elsewhere the relative is the subject of its own clause: anhr oJv etc. James 1:12; pav oJv, Luke 14:33; oudeiv oJv, Mark 10:29; Luke 18:29, and many other examples

2. in constructions peculiar in some respect;

a. the gender of the relative is sometimes made to conform to that of the following noun: thv aulhv, oJ esti praitwrion, Mark 15:16; lampadev, aJ eisi (L estin) ta pneumata, Revelation 4:5 (L T WH); spermati, oJv esti Cristov, Galatians 3:16; add, Ephesians 1:14 (L WH text Tr marginal reading oJ); 6:17; 1 Timothy 3:15; Revelation 5:8 (T WH marginal reading aJ); cf. Herm. ad Vig., p. 708; Matthiae, sec. 440, p. 989f; Winer’s Grammar, sec. 24, 3; Buttmann, sec. 143, 3.

b. in constructions ad sensum (cf. Buttmann, sec. 143, 4); [a]. the plural of the relative is used after collective nouns in the singular (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 21, 3; Buttmann, as above): plhqov polu, oJi hlqon, Luke 6:17; pan to presbuterion, par’ wJn, Acts 22:5; geneav, en oJiv, Philippians 2:15. [b]. kata pasan polin, en aJiv, Acts 15:36; tauthn deuteran uJmin grafw epistolhn, en aJiv (because the preceding context conveys the idea of two Epistles), 2 Peter 3:1. [g]. the gender of the relative is conformed not to the grammatical but to the natural gender its antecedent (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 21, 2; Buttmann, as above): paidarion oJv, John 6:9 L T Tr WH; qhrion oJv, of Nero, as antichrist, Revelation 13:14 L T Tr WH; kefalh oJv, of Christ, Colossians 2:19; (add musthrion oJv etc. 1 Timothy 3:16 G L T Tr WH; cf. Buttmann, as above; Winer’s Grammar, 588f (547)); skeuh (of men) oJuv,Ro. 9:24; eqnh oJi, Acts 15:17; 26:17; tekna, teknia oJi, John 1:13; Galatians 4:19; 2 John 1:1 (Euripides, suppl. 12); teknon oJv, Philemon 1:10.

c. In attractions (Buttmann, sec. 143, 8; Winer’s Grammar, sections 24, 1; 66, 4ff); 277 [a]. the accusative of the relative pronoun depending on a transitive, verb is changed by attraction into the oblique case of its antecedent: ktisewv hJv ektisen oJ Qeov, Mark 13:19 (R G); tou rhmatov oJu eipen, Mark 14:72 (Rec.); add, John 4:14; 7:31,39 (but Tr marginal reading WH marginal reading oJ); 15:20; 21:10; Acts 3:21,25; 7:17,45; 9:36; 10:39; 22:10; Romans 15:18; 1 Corinthians 6:19; 2 Corinthians 1:6; 10:8,13; Ephesians 1:8; Titus 3:5(RG),6; Hebrews 6:10; 9:20; James 2:5; 1 John 3:24; Jude 1:15; for other examples see below; en aJra hJ ou ginwskei, Matthew 24:50; th paradosei hJ paredwkate, Mark 7:13; add, Luke 2:20; 5:9; 9:43; 12:46; 24:25; John 17:5; Acts 2:22; 17:31; 20:38; 2 Corinthians 12:21; 2 Thessalonians 1:4; Revelation 18:6; cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 24, 1; (Buttmann, as above). Rarely attraction occurs where the verb governs the dative (but see below): thus, katenanti oJu episteuse Qeou for katenanti Qeou, wJ episteuse (see katenanti), Romans 4:17; fwnhv, hJv ekraxa (for hJ (others, hJn, cf. Winer’s Grammar, 164 (154f) Buttmann, 287 (247))), Acts 24:21, cf. The following expressions, however, can hardly be brought under this construction: thv caritov hJv ecaritwsen (as if for hJ), Ephesians 1:6 L T Tr WH; thv klhsewv, hJv eklhqhte, Ephesians 4:1; dia thv paraklhsewv hJv parakaloumeqa, 2 Corinthians 1:4, but must be explained agreeably to such phrases as carin caritoun, klhsin kalein, etc. ((i.e. accusative of kindred abstract substantive; cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 32, 2; Buttmann, sec. 131, 5)); cf. Winer’s Grammar, (and Buttmann, as above). [b]. The noun to which the relative refers is so conformed to the case of the relative clause that either [aa]. it is itself incorporated into the relative construction, but without the article (Buttmann, sec. 143, 7; Winer’s Grammar, sec. 24, 2 b.): oJn 278 egw apekefalisa Iwannhn, oJutov hgerqh, for Iwannhv, oJn k.t.l., Mark 6:16; add, Luke 24:1; Philemon 1:10; Romans 6:17; eiv hJn oikian, ekei, equivalent to en th oikia, eiv hJn, Luke 9:4; or [bb]. it is placed before the relative clause, either with or without the article (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 24, 2 a.; Buttmann, sec. 144, 13): ton arton oJn klwmen, ouci koinwnia tou swmatov, 1 Corinthians 10:16; liqon oJn apedokimasan oJi oikodomountev, oJutov egenhqh (for oJ liqov, oJv k.t.l.), Matthew 21:42; Mark 12:10; Luke 20:17; 1 Peter 2:7. [g]. [d]. A noun common to both the principal clause and the relative is placed in the relative clause after the relative pronoun (Winer’s Grammar, 165 (156)): en wJ krimati krinete, kriqhsesqe, for kriqhsesqe en tw krimati, en wJ krinete, Matthew 7:2; 24:44; Mark 4:24; Luke 12:40, etc.

Buttmann, sec. 129, 6): lepta duo, oJ esti kodranthv, Mark 12:42; agaphn, oJ esti sundesmov, Colossians 3:14 L T Tr WH; artouv, oJ etc. Matthew 12:4 L text T Tr WH.

b. is used in the phrases (Buttmann, as above] — oJ estin, “which (term) signifies”: Boanergev oJ estin uJioi bronthv, Mark 3:17; add, 5:41; 7:11, 34; Hebrews 7:2; oJ esti meqermhneuomenon, and the like: Matthew 1:23; Mark 15:34; John 1:38 (39), 41f (42f); 9:7; 20:16.

Buttmann, sec. 143, 3)) estin alhqev, 1 John 2:8; oJ (namely, to have one’s lot assigned in the lake of fire) estin oJ qanatov oJ deuterov, Revelation 21:8.

osfuv (or osfuv, so R Tr in Ephesians 6:14; G in Matthew 3:4; cf. Chandler sections 658, 659; Tdf. Proleg., p. 101), osfuov, hJ, from Aeschylus and Herodotus down;
