2. “a loin,” the Septuagint several times for µyixæl]j}, “the (two) loins,” where the Hebrews thought the generative power (semen) resided (?); hence, karpov thv osfuov, fruit of the loins, offspring, Acts 2:30 (see karpov, 1 at the end); exercesqai ek thv osfuov tinov, to come forth out of one’s loins i.e. derive one’s origin or descent from one, Hebrews 287 7:5 (see exercomai, 2 b.); eti en th osfui tinov, to be yet in the loins of someone (an ancestor), Hebrews 7:10.*

oJtan, a particle of time, compound of oJte and an, “at the time that, whenever” (German dann wann; wann irgend); used of things which one assumes will really occur, but the time of whose occurrence he does not definitely fix (in secular authors often also of things which one assumes can occur, but whether they really will or not he does not know; hence, like our “in case that,” as in Plato, Prot., p. 360 b.; Phaedr., p. 256 e.; Phaedo,

p. 68 d.); (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 42, 5; Buttmann, sec. 139, 33);

a. with the subjunctive present: Matthew 6:2,5; 10:23; Mark 13:11 (here Rec. aorist); 14:7; Luke 11:36; 12:11; 14:12f; 21:7; John 7:27; 16:21; Acts 23:35; 1 Corinthians 3:4; 2 Corinthians 13:9; 1 John 5:2; Revelation 10:7; 18:9; preceded by a specification of time: eJwv thv hJmerav ekeinhv, oJtan etc., Matthew 26:29; Mark 14:25; followed by tote, 1 Thessalonians 5:3; 1 Corinthians 15:28; equivalent to “as often as,” of customary action, Matthew 15:2; John 8:44; Romans 2:14; “at the time when” equivalent to “as long as,” Luke 11:34; John 9:5.

b. with the subjunctive aorist: equivalent to the Latin quando acciderit, ut with subjunctive present, Matthew 5:11; 12:43; 13:32; 23:15, 24:32; Mark 4:15f,29 (R G), 31f; 13:28; Luke 6:22, 26; 8:13; 11:24; 12:54f; 21:30; John 2:10; 10:4; 16:21; 1 Timothy 5:11 (here L marginal reading future); Revelation 9:5. equivalent to quando with future perfect, Matthew 19:28; 21:40; Mark 8:38; 9:9; 12:23 (G Tr WH omit; L brackets the clause), 25; Luke 9:26; 16:4,9; 17:10; John 4:25; 7:31; 13:19; 14:29; 15:26; 16:4,13,21; 21:18; Acts 23:35; 24:22; Romans 11:27; 1 Corinthians 15:24 (here L T Tr WH present), 27 (where the meaning is, ‘when he shall have said that the uJpotaxiv predicted in the Psalm is now accomplished’; cf. Meyer ad loc.); 16:2,5,12; 2 Corinthians 10:6; Colossians 4:16; 1 John 2:28 (L T Tr WH ean); 2 Thessalonians 1:10; Hebrews 1:6 (on which see eisagw, 1); Revelation 11:7; 12:4; 17:10; 20:7. followed by tote, Matthew 9:15; 24:15; 25:31; Mark 2:20; 13:14; Luke 5:35; 21:20; John 8:28; 1 Corinthians 13:10 (G L T Tr WH omit tote); 15:28, 54; Colossians 3:4. 288

c. According to the usage of later authors, a usage, however, not altogether unknown to the more elegant writers (Winer’s Grammar, 309 (289f); Buttmann, 222f (192f); (Tdf. Proleg., p. 124f; WH’s Appendix, p. 171; for examples additional to these given by Winer’s Grammar, and Buttmann, as above see Sophocles’ Lexicon, under the word; cf. Jebb in Vincent and Dickson’s Handbook to Modern Greek, Appendix, sec. 78)), with the indicative; [a]. future: “when” (Matthew 5:11 Tdf.); Luke 13:28 T Tr text WH marginal reading; (1 Timothy 5:11 L marginal reading); “as often as,” Revelation 4:9 (cf. Bleek ad loc.). [b]. present: Mark 11:25 L T Tr WH; Mark 13:7 Tr text; (Luke 11:2 Tr marginal reading). [g]. very rarely indeed, with the imperfect: “as often as,” (whensoever), oJtan eqewroun, Mark 3:11 (Genesis 38:9; Exodus 17:11; 1 Samuel 17:34; see an, II. 1). [d]. As in Byzantine authors equivalent to oJte, “when,” with the indicative aorist: oJtan hnoixen, Revelation 8:1 L T Tr WH; (add oJtan oye egeneto, Mark 11:19 T Tr text WH, cf. Buttmann, 223 (193); but others take this of customary action, “whenever evening came” (i.e. “every evening,” R.V.)). oJtan, does not occur in the Epistles of Peter and Jude.

oJte, a particle of time (from Homer down), “when”;

1. with the indicative (Winer’s Grammar, 296f (278f)); indicative present (of something certain and customary, see Herm. ad Vig., p. 913f), “while”: John 9:4; Hebrews 9:17; with an historical present Mark 11:1. with the imperfect (of a thing done on occasion or customary); Mark 14:12; 15:41; Mark 6:21 R G; John 21:18; Acts 12:6; 22:20; Romans 6:20; 7:5; 1 Corinthians 13:11; Galatians 4:3; Colossians 3:7; 1 Titus 3:4; 2 Thessalonians 3:10; 1 Peter 3:20. with an indicative aorist, Latin quom with pluperfect (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 40, 5; (Buttmann, sec. 137, 6)): Matthew 9:25; 13:26,48; 17:25 (R G); 21:34; Mark 1:32; 4:10; 8:19; 15:20; Luke 2:21f,42; 4:25; 6:(3 L T WH), 13; 22:14; 23:33; John 1:19; 2:22; 4:45 (where Tdf. wJv), etc.; Acts 1:13; 8:12,39; 11:2; 21:5,35; 27:39; 28:16; Romans 13:11 (“than when we gave in our allegiance to Christ;” Latin quom Christo nomen dedissemus (R.V. “than when we first believed”)); 289 Galatians 1:15; 2:11,12,14; 4:4; Philippians 4:15; Hebrews 7:10; Revelation 1:17; 6:3,5,7,9,12; 8:1, etc.; so also Matthew 12:3; Mark 2:25; (John 12:41 R Tr marginal reading oJte eiden, when it had presented itself to his sight (but best texts oJti: “because” he saw etc.)). egeneto, oJte etelesen, a common phrase in Matthew, viz. Matthew 7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1. oJte ... tote, Matthew 21:1; John 12:16. with the indicative perfect, “since” (R.V. “now that” I am become), 1 Corinthians 13:11; with the indicative future: Luke 17:22; John 4:21,23; 5:25; 16:25; Romans 2:16 (R G T Tr text WH marginal reading) (where Lachmann hJ (others besides)); 2 Timothy 4:3.

2. with the aorist subjunctive: eJwv an hJxh, oJte eiphte (where oJtan, might have been expected), until the time have come, when ye have said, Luke 13:35 (R G (cf. Tr brackets)); cf. Matthiae, ii., p. 1196f; Bornemann, Scholia in Lucae evang., p. 92; Winer’s Grammar, 298 (279); (Bernhardy (1829), p. 400; cf. Buttmann, 231f (199)).

ou before a consonant, ouk before a vowel with a smooth breathing, and ouc before an aspirated vowel; but sometimes in the best manuscripts ouc occurs even before a smooth breathing; accordingly, L T WH marginal reading have adopted ouc idou, Acts 2:7; L T ouc Ioudaikwv, Galatians 2:14 (see WH, Introduction, sec. 409); L ouc oligov, Acts 19:23; ouc hgaphsan, Revelation 12:11; and 294 contrariwise ouk before an aspirate, as ouk eJsthken, John 8:44 T; (ouk eJneken, 2 Corinthians 7:12 T); (ouk eJuron, Luke 24:3; (ouk uJparcei, Acts 3:6) in manuscript a (also C*; cf. the Alexandrian LXX manuscript in 1 Esdr. 4:2,12; Job 19:16; 38:11, 26)); cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 5, 1 d. 14; Buttmann, 7; (A.V. Schütz, Hist. Alphab. Art., Berol. 1875, pp. 54-58; Sophocles, Hist. of Greek Alphab., 1st edition 1848, p. 64f (on the breathing); Tdf., the Septuagint, edition 4, Proleg., pp. xxxiii. xxxiv.; Scrivener, Collation etc., 2nd edition, p. 55: no. 9; id. manuscript Bezae, p. xlvii. no. 11 (cf. p. xiii. no. 5); Kuenen and Cobet, N.T. etc., p. 87f; Tdf. Proleg., p. 90f; WH. Introductory sections 405ff, and Appendix, p. 143f); the Septuagint for alo, ˆyiaæ, ˆyae; a particle of negation, “not” (how it differs from mh has been explained in mh, at the beginning); it is used:

1. absolutely and accented, ou, “nay, no” (Winer’s Grammar, 476 (444)): in answers, oJ de fhsin. ou, Matthew 13:29; apekriqh. Ou, John 1:21; (21:5), cf. 7:12; repeated, ou ou, it strengthens the negation, “nay, nay, by no means,” Matthew 5:37; htw uJmwn to ou ou, let your denial be truthful, James 5:12; on 2 Corinthians 1:17-19, see nai.

2. It is joined to other words — to a finite verb, simply to deny that what is declared in the verb applies to the subject of the sentence: Matthew 1:25 (ouk eginwsken authn); Mark 3:25; Luke 6:43; John 10:28; Acts 7:5; Romans 1:16, and times without number. It has the same force when conjoined to participles: wJv ouk aera derwn, 1 Corinthians 9:26; ouk ontov autw teknou, at the time when he had no child, Acts 7:5 (mh ontov would be, “although he had no child”); add, Romans 8:20; 1 Corinthians 4:14; 2 Corinthians 4:8; Galatians 4:8,27; Colossians 2:19; Philippians 3:3; Hebrews 11:35; 1 Peter 1:8; oJ ... ouk wn poimhn, John 10:12 (where according to classical usage mh must have been employed, because such a person is imagined as is not a shepherd; (cf. Buttmann, 351 (301) and mh,

I. 5 b.)). in relative sentences: eisin ... tinev oJi ou pisteuousin, John 6:64; add, Matthew 10:38; 12:2; Luke 6:2; Romans 15:21; Galatians 3:10, etc.; ouk estin oJv and ouden estin oJ followed by a future: Matthew 10:26; Luke 8:17; 12:2; tiv estin, oJv ou followed by a present indicative: Acts 19:35; Hebrews 12:7; cf. Winer’s Grammar, 481 (448); Buttmann, 355 (305); in statements introduced by oJti after verbs of understanding, perceiving, saying, etc.: 295 John 5:42; 8:55, etc.; oJti ouk (where ouk is pleonastic) after arneisqai, 1 John 2:22; cf. Buttmann, sec. 148, 13; (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 65, 2 [b].); — to an infinitive, where mh might have been expected: tiv eti creia kata thn taxin Melcisedek eJteron anistasqai iJerea kai ou kata thn taxin Aarwn legesqai, Hebrews 7:11 (where the difficulty is hardly removed by saying (e.g. with Winer’s Grammar, 482 (449)) that ou belongs only to kata thn taxin Aarwn, not to the infinitive). it serves to deny other parts of statements: ouk en sofia logou, 1 Corinthians 1:17; ou melani, ouk en plaxi liqinaiv, 2 Corinthians 3:3, and many other examples; — to deny the object, eleov (R G eleon) qelw, ou qusian, Matthew 9:13; 12:7; ouk eme decetai, Mark 9:37. It blends with the term to which it is prefixed into a single and that an affirmative idea (Winer’s Grammar, 476 (444); cf. Buttmann, 347 (298)); as, ouk eaw, “to present, hinder,” Acts 16:7; 19:30 (cf., on this phrase, Herm. ad Vig., p. 887f); ouk ecw, “to be poor,” Matthew 13:12; Mark 4:25 (see ecw, I. 2 a.,

p. 266{b}); ta ouk anhkonta (or aJ ouk anhken, L T Tr WH), “unseemly, dishonorable,” Ephesians 5:4 (see mh, I. 5 d. at the end, p. 410a; (cf. Buttmann, sec. 148, 7{a}.; Winer’s Grammar, 486 (452))); often so as to form a litotes; as, ouk agnoew, “to know well,” 2 Corinthians 2:11 (Sap. 12:10); ouk oligoi, not a few, i.e. very many, Acts 17:4,12; 19:23f; 15:2; 14:28; 27:20; ou pollai hJmerai, a few days, Luke 15:13; John 2:12; Acts 1:5; ou polu, Acts 27:14; ou metriwv, Acts 20:12; ouk ashmov, not undistinguished (A.V. “no mean” etc.), Acts 21:39; ouk ek metrou, John 3:34. it serves to limit the term to which it is joined: ou pantwv, “not altogether, not entirely” (see pantwv, c. [b].); ou pav, “not any and every one,” Matthew 7:21; plural, ou pantev, “not all,” Matthew 19:11; Romans 9:6; 10:16; ou pasa sarx, not every kind of flesh, 1 Corinthians 15:39; ou panti tw law, not to all the people, Acts 10:41; on the other hand, when ou is joined to the verb, pav ... ou must be rendered “no one, no” (as in Hebrew, now lK; ... alo, now alo ... lK;; cf. Winer, Lex. Hebrew et Chald., p. 513f): Luke 1:31; Ephesians 5:5; 1 John 2:21; Revelation 22:3; pasa sarx ... ou with a verb, “no flesh, no mortal,” Matthew 24:22; Mark 13:20; Romans 3:20; Galatians 2:16; cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 26, 1; (Buttmann, 121 (106)). Joined to a noun it denies and annuls the idea of the noun; as, ton ou laon, a people that is not a people (German ein Nichtvolk, “a no 296 people”), Romans 9:25, cf. 1 Peter 2:10; ep’ ouk eqnei (R.V. “with that which is no nation”), Romans 10:19 (so alo µ[;; alo laæ, a no-god, Deuteronomy 32:21; alo x[e, “a not-wood,” Isaiah 10:15; ouk arciereuv, 2 Macc. 4:13; hJ ou dialusiv, Thucydides 1, 137, 4; hJ ou periteicisiv 3, 95, 2; hJ ouk exousia 5, 50, 3; di’ apeirosunan ... kouk apodeixin, Euripides, Hippolytus 196, and other examples in Greek writings; “non sutor,” Horace sat. 2, 3, 106; “non corpus,” Cicero, acad. 1, 39 at the end); cf. Winer’s Grammar, 476 (444); (Buttmann, sec. 148, 9); hJ ouk hgaphmenh, Romans 9:25; oJi ouk hlhemenoi, 1 Peter 2:10.

3. followed by another negative,

a. it strengthens the negation: ou krinw oudena, John 8:15; add, Mark 5:37; 2 Corinthians 11:9 (8); oJu ouk hn oudepw oudeiv keimenov, Luke 23:53 (see oudepw); ouk ... ouden, nothing at all, Luke 4:2; John 6:63; 11:49; 12:19; 15:5; ou melei soi peri oudenov, Matthew 22:16; ouk ... ouketi, Acts 8:39; cf. Matthiae, sec. 609, 3; Kühner, ii. sec. 516; Winer’s Grammar, sec. 55, 9{b}; (Buttmann, sec. 148, 11).

b. as in Latin, it changes a negation into an affirmation (cf. Matthiae, sec. 609, 2; Klotz ad Devar. ii. 2, p. 695f; Winer’s Grammar, sec. 55, 9 a.; Buttmann, sec. 148, 12); ou para touto ouk estin ek tou swmatov, “not on this account is it not of the body,” i.e. it belongs to the body, does not cease to be of the body, 1 Corinthians 12:15; ou dunameqa aJ eidomen kai hkousamen mh lalein, “we are unable not to speak” (A.V. “we cannot but speak”), Acts 4:20.

4. It is used in disjunctive statements where one thing is denied that another may be established (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 55, 8; cf. Buttmann, 356 (306)): ouk ... alla, Luke 8:52; 24:6 (WH reject the clause); John 1:33; 7:10,12,16; 8:49; Acts 10:41; Romans 8:20; 1 Corinthians 15:10; 2 Corinthians 3:3; 8:5; Hebrews 2:16, etc.; see alla II. 1; ouc iJna ... all’ iJna, John 3:17; ouc iJna ... alla, John 6:38; ou monon ... alla kai, see alla, II. 1 and monov, 2; ouk ... ei mh, see ei, III. 8 c., p. 171{b}; ou mh with subjunctive aorist followed by ei mh, Revelation 21:27 (see ei as above, [b].).

5. It is joined to other particles: ou mh, “not at all, by no means, surely not, in no wise,” see mh, IV.; ou mhketi with aorist subjunctive Matthew 297 21:19 L T Tr marginal reading WH. mh ou, where mh is interrogative (Latin num) and ou negative (cf. Buttmann, 248 (214), 354 (304); Winer’s Grammar, 511 (476)): Romans 10:18f; 1 Corinthians 9:4f; 11:22. ei ou, see ei, III. 11, p. 172a. ou gar (see gar, I., p. 109b), Acts 16:37.

6. As in Hebrew alo with imperfect, so in Biblical Greek ou with 2 person future is used in emphatic prohibition (in secular authors it is milder; cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 43, 5 c.; also 501f (467f); (Buttmann, sec. 139, 64); Fritzsche on Matthew, p. 259f (cf. p. 252f) thinks otherwise, but not correctly): Matthew 6:5; and besides in the moral precepts of the O.T., Matthew 4:7; 19:18; Luke 4:12; Acts 23:5; Romans 7:7; 13:9.

7. ou is used interrogatively — when an affirmative answer is expected (Latin nonne; (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 57, 3{a}; Buttmann, 247 (213))): Matthew 6:26,30; 17:24; Mark 4:21; 12:24; Luke 11:40; John 4:35; 7:25; Acts 9:21; Romans 9:21; 1 Corinthians 9:1,6f,12; James 2:4, and often; ouk oidate k.t.l.; and the like, see eidw, II. 1,

p. 174{a}; all’ ou, Hebrews 3:16 (see alla, I. 10, p. 28{a}); ouk apokrinh ouden; answerest thou nothing at all? Mark 14:60; 15:4; — where an exclamation of reproach or wonder, which denies directly, may take the place of a negative question: Mark 4:13,38; Luke 17:18; Acts 13:10 (cf. Buttmann, sec. 139, 65); 21:38 (on which see ara, 1); cf. Winer’s Grammar, as above; ou mh piw auto; shall I not drink it? John 18:11; cf. Winer’s Grammar, p. 512 (477); (cf. Buttmann, sec. 139, 2).

oua, Tdf. oua (see Proleg., p. 101; cf. Chandler sec. 892), “Ah! Ha!” an interjection of wonder and amazement: Epictetus diss. 3, 22, 34; 3, 23, 24; Dio Cassius, 63, 20; called out by the overthrow of a boastful adversary, Mark 15:29.*

ouai, an interjection of grief or of denunciation; the Septuagint chiefly for ywOh and ywOa; “Alas! Woe!” with a dat of person added, Matthew 11:21; 18:7; 23:13-16,23,25,27,29; 24:19; 26:24; Mark 13:17; 14:21; Luke 6:24-26; 10:13; 11:42-44,46f,52; 21:23; 22:22; Jude 1:11; Revelation 12:12 R G L, small edition. (see below) (Numbers 21:29; Isaiah 3:9, and often in the Septuagint); thrice repeated, and followed by a dative, Revelation 8:13 R G L WH marginal reading (see below); the dative is omitted in Luke 17:1; twice 298 repeated and followed by a nominative in place of a vocative, Revelation 18:10,16,19 (Isaiah 1:24; 5:8-22; Habakkuk 2:6, 12, etc.); exceptionally, with an accusative of the person, in Revelation 8:13 T Tr WH text, and 12:12 L T Tr WH; this accusative, I think, must be regarded either as an accusative of exclamation (cf. Matthiae, sec. 410), or as an imitation of the construction of the accusative after verbs of injuring (Buttmann, sec. 131, 14 judges otherwise); with the addition of apo and a genitive of the evil the infliction of which is deplored (cf. Buttmann, 322 (277); Winer’s Grammar, 371 (348)), Matthew 18:7; also of ek, Revelation 8:13. As a substantive, hJ ouai (the writer seems to have been led to use the feminine by the similarity of hJ qliyiv or hJ talaipwria; cf. Winer’s Grammar, 179 (169)) “woe, calamity”: Revelation 9:12; 11:14; duo ouai, Revelation 9:12 (ouai epi ouai estai, Ezekiel 7:26; ouai hJmav lhyetai Evang. Nicod. c. 21 (Pars ii., v. 1 (edited by Tdf.))); so also in the phrase ouai moi estin, “woe is unto me,” i.e. divine penalty threatens me, 1 Corinthians 9:16, cf. Hosea 9:12; (Jeremiah 6:4); Epictetus diss. 3, 19, 1 (frequent in ecclesiastical writings).*

oudamwv (from oudamov, not even one; and this from oude and amov (allied perhaps with aJma; cf. Vanicek, p. 972; Curtius, sec. 600)), adverb, from Herodotus (and Aeschylus) down, “by no means, in no wise”: Matthew 2:6.*

oude (from Homer down), a neg. disjunctive conjunction, compounded of ou and de, and therefore properly, equivalent to “but not”; generally, however, its oppositive force being lost, it serves to continue a negation. (On the elision of e when the next word begins with a vowel (observed by Tdf. in eight instances, neglected in fifty-eight), see Tdf. Proleg., p. 96; cf. WH’s Appendix, p. 146; Winer’s Grammar, sec. 5, 1 a.; Buttmann, p. 10f) It signifies:

1. “and not,” continuing a negation, yet differently from oute; for the latter connects parts or members of the same thing, since te is adjunctive like the Latin que; but oude places side by side things that are equal and mutually exclude each other ((?). There appears to be some mistake here in what is said about ‘mutual exclusion’ (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 55, 6): oude, like de, always makes reference to something preceding; oute to what follows also; the connection of clauses made negative by oute is close and internal, so that they are mutually complementary and combine into a unity, whereas 299 clauses negatived by oude follow one another much more loosely, often almost by accident as it were; see Winer’s Grammar, at the passage cited, and especially the quotations there given from Benfey and Klotz.) It differs from mhde as ou does from mh (which see ad at the beginning); after ou, where each has its own verb: Matthew 5:15 6:28; Mark 4:22; Luke 6:44; Acts 2:27; 9:9; 17:24f; Galatians 1:17; 4:14; ouk oida oude epistamai, Mark 14:68 R G L marginal reading (others, oute ... oute) (Cicero, pro Rosc. American 43, non novi neque scio); cf. Winer’s Grammar, 490 (456) c.; (Buttmann, 367 (315) note); ou ... oude ... oude, “not ... nor ... nor,” Matthew 6:26; oudeiv ... oude ... oude ... oude, Revelation 5:3 (R G; cf. Buttmann, 367 (315); Winer’s Grammar, 491 (457)); ou ... oude; followed by a future ... oude mh followed by subjunctive aorist ... oude, Revelation 7:16. ou ... oude, the same verb being common to both: Matthew 10:24; 25:13; Luke 6:43; 8:17 (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 300 (281); Buttmann, 355 (305) cf. sec. 139, 7); John 6:24; 13:16; Acts 8:21; 16:21; 24:18; Romans 2:28; 9:16; Galatians 1:1; 3:28; 1 Thessalonians 5:5; 1 Timothy 2:12; Revelation 21:23. preceded by oupw, Mark 8:17; — by oudeiv, Matthew 9:17; — by iJna mh, which is followed by oude ... oude, where mhde ... mhde might have been expected (cf. Buttmann, sec. 148, 8; (Winer’s Grammar, 474 (442))) Revelation 9:4. oude gar, “for neither,” John 8:42; Romans 8:7.

2. “also not” (A.V. generally “neither”): Matthew 6:15; 21:27; 25:45; Mark 11:26 (R L); Luke 16:31; John 15:4; Romans 4:15; 11:21; 1 Corinthians 15:13,16; Galatians 1:12 (oude gar egw (cf. Buttmann, 367 (315) note; 492 (458))); Hebrews 8:4, etc.; all’ oude, Luke 23:15; h oude, in a question, “or doth not even” etc.? 1 Corinthians 11:14 Rec.; the simple oude, num ne quidem (“have ye not even” etc.) in a question where a negative answer is assumed (see ou, 7): Mark 12:10; Luke 6:3; 23:40; and G L T Tr WH in 1 Corinthians 11:14.

3. “not even” (Buttmann, 369 (316)): Matthew 6:29; 8:10; Mark 6:31; Luke 7:9; 12:27; John 21:25 (Tdf. omits the verse); 1 Corinthians 5:1; 14:21; oude eJiv (Winer’s Grammar, 173 (163); Buttmann, sec. 127, 32), Acts 4:32; Romans 3:10; 1 Corinthians 6:5 (L T Tr WH oudeiv); oude eJn, John 1:3; all’ oude, Acts 19:2; 1 Corinthians 3:2 (Rec. all’ oute); 4:3; Galatians 2:3. in a 300 double negative for the sake of emphasis, ouk ... oude (Buttmann, 369 (316); Winer’s Grammar, 500 (465)): Matthew 27:14; Luke 18:13; Acts 7:5.

oudeiv, oudemia (the feminine only in these passages: Mark 6:5; Luke 4:26; John 16:29; 18:38; 19:4; Acts 25:18; 27:22; Philippians 4:15; 1 John 1:5, and Rec. in James 3:12), ouden (and, according to a pronunciation not infrequent from Aristotle, and Theophrastus down, ouqeiv, ouqen: 1 Corinthians 13:2 Rst L T Tr WH; Acts 19:27 L T Tr WH; 2 Corinthians 11:8 (9) L T Tr WH; Luke 22:35 T Tr WH; 23:14 T Tr WH; Acts 15:9 T Tr WH text; Acts 26:26 T WH Tr brackets; 1 Corinthians 13:3 Tdf.; see mhdeiv at the beginning and Göttling on Aristotle, pol., p. 218; (Meisterhans, Grammatik d. Attisch. Inschriften, sec. 20, 5; see Liddell and Scott, under the word ouqeiv; cf. Lob. Pathol. Elem. ii. 344); Alexander Buttmann (1873) Ausf. Spr. sec. 10 Anm. 7) (from oude and eJiv) (fr. Homer down), “and not one, no one, none, no”; it differs from mhdeiv as ou does from mh (which see at the beginning);

1. with nouns: masc, Luke 4:24; 16:13; 1 Corinthians 8:4; oudeiv allov, John 15:24; oudemia in the passages given above; neuter, Luke 23:4; John 10:41; Acts 17:21; 23:9; 28:5; Romans 8:1; 14:14; Galatians 5:10, etc.

2. absolutely: oudeiv, Matthew 6:24; 9:16; Mark 3:27; 5:4; 7:24; Luke 1:61; 5:39 (WH in brackets); 7:28; John 1:18; 4:27; Acts 18:10; 25:11; Romans 14:7, and very often. with a partitive genitive: Luke 4:26; 14:24; John 13:28; Acts 5:13; 1 Corinthians 1:14; 2:8; 1 Timothy 6:16. oudeiv ei mh, Matthew 19:17 Rec.; 17:8; Mark 10:18; Luke 18:19; John 3:13; 1 Corinthians 12:3; Revelation 19:12, etc.; ean mh, John 3:2; 6:44,65. ouk ... oudeiv (see ou, 3 a.), Matthew 22:16; Mark 5:37; 6:5; 12:14; Luke 8:43; John 8:15; 18:9,31; Acts 4:12; 2 Corinthians 11:9 (8); ouketi ... oudeiv, Mark 9:8; oudepw ... oudeiv, Luke 23:53 (Tdf. oudeiv ... oudepw; L Tr WH oudeiv oupw); John 19:41; Acts 8:16 (L T Tr WH); oudeiv ... ouketi, Mark 12:34; Revelation 18:11. neuter ouden, “nothing,” Matthew 10:26 (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 300 (281); Buttmann, 355 (305)); Matthew 17:20; 26:62; 27:12, and very often; with a partitive genitive, Luke 9:36; 18:34; Acts 18:17; 1 Corinthians 9:15; 14:10 (R G); ouden ei mh, Matthew 5:13; 301 21:19; Mark 9:29; 11:13; mh tinov; with the answer oudenov, Luke 22:35; ouden ektov with genitive, Acts 26:22; ouden moi diaferei, Galatians 2:6; it follows another negative, thereby strengthening the negation (see ou, 3 a.): Mark 15:4f; 16:8; Luke 4:2; 9:36; 20:40; John 3:27; 5:19,30; 9:33; 11:49; 14:30; Acts 26:26 (Lachmann omits); 1 Corinthians 8:2 (R G); 9:15 (G L T Tr WH); ouden ou mh with aorist subjunctive Luke 10:19 (Rst G WH marginal reading; see mh,

IV. 2). ouden, absolutely, “nothing whatever, not at all, in no wise” (cf. Buttmann, sec. 131, 10): adikein (see adikew, 2 b.), Acts 25:10; Galatians 4:12; ouden diaferein tinov, Galatians 4:1; uJsterein, 2 Corinthians 12:11; wfelein, John 6:63; 1 Corinthians 13:3. ouden estin, it is nothing, of no importance, etc. (cf. Buttmann, sec. 129, 5): Matthew 23:16,18; John 8:54; 1 Corinthians 7:19; with a genitive, “none of these things is true,” Acts 21:24; 25:11; ouden eimi, I am nothing, of no account: 1 Corinthians 13:2; 2 Corinthians 12:11, (see examples from Greek authors in Passow, under the word, 2; (Liddell and Scott, under the word, II. 2; Meyer on 1 Corinthians, the passage cited)); eiv ouden logisqhnai (see logizomai, 1 a.), Acts 19:27; eiv ouden ginesqai, to come to nought, Acts 5:36 (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 29, 3 a.; en oudeni, in no respect, in nothing, Philippians 1:20 (cf. mhdeiv, g.)).

oudepote, adverb, denying absolutely and objectively (from oude and pote, properly, “not ever”) (from Homer down), “never”: Matthew 7:23; 9:33; 26:33; Mark 2:12; (Luke 15:29 (bis)); John 7:46; Acts 10:14; 11:8; 14:8; 1 Corinthians 13:8; Hebrews 10:1,11. interrogatively, “did ye never,” etc.: Matthew 21:16,42; Mark 2:25.*

oudepw, adverb, simply negative (from oude and the enclitic pw) (from Aeschylus down), “not yet, not as yet”: John 7:39 (where L Tr WH oupw); John 20:9. oudepw oudeiv, “never anyone” (A.V. “never man yet”), John 19:41; (oudepw ... ep’ oudeni, “as yet ... upon none,” Acts 8:16 L T Tr WH); ouk ... oudepw oudeiv (see ou, 3 a.), Luke 23:53 (L Tr WH ouk ... oudeiv oupw; Tdf. ouk ... oudeiv oudepw); oudepw ouden (L T Tr WH simply oupw) “not yet” (anything), 1 Corinthians 8:2.*

ouketi (also written separately by Rec.st (generally), Tr (nine times in John), Tdf. (in Philemon 1:16)) (ouk, eti), an adverb which denies simply, and thus differs from mhketi (which see), “no longer, no more, no further”: Matthew 19:6; Mark 10:8: Luke 15:19,21; John 4:42; 6:66; Acts 20:25,38; Romans 6:9; 14:15; 2 Corinthians 5:16; Galatians 3:25; 4:7; Ephesians 2:19; Philemon 1:16; Hebrews 10:18, 26, etc.; ouketi hlqon, I came not again (R.V. “I forebore to come”), 2 Corinthians 1:23. with another neg. particle in order to strengthen the negation: oude ... ouketi, Matthew 22:46; ouk ... ouketi, Acts 8:39; oudeiv ... ouketi, Mark 12:34; Revelation 18:11; ouketi ... ouden, Mark 7:12; 15:5; Luke 20:40; ouketi ... oudena, Mark 9:8; ouketi ou mh, Mark 14:25; Luke 22:16 (WH omits; L Tr brackets ouketi); Revelation 18:14 (Tr omits); oude ... ouketi oudeiv, Mark 5:3 L T WH Tr text ouketi is used logically (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 65, 10); as, ouketi egw for “it cannot now be said” oJti egw etc., Romans 7:17,20; Galatians 2:20; add, Romans 11:6; Galatians 3:18. ((Homer, Hesiod, Herodotus, others))

oukoun (from ouk and oun), adverb, “not therefore”; and since a speaker often introduces in this way his own opinion (see Krüger, as below), the particle is used affirmatively, “therefore, then,” the force of the negative disappearing. Hence, the saying of Pilate oukoun basileuv ei su must be taken affirmatively: “then (since thou speakest of thy basileia) thou art a king!” (German also bist du doch ein König!), John 18:37 (cf. Buttmann, 249 (214)); but it is better to write oukoun, so that Pilate, arguing from the words of Christ, asks, not without irony, “art thou not a king then?” or “in any case, thou art a king, art thou not?” cf. Winer’s Grammar, 512 (477). The difference between oukoun and oukoun is differently stated by different writers; cf. Herm. ad Vig., p. 792ff; Krüger, sec. 69, 51, 1 and 2; Kühner, sec. 508, 5 ii., p. 715ff, also the 3rd excurs. appended to his edition of Xenophon, memor.; (Bäumlein, Partikeln, pp. 191-198).*

oun a conjunction indicating that something follows from another necessarily; (others regard the primary force of the particle as confirmatory or continuative, rather than illative; cf. Passow, or Liddell and Scott, under 303 the word; Kühner, sec. 508, 1 ii., p. 707ff; Bäumlein, p. 173ff; Krüger, sec. 69, 52; Donaldson, p. 571; Rost in a program “Ueber Ableitung,” as above, p. 2; Klotz, p. 717; Hartung 2:4). Hence, it is used in drawing a conclusion and in connecting sentences together logically, “then, therefore, accordingly, consequently, these things being so” ((Klotz, Rost, others, have wished to derive the word from the neuter participle on (cf. ontwv); but see Bäumlein or Kühner, as above); cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 53, 8): Matthew 3:10; 10:32 (since persecutions are not to be dreaded, and consequently furnish no excuse for denying me (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 455 (424))); Matthew 18:4; Luke 3:9; 16:27; John 8:38 (kai uJmeiv oun, “and ye accordingly,” i.e. ‘since, as is plain from my case, sons follow the example of their fathers’; Jesus says this in sorrowful irony (Winer’s Grammar, 455 (424))); Acts 1:21 (since the office of the traitor Judas must be conferred on another); Romans 5:9; 6:4; 13:10; 1 Corinthians 4:16 (since I hold a father’s place among you); 2 Corinthians 5:20; James 4:17, and many other examples As respects details, notice that it stands

a. in exhortations (to show what ought now to be done by reason of what has been said), equivalent to “wherefore” (our transitional “therefore”): Matthew 3:8; 5:48; 9:38; Luke 11:35; 21:14,36 (R G L marginal reading Tr marginal reading); Acts 3:19; 13:40; Romans 6:12; 14:13; 1 Corinthians 16:11; 2 Corinthians 8:24; Ephesians 5:1; 6:14 Philippians 2:29; Colossians 2:16; 2 Timothy 1:8; Hebrews 4:1,11; 10:35; James 4:7; 5:7; 1 Peter 4:7; 5:6; Revelation 1:19 (G L T Tr WH); 3:3, 19, and often; nun oun, “now therefore,” Acts 16:36.

b. in questions, “then, therefore” (Latin igitur); [a]. when the question is, what follows or seems to follow from what has been said: Matthew 22:28; 27:22 (Winer’s Grammar, 455 (424)); Mark 15:12; Luke 3:10; 20:15,33; John 8:5; ti oun eroumen; Romans 6:1; 7:7; 9:14; ti oun fhmi; 1 Corinthians 10:19; ti oun; “what then?” i.e. how then does the matter stand? (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 64, 2 a.), John 1:21 (here WH marginal reading punct. ti oun su;) Romans 3:9; 6:15; 11:7; also ti oun estin; (“what is it then?”) Acts 21:22; 1 Corinthians 14:15,26. 304 [b]. when it is asked, whether this or that follows from what has just been said: Matthew 13:28; Luke 22:70; John 18:39; Romans 3:31; Galatians 3:21. [g]. when it is asked, how something which is true or regarded as true, or what someone does, can be reconciled with what has been previously said or done: Matthew 12:26; 13:27; 17:10 (where the thought is, ‘thou commandest us to tell no one about this vision we have had of Elijah; what relation then to this vision has the doctrine of the scribes concerning the coming of Elijah? Is not this doctrine confirmed by the vision?’); Matthew 19:7; 26:54; Luke 20:17; John 4:11 (Tdf. omits oun); Acts 15:10 (nun oun, “now therefore,” i.e. at this time, therefore, when God makes known his will so plainly); Acts 19:3; Romans 4:1 (where the meaning is, ‘If everything depends on faith, what shall we say that Abraham gained by outward things, i.e. by works?’ (but note the critical texts)); 1 Corinthians 6:15; Galatians 3:5. [d]. in general, it serves simply to subjoin questions suggested by what has just been said: Romans 3:27; 4:9f.; 6:21; 11:11; 1 Corinthians 3:5, etc.

c. in epanalepsis, i.e. it serves to resume a thought or narrative interrupted by intervening matter (Matthiae, 2, p. 1497; (Winer’s Grammar, 444 (414))), like Latin igitur, inquam, our “as was said, say I, to proceed,” etc.; Mark 3:31 (R G) (cf. Mark 3:21); Luke 3:7 (cf. Luke 3:3); John 4:45 (cf. John 4:43); 6:24 (cf. 22); 1 Corinthians 8:4; 11:20 (cf. John 11:18); add, Mark 16:19 (Tr marginal reading brackets oun); Acts 8:25; 12:5; 13:4; 15:3,30; 23:31; 25:1; 28:5. It is used also when one passes at length to a subject about which he had previously intimated an intention to speak: Acts 26:4,9.

d. it serves to gather up summarily what has already been said, or even what cannot be narrated at length: Matthew 1:17; 7:24 (where no reference is made to what has just before been said (?), but all the moral precepts of the Serm. on the Mount are summed up in a single rule common to all); Luke 3:18; John 20:30; Acts 26:22.

e. it serves to adapt examples and comparisons to the case in hand: John 3:29; 16:22; — or to add examples to illustrate the subject under consideration: Romans 12:20 Rec. 305

f. In historical discourse it serves to make the transition from one tiring to another, and to connect the several parts and portions of the narrative, since the new occurrences spring from or are occasioned by what precedes (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 60, 3): Luke 6:9 R G; numberless times so in John, as 1:22 (Lachmann omits); 2:18; 4:9 (Tdf. omits); 6:60,67; 7:6 (G T omit), 25,28,33,35,40; 8:13,19,22,25,31,57; 9:7f,10,16; 11:12,16,21,32,36; 12:1-4; 13:12; 16:17,22; 18:7,11f,16,27-29; 19:2024,32,38,40; 21:5-7, etc.

g. with other conjunction oun, “so then,” Latin hinc igitur, in Paul; see ara, 5. ei oun, “if then” (where what has just been said and proved is carried over to prove something else), see ei, III. 12; (ei men oun, see men, II. 4, p. 398{b}). eite oun ... eite, “whether then ... or”: 1 Corinthians 10:31; 15:11. epei oun, “since then”: Hebrews 2:14; 4:6; for which also a participle is put with oun, as Acts 2:30; 15:2 (T Tr WH de); 17:29; 19:36; 25:17; 26:22; Romans 5:1; 15:28; 2 Corinthians 3:12; 5:11; 7:1; Hebrews 4:14; 10:19; 1 Peter 4:1; 2 Peter 3:11 (WH Tr marginal reading oJutwv). ean oun, “if then ever, in case then,” or rather, “therefore if, therefore in case” (for in this formula, oun, although placed in the protasis, yet belongs more to the apodosis, since it shows what will necessarily follow from what precedes if the condition introduced by ean shall ever take place): Matthew 5:23 (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 455 (424)); 6:22 (here Tdf. omits oun); 24:26; Luke 4:7; John 6:62; 8:36; Romans 2:26; 1 Corinthians 14:11,23; 2 Timothy 2:21; ean oun mh, Revelation 3:3; so also oJtan oun, “when therefore”: Matthew 6:2; 21:40; 24:15, and R G in Luke 11:34. oJte oun, “when (or after) therefore, so when”: John 13:12,31 ((30) Rec.bez elz L T Tr WH); 19:30; 21:15; equivalent to “hence, it came to pass that, when” etc., John 2:22; 19:6,8. wJv oun, “when (or after) therefore”: John 4:1,40; 11:6; 18:6; 20:11; 21:9; wJv oun, “as therefore,” Colossians 2:6. wJsper oun, Matthew 13:40. men oun, followed by de (cf. Buttmann, sec. 149, 16), Mark 16:19 (Tr marginal reading brackets oun); John 19:25; Acts 1:6; 8:4,25; 1 Corinthians 9:25, etc.; without an adversative conjunc. following, see men, II. 4. nun oun, see above under a., and b. [g].

h. As to position, it is never the first word in the sentence, but generally the second, sometimes the third (sometimes even the fourth, Winer’s Grammar, sec. 61, 6); as (peri thv brwsewv oun etc. 1 Corinthians 306 8:4); oJi men oun, Acts 2:41, and often; polla men oun, John 20:30. John uses this particle in his Gospel far more frequently ((more than two hundred times in all)) than the other N.T. writers; in his Epistles only in the following passages: 1 John 2:24 (where G L T Tr WH have expunged it); 4:19 Lachmann; 3 John 1:8. ((From Homer down.))

oupw (from ou and the enclitic pw), adverb (fr. Homer down) (differing from mhpw, as ou does from mh (which see ad init:) “not yet”; a. in a negation: Matthew 24:6; Mark 13:7; John 2:4; 3:24; 6:17 L text T Tr WH; John 7:6, 8a R L WH txt, 8b, 30,39; 8:20,57; 11:30; 20:17; 1 Corinthians 3:2; Hebrews 2:8; 12:4; 1 John 3:2; Revelation 17:10,12 (where Lachmann ouk); oudeiv oupw, “no one ever yet” (see oudeiv, 2, and cf. ou, 3 a.), Mark 11:2 L T Tr WH; Luke 23:53 L Tr WH; Acts 8:16 Rec. b. in questions, nondumne? “do ye not yet” etc.: Matthew 15:17 R G; 16:9; Mark 4:40 L Tr WH; Mark 8:17 (21 L text T Tr WH).*
oura, ourav, hJ, “a tail”: Revelation 9:10,19; 12:4. (From Homer down. The Septuagint several times for bn;z;.)*

ouraniov, ouranion, in classical Greek generally of three term. (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 11, 1; Buttmann, 25 (23)) (ouranov), “heavenly,” i.e. a. “dwelling in heaven”: oJ pathr oJ ouraniov, Matthew 6:14,26,32; 15:13; besides L T Tr WH in 5:48; 18:35; 23:9; stratiav ouraniou Luke 2:13 (where Tr text WH marginal reading ouranou).

b. “coming from heaven”: ouraniw optasia, Acts 26:19. (Homer in Cer. 55; Pindar, Tragg., Aristophanes, others.)*
ouranoqen (ouranov), adverb, “from heaven”: Acts 14:17; 26:13. (Homer, Hesiod, the Orphica, 4 Macc. 4:10.) Cf. Lob. ad Phryn., p. 93f.*

ouranov, ouranou, oJ (from a root meaning ‘to cover,’ ‘encompass’; cf. Vanicek, p. 895; Curtius, sec. 509), “heaven”; and, in imitation of the Hebrew µyimæv; (i.e. properly, “the heights above, the upper regions”), ouranoi, ouranwn, oJi, “the heavens” (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 27, 3; Buttmann, 24 (21)) (on the use and the omission of the article cf. Winer’s Grammar, 121 (115)), i.e.:

1. “the vaulted expanse of the Sky with all the things visible in it”; 307

a. generally: as opposed to the earth, Hebrews 1:10; 2 Peter 3:5,10,12; oJ ouranov kai hJ gh (heaven and earth) equivalent to “the universe, the world” (according to the primitive Hebrew manner of speaking, inasmuch as they had neither the conception nor the name of “the universe,” Genesis 1:1; 14:19; Tobit 7:17 (18); 1 Macc. 2:37, etc.): Matthew 5:18; 11:25; 24:35; Mark 13:31; Luke 10:21; 16:17; 21:33; Acts 4:24; 14:15; 17:24; Revelation 10:6; 14:7; 20:11. The ancients conceived of the expanded sky as an arch or vault the outmost edge of which touched the extreme limits of the earth (see B. D. under the word Firmament, cf. Heaven); hence, such expressions as ap’ akrwn ouranwn eJwv akrwn autwn, Matthew 24:31; ap’ akrou ghv eJwv akrou ouranou, Mark 13:27; uJpo ton ouranon (tjæTæ µyimæV;hæ, Ecclesiastes 1:13; 2:3, etc.), “under heaven,” i.e. on earth, Acts 2:5; 4:12; Colossians 1:23; ek thv (namely, cwrav, cf. Winer’s Grammar, 591 (550); (Buttmann, 82 (71f))) uJp’ (here L T Tr WH uJpo ton ouranon) ouranon eiv thn uJp’ ouranon, “out of lite one part under the heaven unto the other part under heaven” i.e. from one quarter of the earth to the other, Luke 17:24; as by this form of expression the greatest longitudinal distance is described, so to one looking up from the earth heaven stands as the extreme measure of altitude hence, kollasqai acri tou ouranou, Revelation 18:5 (L T Tr WH) (on which see kollaw); uJywqhnai eJwv tou ouranou, metaphorically, of a city that has reached the acme, zenith, of glory and prosperity, Matthew 11:23; Luke 10:15 (kleov ouranon iJkei, Homer, Iliad 8, 192; Odyssey 19, 108; prov ouranon bibazein tina, Sophocles O. C. 382 (381); examples of similar expressions from other writings are given in Kypke, Observations, i., p. 62); kainoi ouranoi (kai gh kainh), better heavens which will take the place of the present after the renovation of all things, 2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1; oJi nun ouranoi, the heavens which now are, and which will one day be burnt up, 2 Peter 3:7; also oJ prwtov ouranov, Revelation 21:1, cf. Hebrews 12:26. But the heavens are also likened in poetic speech to an expanded curtain or canopy (<19A302>Psalm 103:2 (<19A402>Psalm 104:2); Isaiah 40:22), and to an unrolled scroll; hence, eJlissein (T Tr marginal reading allassein) touv ouranouv wJv peribolaion, Hebrews 1:12 (from the Septuagint of <19A102>Psalm 101:26 (<19A226>Psalm 102:26) manuscript Alexandrian LXX); kai oJ ouranov apecwrisqh wJv biblion eJlissomenon (or eJilissomenon), Revelation 6:14. 308

b. “the aerial heavens” or sky, the region where the clouds and tempests gather, and where thunder and lightning are produced: oJ ouranov purrazei, Matthew 16:2 (T brackets WH reject the passage); stugnazwn, Matthew 16:3 (see last reference); uJeton edwke, James 5:18; add Luke 9:54; 17:29; Acts 9:3; 22:6; Revelation 13:13; 16:21; 20:9; shmeion or apo tou ouranou, Matthew 16:1; Mark 8:11; Luke 11:16; 21:11; terata en tw ouranw Acts 2:19; kleiein ton ouranon, to keep the rain in the sky, hinder it from falling on the earth, Luke 4:25; Revelation 11:6, (sunecein ton ouranou for rxæ[; µyimæV;hæ, Deuteronomy 11:17; 2 Chronicles 6:26; 7:13; anecein ton ouranon, Sir. 48:3); aJi nefelai tou ouranou, Matthew 24:30; 26:64; Mark 14:62; to proswpon tou ouranou, Matthew 16:3 (T brackets WH reject the passage); Luke 12:56; ta peteina tou ouranou (genitive of place), that fly in the air (Genesis 1:26; Psalm 8:9; Baruch 3:17; Judith 11:7), Matthew 6:26; 8:20; 13:32; Mark 4:32; Luke 8:5; 9:58; 13:19; Acts 10:12. These heavens are opened by being cleft asunder, and from the upper heavens, or abode of heavenly beings, come down upon earth — now the Holy Spirit, Matthew 3:16; Mark 1:10; Luke 3:21f; John 1:32; now angels, John 1:51 (52); and now in vision appear to human sight some of the things within the highest heaven, Acts 7:55; 10:11,16; through the aerial heavens sound voices, which are uttered in the heavenly abode: Matthew 3:17; Mark 1:11; Luke 3:22; John 12:28; 2 Peter 1:18.

c. “the sidereal or starry heavens”: ta astra tou ouranou Hebrews 11:12 (Deuteronomy 1:10; 10:22; Euripides, Phoen. 1); oJi asterev ... tou ouranou, Mark 13:25; Revelation 6:13; 12:4 (Isaiah 13:10; 14:13); aJi dunameiv twn ouranwn, “the heavenly forces” (hosts), i.e. “the stars” (others take dunameiv in this phrase in a general sense (see dunamiv, f.) of the powers which uphold and regulate the heavens): Matthew 24:29; Luke 21:26; aJi en toiv ouranoiv, Mark 13:25 (Hebrew µyimæV;hæ ab;x], Deuteronomy 17:3; Jeremiah 33:22; Zephaniah 1:5); so hJ stratia tou ouranou, Acts 7:42.

2. “the region above the sidereal heavens, the seat of an order of things eternal and consummately perfect, where God dwells and the other heavenly beings”: this heaven Paul, in 2 Corinthians 12:2, seems to designate by the name of oJ tritov ouranov, but certainly not the third of 309 the seven distinct heavens described by the author of the Test xii. Patr., Levi sec. 3, and by the rabbis ((cf. Wetstein at the passage; Hahn, Theol. d. N.T. 1:247f; Drummond, Jewish Messiah, chapter xv.)); cf. DeWette at the passage Several distinct heavens are spoken of also in Ephesians 4:10 (uJperanw pantwn twn ouranwn); cf. Hebrews 7:26, if it be not preferable here to understand the numerous regions or parts of the one and the same heaven where God dwells as referred to. The highest heaven is “the dwelling-place of God”: Matthew 5:34; 23:22; Acts 7:49; Revelation 4:1ff (Psalm 10:4 (Psalm 11:4); 113:24 (<19B516>Psalm 115:16f)); hence, Qeov tou ouranou, Revelation 11:13; 16:11 (Genesis 24:3); oJ en (toiv) ouranov, Matthew 5:16,45; 6:1,9; 7:21; 10:33; 7:50; 16:17; 18:10 (here L WH marginal reading en tw ouranw in brackets), 14, 19; Mark 11:25f, etc. From this heaven the pneuma aJgion is sent down, 1 Peter 1:12 and the passages already cited (cf. 1 b. under the end); and Christ is said to have come, John 3:18,31; 6:38,41f; 1 Corinthians 15:47; it is the abode of the angels, Matthew 24:36; 22:30; 18:10; 28:2; Mark 12:25; 13:32; Luke 2:15; 22:43 (L brackets WH reject the passage); Galatians 1:8; 1 Corinthians 8:5; Ephesians 3:15; Hebrews 12:22; Revelation 10:1; 12:7; 18:1; 19:14 (Genesis 21:17; 22:11); ta en toiv ouranoiv kai ta epi thv ghv, the things and beings in the heavens (i.e. angels) and on the earth, Ephesians 1:10; Colossians 1:16, 20; ginetai to qelhma tou Qeou en ouranw, i.e. by the inhabitants of heaven, Matthew 6:10; cara estai en tw ouranw, God and the angels will rejoice, Luke 15:7. this heaven is the abode to which Christ ascended after his resurrection, Mk, 16:19; Luke 24:51 (T omits; WH reject the clause); Acts 1:10f; 2:34; 3:21; Romans 10:6; (Ephesians 1:20 Lachmann text); 1 Peter 3:22; Hebrews 1:4 (en uJyhloiv); 8:1; 9:24; Revelation 4:2, and from which he will hereafter return, 1 Thessalonians 1:10; 4:16; 2 Thessalonians 1:7; into heaven have already been received the souls (pneumata) both of the O.T. saints and of departed Christians, Hebrews 12:23 (see apografw, b. at the end), and heaven is appointed as the future abode of those who, raised from the dead and clothed with superior bodies, shall become partakers of the heavenly kingdom, 2 Corinthians 5:1, and enjoy the reward of proved virtue, Matthew 5:12; Luke 6:23; hence, eternal blessings are called qhsaurov en ouranw, Matthew 6:20; Luke 12:33, and those on whom God has conferred eternal salvation are said ecein qhsauron en ouranw (ouranoiv), Matthew 19:21; Mark 10:21; Luke 18:22, 310 cf. Hebrews 10:34 (R G); or the salvation awaiting them is said “to be laid up for them in heaven,” Colossians 1:5; 1 Peter 1:4; or their names are said to have been written in heaven, Luke 10:20; moreover, Christ, appointed by God the leader and lord of the citizens of the divine kingdom, is said to have all power in heaven and on earth, Matthew 28:18; finally, the seer of the Apocalypse expects a new Jerusalem to come down out of heaven as the metropolis of the perfectly established Messianic kingdom, Revelation 3:12; 21:2,10. By metonymy, oJ ouranov is put for the inhabitants of heaven: eufrainou ourane, Revelation 18:20, cf. Revelation 12:12 (Psalm 95:11 (Psalm 46:11); Isaiah 44:23; Job 15:15); in particular for “God” (Daniel 4:23, and often by the rabbis, influenced by an over-scrupulous reverence for the names of God himself; cf. Schürer in the Jahrbb. f. protest. Theol., 1876, p. 178f; (Keil, as below)): aJmartanein eiv ton ouranon, Luke 15:18, 21; ek tou ouranou, equivalent to by God, John 3:27; ex ouranou, of divine authority, Matthew 21:25; Mark 11:30; Luke 20:4; enantion tou ouranou, 1 Macc. 3:18 (where the tou Qeou before tou ouranou seems questionable); ek tou ouranou hJ iscuv, 1 Macc. 3:19; hJ ex ouranou bohqeia, 12:15; 16:3, cf. 3:5053,59; 4:10,24,30,40,55; 5:31; 7:37,41; 9:46; cf. Keil, Comm. üb. d. Büch.

d. Macc., p. 20. On the phrase hJ basileia twn ouranwn and its meaning, see basileia, 3; (Cremer, under the word basileia; Edersheim 1:265).

Ourbanov, Ourbanou, oJ (a Latin name; cf. Lightfoot on Philip.,

p. 174), “Urbanus,” a certain Christian: Romans 16:9.*
Ouriav, Ouriou (Buttmann, 17f (16) no. 8), oJ (hY;riWa light of Jehovah (or, my light is Jehovah)), “Uriah,” the husband of Bathsheba the mother of Solomon by David: Matthew 1:6.*

ouv, genitive wtov, plural wta, dative wsin, to (cf. Latin auris, ausculto, audio, etc.; akin to aiw, aisqanomai; cf. Curtius, sec. 619; Vanicek, p. 67); from Homer down; Hebrew ˆz,ao; “the ear”;

1. properly: Matthew 13:16; Mark 7:33; Luke 22:50; 1 Corinthians 2:9; 12:16; wta tinov eiv dhesin, to hear supplication, 1 Peter 3:12; hJ grafh plhroutai en toiv wsi tinov, while present and hearing, Luke 4:21 (Baruch 1:3f); those unwilling to hear a thing are said sunecein (which see 2 a.) ta wta, “to stop their ears,” Acts 7:57; 311 hkousqh ti eiv ta wta tinov, something was heard by, came to the knowledge of (A.V. “came to the ears of”) one, Acts 11:22; likewise eisercesqai, James 5:4; ginesqai, to come unto the ears of one, Luke 1:44; akouein eiv to ouv, to hear (A.V. “in the ear” i.e.) in familiar converse, privately, Matthew 10:27 (eiv ouv often so in classical Greek; cf. Passow (Liddell and Scott), under the word, 1); also prov to ouv lalein, Luke 12:3.

2. metaphorically equivalent to: “the faculty of perceiving with the mind, the faculty of understanding and knowing”: Matthew 13:16; oJ ecwn (or ei tiv ecei) wta (or ouv, in Rev.) (sometimes (especially in Mark and Luke) with akouein added; cf. Buttmann, sec. 140, 3) akouetw, whoever has the faculty of attending and understanding, let him use it, Matthew 11:15; 13:9,43; Mark 4:9,23; 7:16 (T WH omit; Tr brackets the verse); Luke 8:8; 14:35 (34); Revelation 2:7,11,17,29; 3:6,13,22; 13:9; toiv wsi barewv akouein, to be slow to understand or obey (A.V. “their ears are dull of hearing”), Matthew 13:15; Acts 28:27 (from Isaiah 6:10); wta econtev ouk akouete, Mark 8:18; wta tou mh akouein, (“ears that they should not hear”; cf. Buttmann, 267 (230)), Romans 11:8; qesqe touv logouv toutouv eiv ta wta (A.V. “let these words sink into your ears” i.e.) take them into your memory and hold them there, Luke 9:44; aperitmhtov toiv wsin (see aperitmhtov), Acts 7:51.*

ousia, ousiav, hJ (from wn, ousa, on, the participle of eimi), “what one has,” i.e. “property, possessions, estate” (A.V. “substance”): Luke 15:12f. (Tobit 14:13; Herodotus 1, 92; Xenophon, Plato, Attic orators, others.)*

oute (ou and te), an adjunctive negative conjunction (from Homer down) (differing fr., mhte as ou does from mh (which see ad at the beginning), and from oude as mhte does from mhde; see mhte and oude), “neither; and not”.

1. Examples in which oute stands singly:

a. ou ... oute, Revelation 12:8 Rec. (where G L T Tr WH oude); Revelation 20:4 R G (where L T Tr WH oude); oudeiv axiov eJureqh anoixai to biblion oute blepein auto, Revelation 5:4; cf. Winer’s Grammar, 491 (457); Buttmann, 367 (315); ou ... oude ... oute, 1 312 Thessalonians 2:3 R G (where L T Tr WH more correctly oude) (Winer’s Grammar, 493 (459); Buttmann, 368 (315)); oude ... oute (so that oute answers only to the ou in oude), Galatians 1:12 R G T WH text (Winer’s Grammar, 492 (458); Buttmann, 366 (314)).

b. oute ... kai, like Latin neque ... et, “neither ... and”: John 4:11; 3 John 1:10 (Euripides, Iph. T. 591; but the more common Greek usage was ou ... te, cf. Klotz ad Devar. 2:2, p. 714; Passow, under the word, B. 2; (Liddell and Scott, under the word, II. 4); Winer’s Grammar, sec. 55, 7; (Buttmann, sec. 149, 13 c.)).

c. By a solecism oute is put for oude, “not ... even”: 1 Corinthians 3:2 Rec. (where G L T Tr WH oude) (Winer’s Grammar, 493 (459); Buttmann, 367 (315); sec. 149, 13 f.); Mark 5:3 R G (where L T Tr WH have restored oude (Winer’s Grammar, 490 (456); Buttmann, as above)); Luke 12:26 R G (where L T Tr WH oude (Winer’s Grammar, as above and 478 (445); Buttmann, 347 (298))); oute metenohsan, Revelation 9:20 R L Tr (where G WH text ou, T oude “not ... even”; WH marginal reading oute or oude (cf. Buttmann, 367 (315))); after the question mh dunatai ... suka; follows oute aJlukon gluku poihsai uJdwr, James 3:12 G L T Tr WH (as though oute dunatai ... suka had previously been in the writer’s mind (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 493 (459); Buttmann, as above)).

2. used twice or more, “neither ... nor” (Latin nec ... nec; neque ... neque): Matthew 6:20; 22:30; Mark 12:25; (Mark 14:68 L text T Tr WH); Luke 14:35 (34); John 4:21; 5:37; 8:19; 9:3; Acts 15:10; 19:37; 25:8; 28:21; Romans 8:38f (where oute occurs ten times); 1 Corinthians 3:7; 6:9f; (oute eight times (yet T WH Tr marginal reading the eighth time ou)); 11:11; Galatians 5:6; 6:15; 1 Thessalonians 2:6; Revelation 3:15f; 9:20; 21:4; oute ... oute ... oude (German auch nicht, “also not”), L Tr WH in Luke 20:35f, and L T Tr marginal reading WH in Acts 24:12f; cf. Winer’s Grammar, 491 (457f); Buttmann, 368 (315) note.

oJutov, aJuth, touto, demonstrative pronoun (cf. Curtius, p. 543), Hebrew hz,, tazo, “this”; used:

I. absolutely. 313

1. a. “this one,” visibly present here: Matthew 3:17; 17:5; Mark 9:7; Luke 7:44f; 9:35; 2 Peter 1:17. Matthew 9:3; 21:38; Mark 14:69; Luke 2:34; 23:2; John 1:15,30; 7:25; 9:8f,19; 18:21,30; 21:21; Acts 2:15; 4:10; 9:21; according to the nature and character of the person or thing mentioned, it is used with a suggestion — either of contempt, as Matthew 13:55f; Mark 6:2f; Luke 5:21; 7:39,49; John 6:42,52; 7:15; or of admiration, Matthew 21:11; Acts 9:21; cf. Wahl, Clavis apocryphoR.V. T., p. 370.

b. it refers to a subject immediately preceding, “the one just named”: Luke 1:32; 2:37 (R G L); John 1:2; 6:71; 2 Timothy 3:6,8, etc.; at the beginning of a narrative about one already mentioned, Matthew 3:3; Luke 16:1; John 1:41 (42); 3:2; 12:21; 21:21; Acts 7:19; 21:24. “this one” just mentioned “and no other”: John 9:9; Acts 4:10 (en toutw); 9:20; 1 John 5:6; “such as I have just described,” 2 Timothy 3:5; 2 Peter 2:17. kai oJutov, “this one” just mentioned “also,” i.e. as well as the rest, Luke 20:30 R G L; Hebrews 8:3. kai touton, “and him too, and him indeed,” 1 Corinthians 2:2.

c. it refers to the leading subject of a sentence although in position more remote (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 23, 1; (Buttmann, sec. 127, 3)): Acts 4:11; 7:19; 8:26 (on which see Gaza under the end); 1 John 5:20 (where oJutov is referred by (many) orthodox interpreters incorrectly ((see Alford at the passage; Winer’s Grammar, and Buttmann’s Grammar, the passages cited)) to the immediately preceding subject, “Christ”); 2 John 1:7.

d. it refers to what follows; oJutov, aJuth esti, “in this appears ... that” etc.; “on this depends ... that” etc.: followed by oJti, as aJuth estin hJ epaggelia, oJti, 1 John 1:5; add, 5:11,14; — by iJna, John 15:12; 1 John 3:11,23; 5:3; 2 John 1:6; touto esti to ergon, to qelhma tou Qeou, iJna, John 6:29,39f.

e. it serves to repeat the subject with emphasis: ou pantev oJi ex Israhl, oJutoi Israhl, Romans 9:6; add, Romans 98; 2:14 (L marginal reading oJi toioutoi); Romans 7:10; Galatians 3:7; it refers, not without special force, to a description given by a participle or by the relative oJv, oJstiv; which description either follows, as Mark 4:16,18; Luke 8:15,21; 9:9; John 11:37; followed by a relative sentence, John 1:15; 1 Peter 5:12; — or precedes: in the form of a participle, Matthew 314 10:22; 13:20,22f; 24:13; 26:23; Mark 12:40; Luke 9:48 (oJ ... uJparcwn, oJutov); John 6:46; 7:18; 15:5; 2 John 1:9; Acts 17:7; (and R G in Revelation 3:5); or of the relative oJv, Matthew 5:19; Mark 3:35; Luke 9:24,26; John 1:33 (here L marginal reading autov); 3:26; 5:38; Romans 8:30; 1 Corinthians 7:20; Hebrews 13:11; 1 John 2:5; 2 Peter 2:19; in the neuter, John 8:26; Romans 7:16; 1 Corinthians 7:24; Philippians 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:2; or of a preceding oJstiv, Matthew 18:4; in the neuter Philippians 3:7. oJsoi ... oJutoi, Romans 8:14; Galatians 6:12; also preceded by ei tiv, 1 Corinthians 3:17 (here Lachmann autov); 8:3; James 1:23; 3:2; by ean tiv, John 9:31; cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 23, 4.

f. with autov annexed, “this” man “himself,” Acts 25:25; plural “these themselves,” Acts 24:15,20; on the neuter see below, 2 a. b. etc.

g. As the relative and interrogative pronoun so also the demonstrative, when it is the subject, conforms in gender and number to the noun in the predicate: oJutoi eisin oJi uJioi thv basileiav, Matthew 13:38; add, Mark 4:15f,18; aJuth estin hJ megalh entolh, Matthew 22:38; oJutov estin oJ planov (German diese sind), 2 John 1:7.

2. The neuter touto

a. refers to what precedes: Luke 5:6; John 6:61; Acts 19:17; touto eipwn, and the like, Luke 24:40 (T omits; Tr brackets WH reject the verse); John 4:18; 8:6; 12:33; 18:38; dia touto, see dia, B.

II. 2 a.; eiv touto, see eiv, B. II. 3 c. [b].; auto touto, “for this very cause,” 2 Peter 1:5 (Lachmann autoi); cf. Matthiae, sec. 470, 7; Passow, under the word, C. 1 a. at the end (Liddell and Scott, under the word, C. IX. 1 at the end; Winer’s Grammar, sec. 21, 3 note 2; Kühner, sec. 410 Anm. 6); meta touto, see meta, II. 2 b. ek toutou, “for this reason” (see ek, II. 8), John 6:66; 19:12; “from this,” i.e. “hereby, by this” note, 1 John 4:6 (cf. Westcott at the passage). en toutw, for this cause, John 16:30; Acts 24:16; “hereby, by this” token, 1 John 3:19. epi toutw, “in the meanwhile,” while this was going on (but see epi, B. 2 e., at the end, p. 234a), John 4:27. toutou carin, Ephesians 3:14. plural tauta, John 7:4 (“these” so great, so wonderful, “things”); meta tauta, see meta, II. 2 b. kata tauta, “in this” same “manner,” Rec. in Luke 6:23, and 17:30 (others, ta auta or 315 tauta). it refers to the substance of the preceding discourse: Luke 8:8; 11:27; 24:26; John 5:34; 15:11; 21:24, and very often. kaqwv ... tauta, John 8:28.

b. it prepares the reader or hearer and renders him attentive to what follows, which tires gets special weight (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 23, 5): 1 John 4:2; auto touto oJti, Philippians 1:6; touto legw followed by direct discourse, Galatians 3:17 (see legw, II. 2 d.). it is prefixed to sentences introduced by the particles oJti, iJna, etc.: touto legw or fhmi followed by oJti, 1 Corinthians 1:12 ((see legw as above); 1 Corinthians 7:29); 15:50; ginwskeiv touto followed by oJti, Romans 6:6; 2 Timothy 3:1; 2 Peter 1:20; 3:3; logizesqai touto oJti, Romans 2:3; after oJmologein, Acts 24:14; after eidwv, 1 Timothy 1:9; en toutw oJti, 1 John 3:16,24; 4:9f; touto, iJna, Luke 1:43; eiv touto, iJna, Acts 9:21; Romans 14:9; 2 Corinthians 2:9; 1 Peter 3:9; 4:6; 1 John 3:8; dia touto, iJna, 2 Corinthians 13:10; 1 Timothy 1:16; Philemon 1:15; toutwn (on this neuter plural referring to a single object see Winer’s Grammar, 162 (153); (cf. Riddell, Platonic Idioms, sec. 41)), iJna, 3 John 4; en toutw, ean, 1 John 2:3; oJtan, 1 John 5:2; touto auto, iJna, “on this very account, that” (see a. above (but others take it here as the accusative of object; see Meyer at the passage (for instances of auto touto see Buttmann, sec. 127, 12))), 2 Corinthians 2:3; eiv auto touto, iJna, Ephesians 6:22; Colossians 4:8; oJpwv, Romans 9:17. In the same manner touto is put before an infinitive with to for the sake of emphasis (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 23, 5; Buttmann, sec. 140, 7, 9, etc.): 2 Corinthians 2:1; before a simple infinitive, 1 Corinthians 7:37 (here R G prefix tou to the infinitive); before an accusative and infinitive Ephesians 4:17; before nouns, as touto eucomai, thn uJmwn katartisin, 2 Corinthians 13:9, cf. 1 John 3:24; 5:4.

c. kai touto, “and this, and that too, and indeed, especially”: Romans 13:11; 1 Corinthians 6:6, L T Tr WH also in 8; Ephesians 2:8; kai tauta, “and that too,” 1 Corinthians 6:8 Rec.; Hebrews 11:12; (so kai tauta also in classical Greek; cf. Devar. edition Klotz i., p. 108; Viger. edition Herm., p. 176f; Matthiae, sec. 470, 6).

d. tauta, “of this sort, such,” spoken contemptuously of men, 1 Corinthians 6:11 (cf. Sophocles O. R 1329; Thucydides 6, 77; Livy 30, 30; cf. Bernhardy (1829), p. 281; (Winer’s Grammar, 162 (153))). 316

e. touto men ... touto de, “partly ... partly,” Hebrews 10:33 (for examples from Greek anth. see Winer’s Grammar, 142 (135); Matthiae, ii., sec. 288 Anm. 2; (Kühner, sec. 527 Anm. 2)). f. tout’ estin, see eimi, II. 3, p. 176{b}.

II. Joined to nouns it is used like an adjective;

a. so that the article stands between the demonstrative and the noun, oJutov oJ, aJuth hJ, touto to (cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 23 at the end; Buttmann, sec. 127, 29): Matthew 12:32; 16:18; 17:21 (T WH omits; Tr brackets the verse); 20:12; 26:29; Mark 9:29; Luke 7:44; 10:36; 14:30; 15:24; John 4:15; 7:46 (L WH omit; Tr brackets the clause); 8:20; 10:6; 11:47; 12:5; Acts 1:11; Romans 11:24; 1 Timothy 1:18; Hebrews 7:1; 8:10; (1 John 4:21); Revelation 19:9; 20:14; 21:5; 22:6. etc.; touto to paidion, “such” a little child “as” ye see here, Luke 9:48; cf. Bornemann at the passage (who takes touto thus as representing the class, ‘this and the like;’ but cf. Meyer (edited by Weiss) at the passage).

b. so that the noun stands between the article and the demonstrative (cf. Winer’s Grammar, 548 (510)); as, oJi liqoi oJutoi, the stones which ye see lying near, Matthew 3:9; 4:3; add, Matthew 5:19; 7:24 (L Tr WH brackets toutouv),26,28; 9:26 (Tr marginal reading WH marginal reading authv); Matthew 10:23, etc.; Mark 12:16; 13:30; Luke 11:31; 23:47; John 4:13,21; 7:49; 11:9; 18:29; Acts 6:13; 19:26; Romans 15:28; 1 Corinthians 1:20; 2:6; 11:26; 2 Corinthians 4:1,7; 8:6; 11:10; 12:13; Ephesians 3:8; 5:32; 2 Timothy 2:19; Revelation 2:24, and very often — (which construction is far more frequent with Paul than the other (see Winer’s Grammar, as above)); it is added to a noun which has another adjective, hJ chra hJ ptwch aJuth, Luke 21:3; panta ta rhmata tauta, Luke 2:19, 51 ((T WH L marginal reading omit; L text Tr marginal reading brackets tauta); apo thv geneav thv skoliav tauthv, Acts 2:40).

c. Passages in which the reading varies between oJutov oJ and oJ ... oJutov: viz. oJutov oJ, Mark 14:30 L text T Tr WH; John 4:20 R L marginal reading; John 6:60 R G; John 7:36 RG; John 9:24 L WH Tr marginal reading; John 21:23 L T Tr WH. oJ ... oJutov, Mark 14:30 R G L marginal reading; John 4:20 G L text T Tr WH; John 6:60 L 317 T Tr WH; John vii 36 L T Tr WH; John 9:24 G T Tr text; John 21:23 R G; etc.

d. with anarthrous nouns, especially numerical specifications (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 37, 5 N. 1): triton touto, “this third time,” 2 Corinthians 13:1; touto triton, John 21:14 (Judges 16:15; deuteron touto, Genesis 27:36; touto dekaton, Numbers 14:22; tetarton touto, Herodotus 5, 76). (The passages which follow, although introduced here by Prof. Grimm, are (with the exception of Acts 1:5) clearly instances of the predicative use of oJutov; cf. Winer’s Grammar, 110 (105) note; Buttmann, sec. 127, 31; Rost sec. 98, 3 A. c. [a]. following): touto palin deuteron shmeion epoihsen, John 4:54; trithn tauthn hJmeran agei, this is the third day that Israel is passing (but see agw, 3), Luke 24:21 (keimai triakosthn tauthn hJmeran, this is now the thirtieth day that I lie (unburied), Lucian, dial. mort. 13, 3); ou meta pollav tautav hJmerav (see meta, II. 2 b. (Winer’s Grammar, 161 (152); Buttmann, sec. 127, 4)), Acts 1:5; oJutov mhn eJktov estin auth, this is the sixth month with her etc. Luke 1:36; aJuth apografh prwth egeneto, Luke 2:2 L (T) Tr WH; tauthn epoihsen archn twn shmeiwn, John 2:11 L T Tr WH.

oJutw and oJutwv (formerly in printed editions oJutw appeared before a consonant, oJutwv before a vowel; but (recent critical editors, following the best manuscripts (“Codex Sinaiticus has oJutw but fourteen times in the N.T.” Scrivener, Collation etc., p. liv.; cf. his Introduction etc.,

p. 561), have restored oJutwv; viz. Treg. uniformly, 205 times; Tdf. 203 times, 4 times oJutw; Lachmann 196 times, 7 times oJutw (all before a consonant); WH 196 tilnes, 10 times oJutw (all before a consonant); cf. Tdf. Proleg., p. 97; WH’s Appendix, p. 146f); cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 5, 1 b.; B. 9; (Lob. Pathol. Elementa ii. 218ff); cf. Krüger, sec. 11, 12, 1; Kühner, sec. 72, 3 a.), adverb (from oJutov) (fr. Homer down), the Septuagint for ˆKe, “in this manner, thus, so”:

1. by virtue of its native demonstrative force it refers to what precedes; “in the manner spoken of; in the way described; in the way it was done; in this manner; in such a manner; thus, so”: Matthew 6:30; 11:26; 17:12; 19:8; Mark 14:59; Luke 1:25; 2:48; 12:28; Romans 11:5; 1 Corinthians 8:12; 15:11; Hebrews 6:9; (2 Peter 3:11 WH Tr marginal reading); ouc oJutwv estai (L Tr WH estin (so also T in 318 Mark)) en uJmin, it will not be so among you (I hope), Matthew 20:26; Mark 10:43; uJmeiv ouc oJutwv namely, esesqe, Luke 22:26; ean afwmen auton oJutwv namely, poiounta, thus as he has done hitherto (see afihmi, 2 b.), John 11:48; it refers to similitudes and comparisons, and serves to adapt them to the case in hand, Matthew 5:16 (“even so,” i.e. as the lamp on the lampstand); Matthew 12:45; 13:49; 18:14; 20:16; Luke 12:21 (WH brackets the verse); 15:7,10; John 3:8; 1 Corinthians 9:24; likewise oJutwv kai, Matthew 17:12; 18:35; 24:33; Mark 13:20; Luke 17:10. oJutwv ecein, “to be so” (Latin sic or ita se habere): Acts 7:1; 12:15; 17:11; 24:9. it serves to resume participles (Josephus, Antiquities 8, 11, 1; b. j. 2, 8, 5; see examples from Greek authors in Passow, under the word, 1 h.; (Liddell and Scott, v. I. 7)): Acts 20:11; 27:17; but John 4:6 must not (with Winer’s Grammar, sec. 65, 9 at the end; Buttmann, sec. 144, 21) be referred to this head, see Meyer (and 5 d. below); on Revelation 3:5, see 5 c. below. It takes the place of an explanatory participial clause, equivalent to “matters being thus arranged, under these circumstances, in such a condition of things” (Buttmann, sec. 149, 1; cf. Winer’s Grammar, sec. 60, 5): Romans 5:12 (this connection between sin and death being established (but this explanation of the oJutwv appears to be too general (cf. Meyer ad loc.))); Hebrews 6:15 (i.e. since God had pledged the promise by an oath); equivalent to “things having been thus settled, this having been done, then”: Matthew 11:26; Acts 7:8; 28:14; 1 Corinthians 14:25; 1 Thessalonians 4:17; 2 Peter 1:11; cf. Fritzsche, Commentary to Romans, i., p. 298. Closely related to this use is that of of oJutwv (like Latin ita for itaque, igitur) in the sense of “consequently” (cf. English “so” at the beginning of a sentence): Matthew 7:17; Romans 1:15; 6:11; Revelation 3:16 ((cf. Fritzsche on Matthew, p. 220); Passow, under the word, 2; (Liddell and Scott, under the word, II.)).

2. it prepares the way for what follows: Matthew 6:9; Luke 19:31; John 21:1; oJutwv hn, was arranged thus, was on this wise (Winer’s Grammar, 465 (434); Buttmann, sec. 129, 11), Matthew 1:18; oJutwv esti to qelhma tou Qeou followed by an infinitive, “so is the will of God, that,” 1 Peter 2:15. before language quoted from the O.T.: Matthew 2:5; Acts 7:6; 13:34,47; 1 Corinthians 15:45; Hebrews 4:4.

3. with adjectives, “so” (Latin tam, marking degree of intensity): Hebrews 12:21; Revelation 16:18; postpositive, ti deiloi este 319 oJutwv; Mark 4:40 (L Tr WH omit); in the same sense with adverbs, Galatians 1:6; or with verbs, “so greatly,” 1 John 4:11; oJutwv ... wJste, John 3:16. oudepote efanh oJutwv, it was never seen in such fashion, i.e. such an extraordinary sight, Matthew 9:33 (efanh must be taken impersonally; cf. Bleek, Synoptative Erklär. i. p. 406 (or Meyer at the passage)); oudepote oJutwv eidomen, we never saw it so, i.e. with such astonishment, Mark 2:12.

4. oJutwv or oJutwv kai in comparison stands antithetic to an adverb or a relative pronoun (Winer’s Grammar, sec. 53, 5; cf. Buttmann, 362 (311) c.): kaqaper ... oJutwv, Romans 12:4f; 1 Corinthians 12:12; 2 Corinthians 8:11; kaqwv ... oJutwv, Luke 11:30; 17:26; John 3:14; 12:50; 14:31; 15:4; 2 Corinthians 1:5; 10:7; 1 Thessalonians 2:4; Hebrews 5:3; oJutwv ... kaqwv, Luke 24:24; Romans 11:26; Philippians 3:17; wJv ... oJutwv, Acts 8:32; 23:11; Romans 5:15,18; 1 Corinthians 7:17; 2 Corinthians 7:14; 1 Thessalonians 2:8; 5:2; oJutwv ... wJv, Mark 4:26; John 7:46 (L WH omit; Tr brackets the clause); 1 Corinthians 3:15; 4:1; 9:26; Ephesians 5:28; James 2:12; oJutwv wJv ... mh wJv, 2 Corinthians 9:5 (G L T Tr WH); wJsper ... oJutwv, Matthew 12:40; 13:40; 24:27,37,39; Luke 17:24; John 5:21,26; Romans 5:12,19,21; 6:4; 11:31; 1 Corinthians 11:12; 15:22; 16:1; 2 Corinthians 1:7 R G; Galatians 4:29; Ephesians 5:24 R G; after kaq’ oJson, Hebrews 9:27f; oJutwv ... oJn tropon, Acts 1:11; 27:25; oJn tropon ... oJutwv, 2 Timothy 3:8 (Isaiah 52:14); kata thn oJdon hJn legousin aJiresin oJutw k.t.l., “after the Way” (i.e. as it requires (cf. oJdov, 2 a. at the end)) “so” etc. Acts 24:14.
